Footnote 957 Mr. Colvin was part of the team that conducted the June 5 & 6, 2007 site visit to the Kabul detention facility, during which three of the four detainees interviewed said they had been whipped with cables, shocked with electricity and/or otherwise “ hurt ” while in NDS custody in Kandahar. Footnote 958 This report has already been described in detail. Mr. Colvin found the accounts of abuse to be “ highly credible ”. Footnote 959 He was not, however, responsible for the distribution of this report, once created. For the purposes of this complaint, i.e. , in terms of MP access to DFAIT information about post-transfer treatment of detainees, Mr. Colvin had no further, significant involvement with the detainee question during the remainder of his time in Afghanistan. 12.3.6 ROTO s 4 & 5 – DFAIT in Afghanistan The Commission heard from three DFAIT witnesses who had information to provide about post-transfer treatment of detainees in Afghanistan during ROTO s 4 & 5, that is, from August 2007 onwards. They were Eelco (Ed) Jager, the policy advisor to MGen Laroche, John Davison, the political director for DFAIT at the PRT , and Nicholas Gosselin, a policy officer in the area of human rights and the individual chiefly responsible for conducting site visits commencing November 5, 2007. 12.3.6.1 Ed Jager, POLAD Mr. Jager arrived in Afghanistan in late July 2007, and spent ten months as General Laroche’s policy advisor ( POLAD ). He left the Afghanistan theatre in May 2008, on the same flight as General Laroche. Footnote 960 Mr. Jager described his role as the “ juncture between the general DFAIT structure and the military in Afghanistan. ” As policy advisor he was to “ help the General understand the political environment in which he was operating. ” Footnote 961 Located at TFHQ , he was a staff of one, but tied into the DFAIT hierarchy via the Head of Mission in Kabul and the Afghanistan department in Ottawa (bearing the acronym FTAG ). Footnote 962 Mr. Jager was stationed at KAF , had a close working relationship with the military personnel there, and had occasion to work with the military police. Mr. Jager was asked about the decision making committee for detainee transfers referred to by Generals Laroche and Juneau in their testimony, and whether he knew the TFPM to be on it. Mr. Jager did not view it as a committee, per se , and could not recall Maj Zybala ever being present at a meeting where detainees were discussed: I don’t remember there being a committee as such. I believe that there was a group of us that the General and the Deputy Commander consulted from time to time. Did that include the Task Force Provost Marshal, Major Zybala? I don’t have a specific memory of him being with us at any particular time. [...] I can remember seeing Major Zybala at various omnibus meetings. Specific meetings dealing with detainees at which he was present, I have no memory of. Footnote 963 Mr. Jager also could not remember if he ever advised the Task Force Commander on issues such as risk to detainees post transfer, although he admitted that it may have been a topic that was discussed that he simply did not recall. Footnote 964 Mr. Jager said he did not provide advice to the Task Force Commander on whether to transfer, and the associated risks. Footnote 965 Mr. Jager was responsible for reading the supplementary transfer arrangement agreement to detainees just prior to their transfer to the NDS , with the assistance of an interpreter. That was his first and last interaction with the detainees. He was not at all involved with the post-transfer monitoring process. Footnote 966 He described the physical transfer process – the portion that he viewed – as follows: [...] The transfer would take place within the confines of the transfer facility on Kandahar Air Field. That transfer facility was completely managed and run by the military police. Unless I happen to run into someone who identified himself as something else, I would have assumed that every single person I met was an MP at some level. Footnote 967 Mr. Jager’s evidence seemed to indicate the military police were present when he read the supplementary transfer arrangement out to the detainees: When you encountered a member of the NDS in the context of an anticipated transfer of a prisoner, that would happen at the transfer facility with MPs present? That is correct. Footnote 968 Elsewhere he said “ [t]o the best of his knowledge, yes, at all times there was always an MP at some level present, simply because I don’t think I would feel comfortable in the room with the detainees by myself. ” Footnote 969 The NDS was not present when he read the arrangement out to the detainees. Footnote 970 He recalled detainees occasionally professed their innocence upon learning of their transfer to the NDS , but he heard no complaints about what might happen to them after transfer in terms of mistreatment. Mr. Jager did not recall any complaints from detainees about their inability to pay their way out of NDS custody: “ No, no one ever expressed that to me or, if they did, it wasn’t translated that way to me. ” Mr. Jager also did not witness any physical resistance to transfer throughout all the transfers he did. Footnote 971 The POLAD was the gatekeeper of the site visit reports coming in over the DFAIT C4 network in KAF . Indeed, he received all the monitoring reports between July 20, 2007 and May 14, 2008. These were secret reports Mr. Jager provided to those on his distribution list, which included, to his recollection, Col Juneau, the Chief of Staff, Chief of Staff (National), the detainee officer and the legal advisor. To the best of his knowledge, the TFPM was not on that list. Footnote 972 Like other witnesses with access to the site visit reports, Mr. Jager was asked whether he would have provided the reports to the military police if asked. Mr. Jager’s answer was somewhat equivocal, although he agreed there was no prohibition on it per se : “ I mean, that never happened so I can’t imagine how I would have reacted at that time. Looking back at it three years ago, no one had ever told me not to give it to them. ” In his view, though, his client was the Task Force Commander, not the military at large or the MPs , so he would have provided information to the military police if the Task Force Commander had asked him to do so. Mr. Jager said there were a number of meetings that took place through that period, with various groups of people present. They were responsible for implementing it, but it was the General and his staff who made the decisions and they kept it – this was a very sensitive matter and they kept it on the basis of who needed to know. CFNIS Investigations On February 1, 2010 the Commission received a voluminous disclosure package of CFNIS investigations into Afghan detainee issues. Most of the investigations in this package related to incidents which pre-date the complaint in this inquiry, and largely relate to allegations of abuse of detainees by members of the CF rather than post-transfer abuse allegations. None of these investigations dealt with the legality of the commanders’ transfer orders. Footnote 1015 A review of these investigations is appropriate nonetheless as they were relied upon by both Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore and LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick in answer to the allegations in the complaint. Footnote 1016 In addition, the examinations of NIS witnesses (including LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick) concerning some of these investigations was instructive with respect to the issue of NIS methodologies, resources and prioritization of investigative files. For ease of reference, the investigations are referred to by their General Occurrence ( GO ) file numbers. 13.1 General Occurrences 13.1.1 GO 2007–2598 Footnote 1017 – Operation Camel Spider Operation Camel Spider was the NIS investigation into the facts underlying allegations brought to this Commission by Dr. Amir Attaran concerning the treatment of three injured detainees who passed through CF custody in Kandahar during ROTO 1. The Commission’s final report is an exhibit in this inquiry Footnote 1018 and the facts underlying that allegation are thoroughly canvassed in that report and elsewhere in this Report. Dr. Attaran contended MPs : (i) failed to investigate the cause of injuries to the three detainees; (ii) failed to treat humanely the three injured detainees while they were in MP custody; (iii) failed to exercise due diligence in safeguarding evidence by transferring the detainees prior to a forensic medical examination; and (iv) failed to seize and inventory the personal effects of at least one of the three detainees. Footnote 1019 The NIS investigation of CF treatment of these detainees was known as “ Operation Camel Spider ”. The Case Manager was RCMP Inspector George Gfellner, who had previously been seconded from the RCMP to the NIS and was assigned to this investigation, WO Steeve Chamberland was the lead NIS investigator. The NIS was ordered by the CFPM to investigate whether any of the three detainees suffered mistreatment or abuse while in CF custody, whether they were given proper medical care, and whether the military police ought to have investigated the cause of the detainees’ injuries. Footnote 1020 By all accounts, the investigation of these allegations was extensive and resource intensive. Inspector Gfellner went so far as to try to locate and interview the detainees themselves. Footnote 1021 None of the subject matter of 2007–2598 dealt with the legality of the orders to transfer detainees or the issue of post-transfer detainee abuse. In the course of this investigation other allegations concerning detainees began to arise, and the NIS did not have the resources to pursue those allegations while conducting the Camel Spider investigation. These other investigations were eventually compiled into Operation Centipede. Footnote 1022 13.1.2 GO 2008–6259 Footnote 1023 – Investigation into Allegations of Extended Detention This investigation was initiated after MPCC personnel alerted the NIS to the fact that during the period of time in late April and early May 2007 a detainee or detainees were held without transfer or release for considerably longer than the 96 hour time period prescribed in the governing TSO . Footnote 1024 This information was conveyed to the NIS in March, 2008 and the GO was initiated by the CFNIS Pacific Region branch on March 12, 2008 when they received the initial information from CFNIS HQ . The focus of this investigation was on the conduct of the MPs who were the custodians of the detainee(s) in question. The investigation included formal interviews of Sgt Utton and Capt Worsfold (the actual custodians) concerning the facts surrounding the extended detention, the conditions, and the efforts made to ensure humane treatment of the detainee(s). There was contact with the TFPM Maj Hudson and the CEFCOM PM Maj Laflamme concerning the circumstances, but this resulted in no relevant evidence. LCdr Siepka, who was legal adviser to MGen ( ret’d ) Grant when these detainees were held under his command, was consulted but offered only a reference to the governing TSO and the suggestion that MGen ( ret’d ) Grant be contacted. WO Chamberland and Inspector Gfellner were spoken to regarding detainee handling issues in general. Further discussions and interviews were held with the MPCC investigator who had initiated the matter. Sgt Utton testified before the Commission about the circumstances and said the detainee(s) were left in extremely hot conditions in a facility not designed at that time to hold a person for so long. Sgt Utton was obviously very concerned for the mental and physical well-being of the detainee(s). The MPs brought in a swamp cooler, and took numerous other steps to help assuage the heat which was apparently somewhere in the range of 140 degrees Fahrenheit. Footnote 1025 Nevertheless, the order remained in place that the detainee(s) could not be released. Sgt Utton and her commander Capt Worsfold both believed the transfers had ceased due to court proceedings in relation to the Amnesty complaint about mistreatment of the detainees by the CF . Although MGen ( ret’d ) Grant’s legal counsel suggested that MGen ( ret’d ) Grant or the CEFCOM J3 could clarify the issue whether the TSO was followed or not, MGen ( ret’d ) Grant does not appear to have been consulted by the NIS . The Commission is aware, from MGen ( ret’d ) Grant’s testimony, that transfers had been suspended due to concerns about allegations of post-transfer abuse and the monitoring provisions that were to take effect following the implementation of the May 3, 2007 transfer arrangement. It is noteworthy the NIS investigators recognized that to get to the root of the investigation “ it is essential to determine the time line regarding the passage of information between the KAF MP Chain of Command and the TFA Cdr , so that it can be precisely determined who made what decisions and when ”. Footnote 1026 Once it was determined the MP company had registered its concerns with the Chain of Command about holding the detainee(s), and the decision to neither transfer nor release the detainee(s) rested with the TFA Cdr , the investigation was concluded and the matter referred to CEFCOM : [...]It shall be noted that this matter was simply a concern brought forward to the CFNIS Chain of Command by the MPCC and that there was no specific allegation or complaint regarding the conduct of MP members. With respect to the fact that the TSO was not followed, it is suggested that the CEFCOM Comd review this issue. Through discussions with Inspector Gfellner and review of information to date, it seems clear that as there is no complaint specific to the MP role or complaint from the detainee or outside agencies; the situation is an issue revolving around the decision to suspend Detainee transfers and not requiring CFNIS investigation at this time. Investigation into this matter is concluded. Footnote 1027 13.1.3 GO 2008–3134 Footnote 1028 – ROTO 4 Human Dimensions Operations ( HDO ) Survey A confidential survey of CF personnel during ROTO 4 disclosed that a small number of CF personnel might have witnessed abuse of detainees and/or non-combatants by members of the CF . Footnote 1029 The Operational Chain of Command conducted an internal investigation when the results of this survey became known. The MP do not appear to have been notified until after the Operations Branch investigation. On February 1, 2008 the CFPM requested the NIS conduct an expedited investigation while potential witnesses were still in theatre and accessible. The CFPM pledged to provide necessary personnel, and asked the NIS to “ [a]dvise me if you encounter resistance that will result in delay ”. Footnote 1030 It is apparent a significant amount of effort and resources were expended on this investigation as the publicly available portion of the GO file disclosed to the Commission comprises three full binder volumes, about half of the disclosed NIS investigations. It should be stressed the incidence of reported abuse was very small – eight persons (1.2% of those polled) reported witnessing one instance of physical abuse of a detainee or non-combatant, and six persons (1% of those polled) reported witnessing this type of incident more than once There is nothing in the Commission’s record indicating whether there could be overlap in reporting, i.e. , more than one person reporting the same incident, such that the actual number of separate incidents could be even lower. Footnote 1031 It is clear that both the Chain of Command and CFPM took even this level of reported abuse seriously, as remedial measures were proposed by the former, and extensive investigations ordered by the CFPM . The investigation disclosed five particular allegations. It was concluded in March 2009 with two allegations being substantiated and pursued (both in relation to one CF member), one allegation being reviewed in theatre, and two found not to involve abuse against detainees or non-combatants. Footnote 1032 None of the allegations related to post-transfer abuse or legality of transfer orders. 13.1.4 GO 2008–6906 Footnote 1033 – Operation Centipede Operation Centipede was a GO generated on March 19, 2008: OP CENTIPEDE was created in order to investigate numerous incidents related to the alleged abuse of CF detainees in Afghanistan. All allegations were placed under one investigative umbrella in order to direct an order of priority based on the severity of the offences and to be able to seek out any possible event-to-event linkages. The mandate was a full time task force utilizing Major Case Management principles to determine if any CF personnel acted illegally or improperly regarding the handling or treatment of Afghan detainees that were in the custody of the CF . From this, eight different General Occurrence ( GO ) reports were created and investigators assigned accordingly. This particular GO was used as an administrative file in order to properly manage the files. Footnote 1034 The alleged abuse being investigated in Operation Centipede was said to have occurred at the hands of the Afghan authorities, not the CF . The investigation was limited to the issue whether any member of the CF was potentially implicated in any service or criminal offence in this context. Maj Bolduc was in charge of Operation Centipede and LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick was his Commanding Officer when the matter commenced. LCol Sansterre was the commanding officer at the conclusion of OP CENTIPEDE and signed off on the completion of the investigation. Footnote 1035 The allegations in question related to incidents from 2006 and reports in the Globe and Mail in March and April 2007, as well as an affidavit of Col Noonan dated May 1, 2007. All of the allegations pre-date the specific time period of this inquiry. Between March and June 2008 the investigators sought TSO s, MP policies, CF doctrine and technical directives, and guidance from CF legal counsel concerning the obligations of members of the CF when they become aware of allegations or witness post-transfer abuse of detainees by Afghan authorities. The relevant documentation was obtained from the investigators in Operation Camel Spider. There were claims of solicitor-client privilege and confidentiality made by legal counsel over the issue of legal guidance, and some exchanges between the CFPM and senior legal counsel to attempt to clarify that it was information being sought, not disclosure of legal advice which had been given. Ultimately, in one particular investigation, questions about the obligations of CF members witnessing abuse were answered by LCol Irwin. The GO ’s initiated within Operation Centipede were numbers 2008–6912 , 2008–6913 , 2008–6917 , 2008–6918 , 2008–6919 , 2008–6920 , 2008–6921 and 2008-23231. The order of priority was determined by first priority being whether the allegation involved an MP member, then whether Canadian soldiers had neglected their duties, then any other kind of allegation Footnote 1036 . A brief description of each investigation is warranted. 13.1.5 GO 2008–6912 Footnote 1037 – Investigation into Allegations of Possible Summary Execution, ROTO 1 This allegation pre-dated Operation Centipede as a distinct investigation, under GO 2007–7482 , but the substance of the investigation occurred between March and May 2008. Significant portions of the GO are redacted but the essence of the allegation can be discerned. An MP at the PRT MP company during ROTO 1 reportedly believed a prisoner who had been seen in the custody of the ANA or ANP was subsequently summarily executed. The particular MP came to this conclusion on the basis of hearing a rumour that human remains had been found in a ditch near the PRT and he felt it could be the same prisoner as he had seen earlier. The MP who reported this incident was suffering from Post Traumatic Stress Disorder ( PTSD ) and had difficulty speaking with NIS investigators. The existence of the human remains was not confirmed, much less the identity of them, and it was confirmed that the prisoner in question was never in CF custody in any event. As a result, the NIS concluded the investigation since it was lacking evidence and beyond the scope of their investigative jurisdiction in any event. This investigation was formally concluded by Maj Bolduc by letter dated June 4, 2008. 13.1.6 GO 2008–6913 Footnote 1038 – Investigation into Allegations of Assault by ANA This allegation was also previously opened under GO 2007–5564 . Footnote 1039 A corporal who had served in Afghanistan during ROTO 1 in 2006 had seen an ANA convoy with a Taliban prisoner restrained in the rear of one vehicle. The prisoner was cross-checked in the head with an RPG barrel, apparently without justification. No further abuse was alleged. On March 5, 2007 the corporal emailed photographs of a prisoner in the custody of the ANA to the MP , with a brief explanation of what he had seen. He was interviewed by the NIS on March 8, 2007 and indicated upon seeing media reports about abuse of prisoners he felt duty bound to come forward with what he knew, and he felt he should have reported what he had seen to the chain of command. The prisoner had never been in the custody of the CF . On March 16, 2007, Col Gleeson at JAG sent a letter to the Globe and Mail in response to detainee abuse issues which had recently been reported. Later that day, the corporal sent copies of the photographs and an email to Col Gleeson with a copy to the MP . On July 18, 2007 the investigation was placed on hold temporarily “ as Detainee Files have been prioritized with the Task Force concentrating on one investigation at this time ”. Footnote 1040 In May of 2008, there were further interviews of the corporal and another CF soldier. The conclusion was that the detainee was never in CF custody, nor did the detainee have significant marks or bruising, nor were any threats made to the detainee. Elements of Maj Bolduc’s closing letter of July 11, 2008 are redacted, but the conclusion was that there was nothing beyond speculation to justify any further investigation. Footnote 1041 13.1.7 GO 2008–6917 Footnote 1042 – Investigation into Allegations of Summary Executions – ROTO 2 A CF medical doctor reported a CF patient being treated for PTSD who claimed that CF detainees who were transferred to the ANA or ANP were taken out of sight and shot. He alleged this was well-known to himself, his colleagues and the chain of command. The patient was suffering from PTSD and in the doctor’s opinion he may have exaggerated his allegation or even made it up. The doctor felt he may have been telling the truth. Investigation including interviews of the platoon commander during June and July, 2008 revealed no evidence to confirm any particulars of detainee transfers and executions, and it appears the patient was in theatre at a time when his unit encountered no detainees being captured or transferred. The patient ultimately did not wish to discuss the allegations with the NIS . As part of this investigation, the NIS sought to obtain the TSO s and other materials or directives which would shed light on the obligations of a CF member who might witness actual or suspected abuse of a detainee at the hands of persons other than a Canadian. After enquiring of CEFCOM legal counsel, they were referred to LCol Irwin, who was the CEFCOM COS at the time. Footnote 1043 It is puzzling to the Commission that the NIS ’s attempts to gain insight into the legal terrain were rebuffed by CF lawyers, and that they were referred for that information to a senior officer in the chain of command rather than a legal officer. LCol Irwin’s information reiterated the CF commitment to living up to the standards of the Geneva Conventions; however, he could not say whether there was any written direction on what to do in the circumstances of a CF member witnessing abuse of detainees by Afghan personnel. He stated he would expect the CF member to report such an incident to the chain of command, but whether there would be any legal authority to intervene in case of abuse outside the scope of CF jurisdiction was not clear to him. LCol Irwin also indicated CF commanders’ expectations emphasized the conduct of CF members, not the conduct of others. He would hope a CF member would intervene to prevent abuse if they were able to – “ the emphasis was placed on can I act, not must I act ”. LCol Irwin did recognize a distinction in CF obligations when handing someone over believing they would get hurt, as opposed to reacting to abuse after the fact. Footnote 1044 This investigation was concluded by Maj Bolduc by letter dated July 16, 2008. The investigation was closed due to a lack of credible evidence supporting the allegations. Footnote 1045 13.1.8 GO 2008–6918 Footnote 1046 – Col Noonan Affidavit The Globe and Mail published an article on May 4, 2007 which described an incident of post-transfer abuse derived from the Federal Court affidavit of Col Noonan dated May 1, 2007. According to the initial description in the GO , a prisoner who was transferred was abused and “ CF persons observed it and took no action. Why did Chain of Command not report this to MP ?” Footnote 1047 The article relates the fact a detainee was abused, but in fact describes an opposition critic who said the government knew about the abuse and did nothing. In the article, the description of the abuse and CF response is substantially the same as is related in Col Noonan’s affidavit. The abuse of detainees was described in two paragraphs of his affidavit and consisted of a threat by the ANA to execute one detainee if he was transferred, and the retrieval of another detainee from the local ANP because the CF had learned this detainee was beaten. This second detainee was then transferred to a provincial branch of the ANP rather than the local branch. The file was initiated on July 10, 2008, assigned to Operation Centipede, and review and analysis of the affidavit took place in January 2009. There were no other steps in the investigation but for the review of the newspaper article and affidavit. Having reviewed the affidavit, the NIS concluded CF personnel took appropriate action with the detainees, and had no jurisdiction over the Afghan officials in question. As a result the investigation was concluded. Footnote 1048 13.1.9 GO 2008–6919 Footnote 1049 – Investigation into Tactical Questioning The Army Provost Marshal was advised on April 30, 2007 of concerns raised by an army captain who was involved in tactical questioning. An email chain describing the incident was forwarded to Operation Camel Spider and was reviewed by the PM . The investigation was placed into Operation Centipede, and not investigated until January 2009 due to resource constraints caused by prioritizing another unrelated high profile investigation. Footnote 1050 The investigation involved review of the email chain disclosing the events and an interview with the recipient of the email from the captain on February 20, 2009. The investigating NIS officer did not interview the captain from whom the information originated, but did read his further commentary in an email thread. The CF captain was relating third-hand information from other CF personnel involved in tactical questioning at the invitation of the ANSF . During this questioning, CF members noticed signs of injury and forced labour on the detainee, and while particulars are redacted, the Captain indicated the ANSF “ don’t necessarily follow our policies on detainee handling if you know what I mean. ” The CF questioner was uncomfortable assisting in the circumstances, but was also aware of the importance of assisting the ANSF as part of Canada’s mission in Afghanistan. Footnote 1051 There was no suggestion the detainee in question was ever in CF custody, although this was not confirmed either way by the NIS investigator. Footnote 1052 Concerns were expressed in the complaint the chain of command knew or ought to have known about potential for abuse during tactical questioning. On March 3, 2009 the NIS concluded its investigation into this matter. While portions of the concluding remarks are redacted, it appears remedial actions were taken by the chain of command to address the concerns raised in the email thread. Additionally, the NIS noted the detainees had not been in the custody of the CF . It was determined, based upon this evidence, that no service or criminal offence had occurred. 13.1.10 GO 2008–6920 and 6921 Footnote 1053 – Investigation into Globe and Mail Reports of Abuse Articles in the Globe and Mail dated March 9, 2007 and April 23, 2007 reported CF transferred detainees had been or would be abused by Afghan authorities after transfer. The March 9 article Footnote 1054 was authored by Professor Attaran and described an incident in the summer of 2006 where CBC reporters allegedly observed CF personnel preparing to transfer a detainee. The Afghan security personnel threatened to kill the detainee once turned over to them. The CF personnel hesitated but then turned over the detainee after the cameras were off. The April 23, 2007 article reported interviews by Globe and Mail reporter Graeme Smith with a number of CF transferred detainees who alleged they were abused by Afghan personnel following transfer. Names and particulars of these people were contained in the article. One of the persons said CF personnel had encouraged him to provide useful information to avoid further abuse. The worst of the abuse was alleged to have occurred at the hands of the NDS and included allegations of beatings, sleep deprivation, whipping with electrical cables, electric shocks, hanging by the ankles for extended periods of time, suffocation and exposure to cold. The investigation into these matters was formalized in Operation Centipede on July 10, 2008. The investigation, such as it was, concluded on November 19, 2008. It is clear the NIS investigation consisted of nothing beyond reading the articles in question. No attempt was made to obtain the CBC video, to confirm (or not) the allegations outlined by Prof Attaran, or to interview Graeme Smith, let alone interview the detainees themselves. The NIS was unaware the CEFCOM PM LCol Boot had conducted, at LGen ( ret’d ) Gauthier’s request, a point-by-point review of the Globe and Mail article and had confirmed certain elements such as the identity of some of the detainees as CF transferees. Not a single external source of information was considered or reviewed in these investigations. The Access to Information “ Details of Release ” sheet for GO 2008–6920 indicates nothing in this investigation was withheld from the Commission or redacted. There appears to be nothing withheld in GO 2008–6921 , although in both instances it is difficult to conclude the file is complete since the articles themselves are not included in the GO and there is no “ Details of Release ” sheet for GO 2008–6921 . The concluding remarks for these investigations are identical; it thus appears to the Commission the two matters were not given independent consideration. The Concluding Remarks are reproduced in full: This report was initially created to investigate the allegations that Afghans that had been capture [sic] by CG personnel were being abused. These allegations stemmed from two reports in the “ Globe and Mail ” dated 9 Mar 07 and 23 Apr 07. In brief, these reports relate that prisoners, specifically those who have captured by [sic] Canadian Forces and then later transferred to Afghan authorities, have been abused, tortured and even summarily executed by the Afghan powers that be. At that time and especially in consideration that Operation Centipede had been recently formed to investigate similar complaints; it was decided that the aforementioned news paper articles would be followed up on with the intention that an investigation(s) would ensue to determine if any service or criminal offences had been committed by CF personnel. However, since these early articles, the media has been inundated with countless reports of a similar nature. Paradoxically, many of these articles report that none of the aforementioned maltreatment was inflicted by Canadians, in fact most of the alleged captives have praised the Canadian soldiers on their civility, good manners and the relatively comfortable detention centre located at KAF . Since then, the Government of Canada ( GOC ) has taken notice and has discussed these reports in great fact. Subsequently the GOC , including the CF and DND have taken action on many levels throughout its various parliamentary affairs in high level national and international menus [sic]. Although these newspaper journalists are reporting that they have interviewed former Afghan captives or at least received information concerning their treatment at the hands of the Afghans, considering the general rules of evidence, the inadmissibility of statements as they pertain to hearsay information, and the lack of any other credible evidence, there is no satisfactory justification to continue this investigation. Likewise, even if these reports were somehow deemed to be credible, the allegations of ill-treatment are directed against the Afghan authorities. This alone excludes our jurisdictional interests and the mandate of the CFNIS . As such, there is no satisfactory justification to proceed with an investigation that focuses on the actions of the Afghan authorities and their handling of prisoners. Upon reflection, it seems to be obvious that there will be additional reports in the far reaching future that will address the manner in which Afghan authorities handle their Afghan captives. To that end, any pending media reports/articles concerning the treatment of Afghan prisoners by Afghan authorities which are void of any direct accusations of criminal wrongdoings of CF members, will not be investigated by this office. This file is concluded. Footnote 1055 13.1.11 GO 2008-23231 Footnote 1056 – Investigation into Disclosure during MP Training Although the particulars are redacted, this was an allegation of detainee abuse related by a Warrant Officer ( WO ) to a group of MP trainees during a lecture at the Canadian Forces Military Police Academy. The investigation was opened on August 21, 2008 and interviews of the WO and some of the lecture attendees occurred shortly thereafter. The WO was interviewed and indicated his information came from a discussion he had in June 2007 with a returning member of the CF , whose identity he could not recall. The member had said he witnessed abuse of a detainee in the hands of Afghan authorities, but the WO indicated, to his knowledge, the detainee was never in CF custody. The witness to the abuse indicated he had tried to intervene and had related the incident to the chain of command. The WO did not confirm that this occurred. The lecture attendees’ accounts were substantially similar to those of the WO . There were no apparent attempts by the NIS to identify who the direct witness to the incident might be although the WO knew his rank, knew he was a returning member of the RCR , and had encountered him during pre-deployment training at CFB Wainwright. The NIS investigation was concluded on November 3, 2008. The conclusion was that there was no evidence to corroborate the allegations, and there was no evidence of CF involvement or wrongdoing. The NIS concluded the allegation was a culmination of several stories, some of which had already been investigated in Operation Centipede, and there was no separate new allegation to be investigated. 13.2 Delays, Investigative Procedures, Resources and Priorities for NIS Investigations The Commission recognizes resource limitations were a very serious issue for the NIS during the period of these investigations. Operation Camel Spider and a major fraud investigation occupied a tremendous amount of NIS resources in 2007. Footnote 1057 The HDO Survey investigation was also very resource intensive during the time period. Operation Centipede was initiated by Maj Bolduc in order to clear the backlog of detainee-related matters which had arisen incidentally during the Camel Spider investigation. In addition to the resource pressure caused by other major investigations, NIS personnel in Afghanistan were faced with the extremely difficult and stressful tasks of investigating CF use of force in combat, forensic investigations concerning CF members who were killed in action, and the difficult task of repatriation of those members, as well as other investigations which did not relate in any way to detainee issues. That being said, it is difficult to reconcile the senior MP and operational commands’ views about the “ mission critical ” nature of detainee abuse issues with the level of priority and attention that was given to some of these investigations. Operation Centipede was placed lower in priority to Maj Bolduc’s existing investigations when he first proposed it. This is why the GO s were opened in March 2008 despite the allegations stemming from 2006–2007 and coming to light during the Camel Spider investigation. NIS personnel acknowledged it is preferable from a policing perspective to investigate matters in a more timely fashion to prevent the loss of potential evidence through the passage of time, Footnote 1058 yet the combination of priorities and resource issues meant these investigations were essentially on the back burner for over a year in some instances. The Commission is also of the view that some of the investigations received short shrift or were half-hearted at best. Several of the investigations involved little more than a review of the complaint and its paper trail, without any attempt to verify whether detainee abuse was or was not occurring and whether any CF personnel, including commanders, were aware of it. There was a paper review of the Globe and Mail article allegations, without any attempt to speak to the author or the detainees, to obtain confirmatory records from CEFCOM , or otherwise test the veracity of these shocking and serious allegations. As noted above, one NIS report concluded by bluntly stating that any other media reports of detainee mistreatment which did not include CF members would not be investigated. This apparent laxity and closed-mindedness is indeed troubling from a policing perspective and appears to be inconsistent with NIS commanders’ own view of proper investigations. Maj Bolduc acknowledged that determining whether an allegedly abused detainee had been in CF custody was a key piece of information in determining whether to move an investigation into abuse forward, Footnote 1059 yet on these two files there was no attempt to obtain this information despite it being readily available at CEFCOM . In the Commission’s view, one cannot expect to obtain further information without asking questions or making inquiries. The allegations were not followed up in part because the newspaper article was said to be “ hearsay ”, but no attempt was made to obtain original evidence. LCol Sansterre was at something of a loss to explain the basis upon which the hearsay nature of information would rule out the investigative pursuit of further information. Footnote 1060 The Commission is well aware that often investigations are initiated and moved forward on the basis of hearsay and untested or uncorroborated evidence –this is consistent with normal police practice. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick and Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore acknowledged this, and both indicated they expected a more thorough investigation to follow upon these allegations. Footnote 1061 It appears to the Commission the main focus of MP concern was CF abuse of detainees, and the significance of post-transfer abuse (and the implications with respect to transfer orders leading to or subsequent to allegations of abuse) was not at the forefront of MP ’s concerns. Perhaps this was because of a tendency to conflate the issue of jurisdiction over charges and relevance to an investigation. Maj Bolduc, the case manager, described Afghan abuse of Afghan detainees as outside the scope of MP jurisdiction, and LCol Sansterre expressed similar views. Footnote 1062 However, as LCol Sansterre noted, the fact abuse was committed by persons outside NIS jurisdiction does not mean that facts cannot be solicited from sources outside NIS charging jurisdiction, Footnote 1063 and it does not preclude the prospect that CF personnel could bear some legal culpability for that abuse in certain circumstances. It appears to the Commission the real significance of post-transfer abuse with respect to the issue of the legality of transfer orders really did not register with the CO of CFNIS until June 12, 2008 when the issue was articulated in writing by the Complainants in this matter. Footnote 1064 At that point, more than a year had passed since the allegations in OP CENTIPEDE had occurred. Both Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore and LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick indicated they expected any evidence relating to the issue of the legality of transfer orders to be substantively addressed in the course of the investigations in Operation Centipede. However, it is clear this issue was not probed during that investigation. XIV. The Analysis of Professors Forcese and Sassoli Relating to Legal Allegations in the Complaint The foundation of the “ failure to investigate ” complaint is an allegation that “ crimes ” were committed by members of the CF in ordering the transfer of detainees to the custody of the Afghan National Directorate of Security despite compelling first hand reports of previous CF detainees being tortured by those authorities. AIC / BCCLA contend there is no reasonable explanation why the Task Force Commander did not halt transfers much sooner than November 5, 2007, when earlier reports of torture were disclosed to Canadian officials. In short, AIC / BCCLA submit that officers in the chain of command ignored much evidence pointing to a substantial risk of torture, thus showing a disregard for the lives and safety of the detainees. The legal basis on which the allegation of “ crimes ” exists is said by AIC / BCCLA to reside in certain provisions of the Criminal Code , the NDA , the Crimes Against Humanity and War Crimes Act , and the Geneva Conventions Act . AIC / BCCLA submit these Acts create a number of offences that would apply to members of the CF who ordered the transfer of detainees when they knew or ought to have known a substantial risk of torture existed. The jurisdiction of this Commission does not extend to making findings of criminal or possible criminal liability against military commanders, and nothing in this Report is to be construed as making such findings or even suggesting such liability exists. However, the underlying legal allegations in the complaint necessarily have to be examined as part of the inquiry into whether a duty to investigate was triggered. As counsel for seven of the subjects acknowledged in written submissions, among the issues the Commission must address is: “ What, if any, were the offences known to law which could have been investigated… ” Footnote 1065 The alleged duty to investigate in this case arises from the Complainants’ allegation that certain offences were committed by commanders in relation to the transfer of detainees. It is therefore necessary to consider whether there are offences that potentially could arise out of detainee transfer orders, as the Complainants allege. If no offences exist under the law that are even potentially applicable to the nature of the complaint, then it is difficult to see how a duty could arise on the part of the MP to investigate, and how they could be faulted for a failure to investigate. To put the matter another way, if there is no offence known to law that could be applicable to orders to transfer detainees, then there would be no act or omission by CF commanders that the MP should reasonably be expected to investigate. The Commission therefore considered it necessary to its investigation to understand the potential scope and application of the various legal enactments cited by AIC / BCCLA in their complaint. To assist the Commission in this regard, two experts were retained (Professor Craig Forcese of the University of Ottawa, and Professor Marco Sassoli of the University of Geneva, Switzerland) to provide a report analyzing whether and how the international and domestic legal instruments cited by AIC / BCCLA could be relevant to the circumstances set out in the complaint. They were instructed not to draw any conclusions as to the actual validity of any of the Complainants’ allegations, and did not do so. For the purpose of framing their analysis they hypothesized certain facts, without opining or concluding whether any of these facts were true. The reports of Professors Sassoli and Forcese were distributed to the parties, and marked as exhibits. Footnote 1066 These experts appeared together as a witness panel on May 6, 2010, to present their reports and to answer questions from the parties. It is clear from the evidence the CF chain of command was aware of its responsibilities and directed that detainees were not to be transferred into situations where a substantial risk of torture was known, or reasonably ought to be known, to exist. On June 18, 2007, LGen ( ret’d ) Gauthier, the Canadian Expeditionary Forces Command ( CEFCOM ) Commander, issued a clear direction to the Task Force Commander, BGen Laroche (as he then was), which stated: 24. The chain of command bears the potential liability should we become aware of torture or mistreatment following the transfer of detainees to Afghan authorities. It is for this reason that I am particularly concerned about the chain of command obligation to satisfy itself that the follow up of transferred detainees is sufficiently robust. I expect a proactive engagement with DFAIT at all levels, but particularly at your level, to ensure monitoring occurs and reporting and analysis is provided. The monitoring, reporting and analysis must be sufficient to enable command decisions regarding continuation of transfers. You are to engage with me directly should a concern arise. Footnote 1067 On September 12, 2007, LGen ( ret’d ) Gauthier issued an Amplifying Guidance on Detainees Reference: Chain of Command Obligations With Respect to Post-Transfer Follow-Up to the Task Force Commander, that stated: 2. The chain of command bears potential legal liability should we transfer a detainee into Afghan custody when we know, or can be reasonably expected to know, that substantial grounds exist for believing that the detainee faces a real risk of subsequent abuse or mistreatment. It is for this reason that I am particularly concerned about the chain of command obligation to satisfy itself that all relevant information regarding the treatment of detainees while in Afghan custody is actively sought and considered. Footnote 1068 On November 25, 2007, when the Task Force Commander ( BGen Laroche) suspended transfers, he gave as reasons: 5. Footnote 1094 The question before the Commission, however, is whether a legal duty to investigate was triggered, as opposed to there being “ sufficiently good reason ” to initiate an investigation. The case law is clear that this duty is not automatically applicable in every situation. The Commission concludes there are offences known to law which could have formed a reasonable basis for a police investigation. In making this finding, the Commission has borne in mind that, while the legal issues may be complex, the police are not expected or required, during the course of an inquiry or investigation, to evaluate the evidence they have gathered against precise legal standards or to make legal judgments as to whether the evidence will support a conviction. That is the task of other participants in the justice system, namely prosecutors, defence counsel and judges. XV. The Legal Standard of Conduct Applicable to Military Police 15.1 The Standard of the Reasonable Police Officer In its ruling on the Motion of Standard of Conduct, dated April 1, 2010, the Commission stated it will be guided generally by the standard of conduct set out in the Hill decision of the Supreme Court of Canada: The Commission will thus be generally guided in the hearings by the standard as set out at para 68 of the Hill judgment, namely, that of a “ reasonable police officer in all the circumstances … ” To this we would add the further clarification at para 73 of Hill that MPs are not required to make optimal decisions, but instead are to be judged on the basis of prevailing circumstances: “ The standard is not perfection, or even the optimum, judged from the vantage of hindsight. It is that of a reasonable officer, judged in the circumstances prevailing at the time the decision was made – circumstances that may include urgency and deficiencies of information. ” Footnote 1095 The Hill case (2007 SCC 41) dealt with the tort of negligent investigation. The Commission is not concerned in this case with the existence, or elements, of this tort. However, the Hill case provides valuable guidance as to the expected standard of conduct when the police are conducting an investigation. In general terms, it is expected police officers will act as a reasonable investigating officer would in the circumstances. The prevailing circumstances may include situations of urgency or deficiencies in information. Police officers are entitled to exercise their investigative discretion as they see fit, so long as they stay within the bounds of reasonableness and their underlying intention is honest, not arbitrary, and not motivated by favouritism or any other dishonest intention. The expected standard of conduct is not perfection, or even the optimum, viewed from the vantage of hindsight. Minor errors, or errors in judgment that any professional might have made, are not “ unreasonable mistakes ” that breach the expected standard even though they might have unfortunate results. The applicable principles are discussed as follows in the Hill judgment: 68 A number of considerations support the conclusion that the standard of care is that of a reasonable police officer in all the circumstances. First, the standard of a reasonable police officer in all the circumstances provides a flexible overarching standard that covers all aspects of investigatory police work and appropriately reflects its realities. The particular conduct required is informed by the stage of the investigation and applicable legal considerations. At the outset of an investigation, the police may have little more than hearsay, suspicion and a hunch. What is required is that they act as a reasonable investigating officer would in those circumstances. Later, in laying charges, the standard is informed by the legal requirement of reasonable and probable grounds to believe the suspect is guilty; since the law requires such grounds, a police officer acting reasonably in the circumstances would insist on them. The reasonable officer standard entails no conflict between criminal standards (Charron J., at para 175). Rather, it incorporates them, in the same way it incorporates an appropriate degree of judicial discretion, denies liability for minor errors or mistakes and rejects liability by hindsight. In all these ways, it reflects the realities of police work. 69 Second, as mentioned, the general rule is that the standard of care in negligence is that of the reasonable person in similar circumstances. In cases of professional negligence, this rule is qualified by an additional principle: where the defendant has special skills and experience, the defendant must “ live up to the standards possessed by persons of reasonable skill and experience in that calling ”. Footnote 1096 These principles suggest the standard of the reasonable officer in like circumstances. 70 Third, the common law factors relevant to determining the standard of care confirm the reasonable officer standard. These factors include: the likelihood of known or foreseeable harm, the gravity of harm, the burden or cost which would be incurred to prevent the injury, external indicators of reasonable conduct (including professional standards) and statutory standards. Footnote 1097 These factors suggest a standard of reasonableness, not something less onerous. There is a significant likelihood that police officers may cause harm to suspects if they investigate negligently. The gravity of the potential harm caused is serious. Suspects may be arrested or imprisoned, their livelihoods affected and their reputations irreparably damaged. The cost of preventing the injury, in comparison, is not undue. Police meet a standard of reasonableness by merely doing what a reasonable police officer would do in the same circumstances — by living up to accepted standards of professional conduct to the extent that it is reasonable to expect in given circumstances. This seems neither unduly onerous nor overly costly. It must be supposed that professional standards require police to act professionally and carefully, not just to avoid gross negligence. The statutory standards imposed by the Police Services Act , R.S.O. 1990, c. P.15, although not definitive of the standard of care, are instructive ( s. 1). 71 Fourth, the nature and importance of police work reinforce a standard of the reasonable officer in similar circumstances. Police conduct has the capacity to seriously affect individuals by subjecting them to the full coercive power of the state and impacting on their repute and standing in the community. It follows that police officers should perform their duties reasonably. It has thus been recognized that police work demands that society (including the courts) impose and enforce high standards on police conduct (Cory Report, at p. 10). This supports a reasonableness standard, judged in the context of a similarly situated officer. A more lenient standard is inconsistent with the standards that society and the law rightfully demand of police in the performance of their crucially important work. 72 Finally, authority supports the standard of the reasonable police officer similarly placed. The preponderance of case law dealing with professionals has applied the standard of the reasonably competent professional in like circumstances. (See Klar, at p. 349; see also the reasons of the trial judge at para 63.) The Quebec Court of Appeal has twice stated that the standard is the ordinarily competent officer in like circumstances. Footnote 1098 73 I conclude that the appropriate standard of care is the overarching standard of a reasonable police officer in similar circumstances. This standard should be applied in a manner that gives due recognition to the discretion inherent in police investigation. Like other professionals, police officers are entitled to exercise their discretion as they see fit, provided that they stay within the bounds of reasonableness. The standard of care is not breached because a police officer exercises his or her discretion in a manner other than that deemed optimal by the reviewing court. A number of choices may be open to a police officer investigating a crime, all of which may fall within the range of reasonableness. So long as discretion is exercised within this range, the standard of care is not breached. The standard is not perfection, or even the optimum, judged from the vantage of hindsight. It is that of a reasonable officer, judged in the circumstances prevailing at the time the decision was made — circumstances that may include urgency and deficiencies of information. The law of negligence does not require perfection of professionals; nor does it guarantee desired results (Klar, at p. 359). Rather, it accepts that police officers, like other professionals, may make minor errors or errors in judgment which cause unfortunate results, without breaching the standard of care. The law distinguishes between unreasonable mistakes breaching the standard of care and mere “ errors in judgment ” which any reasonable professional might have made and therefore, which do not breach the standard of care. Footnote 1099 (Emphasis added). Footnote 1100 The Hill judgment also considered the role of the police in the justice system, namely, to be concerned primarily with gathering and evaluating evidence. Police officers are not expected or required to evaluate evidence according to legal standards, or to make legal judgments. It is the job of prosecutors to determine whether the evidence will support a conviction at law: 49 It was argued that the decision of police to pursue the investigation of a suspect on the one hand, or close it on the other, is a quasi-judicial decision, similar to that taken by the state prosecutor. It is true that both police officers and prosecutors make decisions that relate to whether the suspect should stand trial. But the nature of the inquiry differs. Police are concerned primarily with gathering and evaluating evidence. Prosecutors are concerned mainly with whether the evidence the police have gathered will support a conviction at law. The fact-based investigative character of the police task distances it from a judicial or quasi-judicial role. 50 The possibility of holding police civilly liable for negligent investigation does not require them to make judgments as to legal guilt or innocence before proceeding against a suspect. Police are required to weigh evidence to some extent in the course of an investigation: Chartier v. Attorney General of Quebec , [1979] 2 S.C.R. 474. But they are not required to evaluate evidence according to legal standards or to make legal judgments. That is the task of prosecutors, defence attorneys and judges. This distinction is properly reflected in the standard of care imposed, once a duty is recognized. The standard of care required to meet the duty is not that of a reasonable lawyer or judge, but that of a reasonable police officer . Where the police investigate a suspect reasonably, but lawyers, judges or prosecutors act unreasonably in the course of determining his legal guilt or innocence, then the police officer will have met the standard of care and cannot be held liable either for failing to perform the job of a lawyer, judge or prosecutor, or for the unreasonable conduct of other actors in the criminal justice system. 15.2 The Duty to Self-Initiate an Investigation 15.2.1 Case Law The police have a duty to investigate crime. However, this duty is not absolute; it is subject to the discretion afforded to police officers, with which the Courts will not readily interfere if the discretion is exercised honestly and in an objectively reasonable manner. Police officers have a duty to use their judgment to adapt law enforcement to individual circumstances and the real-life demands of justice. This is the basis of police discretion. In R. v. Beaudry , 2007 SCC 5, the essence of police discretion was described in the following terms: 35 There is no question that police officers have a duty to enforce the law and investigate crimes. The principle that the police have a duty to enforce the criminal law is well established at common law: R. v. Metropolitan Police Commissioner , [1968] 1 All E.R. 763 ( C.A. ), per Lord Denning, M.R., at p. 769; Hill v. Chief Constable of West Yorkshire , [1988] 2 All E.R. 238 (H.L.), per Lord Keith of Kinkel; P. Ceyssens, Legal Aspects of Policing (loose-leaf ed.), vol. 1, at pp. 2-22 et seq .… 36 Nevertheless, it should not be concluded automatically, or without distinction, that this duty is applicable in every situation. Applying the letter of the law to the practical, real-life situations faced by police officers in performing their everyday duties requires that certain adjustments be made. Although these adjustments may sometimes appear to deviate from the letter of the law, they are crucial and are part of the very essence of the proper administration of the criminal justice system, or to use the words of s. 139(2), are perfectly consistent with the “ course of justice ”. The ability — indeed the duty — to use one’s judgment to adapt the process of law enforcement to individual circumstances and to the real-life demands of justice is in fact the basis of police discretion. What La Forest J. said in R. v. Beare , [1988] 2 S.C.R. 387, at p. 410, is directly on point here: Discretion is an essential feature of the criminal justice system. A system that attempted to eliminate discretion would be unworkably complex and rigid. 37 Thus, a police officer who has reasonable grounds to believe that an offence has been committed, or that a more thorough investigation might produce evidence that could form the basis of a criminal charge, may exercise his or her discretion to decide not to engage the judicial process. But this discretion is not absolute. Far from having carte blanche , police officers must justify their decisions rationally. 38 The required justification is essentially twofold. First, the exercise of the discretion must be justified subjectively, that is, the discretion must have been exercised honestly and transparently, and on the basis of valid and reasonable grounds (reasons of Chamberland J.A., at para. 41). Thus, a decision based on favouritism, or on cultural, social or racial stereotypes, cannot constitute a proper exercise of police discretion. However, the officer’s sincere belief that he properly exercised his discretion is not sufficient to justify his decision. 39 Hence, the exercise of police discretion must also be justified on the basis of objective factors. I agree with Doyon J.A. that in determining whether a decision resulting from an exercise of police discretion is proper, it is important to consider the material circumstances in which the discretion was exercised. However, I do not agree with him on the importance of the factors he regarded as part of the legal context, that is, the administrative directives and the administration of justice in the province. 40 First, it is self-evident that the material circumstances are an important factor in the assessment of a police officer’s decision: the discretion will certainly not be exercised in the same way in a case of shoplifting by a teenager as one involving a robbery. In the first case, the interests of justice may very well be served if the officer gives the young offender a stern warning and alerts his or her parents. However, this does not mean that the police have no discretion left when the degree of seriousness reaches a certain level. In the case of a robbery, or an even more serious offence, the discretion can be exercised to decide not to arrest a suspect or not to pursue an investigation. However, the justification offered must be proportionate to the seriousness of the conduct and it must be clear that the discretion was exercised in the public interest. Thus, while some exercises of discretion are almost routine and are clearly justified, others are truly exceptional and will require that the police officer explain his or her decision in greater detail. Footnote 1101 In Chief Constable of the Hertfordshire Police v. Van Colle , [2008] UKHL 50, the UK House of Lords considered a case where the police had failed to act on a threat against a person which culminated in his murder. Much of the reasoning was addressed at the point whether the police owed the victims of the threatened violence a duty to prevent the threatened violence from occurring, and whether they could be sued for breach of such a duty. In his opinion, Lord Bingham stated: […] the court should endeavour to place itself in the chair of DC Ridley and assess events as they unfolded through his eyes. But the application of the test depends not only on what the authorities knew, but also on what they ought to have known. Thus, stupidity, lack of imagination and inertia do not afford an excuse to a national authority which reasonably ought, in the light of what it knew or was told, to make further inquiries or investigations: it is then to be treated as knowing what such further enquiries or investigations would have elicited. Footnote 1102 In the case of R. Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis, Ex Parte Blackburn , [1968] 1 All E.R. 763, Blackburn sought mandamus to compel the police to enforce the gaming laws. In holding that the police had a duty to enforce the law, Lord Denning described the discretion of police officers as follows: Although the chief officers of police are answerable to the law, there are many fields in which they have a discretion with which the law will not interfere. For instance, it is for the Commissioner of Police, or the chief constable, as the case may be, to decide in any particular case whether enquiries should be pursued, or whether an arrest should be made, or a prosecution brought. It must be for him to decide on the disposition of his force and the concentration of his resources on any particular crime or area. No court can or should give him direction on such a matter. As to the outcome of the case, no decision was ultimately necessary due to a policy change and an undertaking by the police to look into the “ goings-on ” in gaming clubs. The Court said that was all that the Complainant could expect. In an Australian case, O’Malley v. Keelty, CMR of the Australian Federal Police , [2005] FCA 861, the Australian Federal Court considered whether the police had breached a duty to investigate allegations by O’Malley that his telephone communications had been illegally intercepted: 31 The primary question in this case is whether the Commissioner, or his officers, have breached any duty by failing to investigate further the allegations made by Mr. O’Malley. In determining whether a breach occurred, the issue to consider is whether a reasonable, honest police officer would have decided to investigate in this case after having given the matter due and proper consideration. […] 36 Nevertheless, a court cannot and should not compel a police force to investigate every breach of the law. There are many mysteries in this world. Some of them involve possible commissions of crime. It is not, however, the responsibility of police officers to investigate all of them. Indeed, the role of the police is not to investigate whether, at large, there has been a breach of the law. In the result, the Court did not find in the O’Malley case the police had breached a duty to investigate. Relevant factors considered by the Court to assess the reasonableness of the police actions were: there was no material that would require an honest and reasonable police officer to conclude that any identifiable person might be successfully prosecuted for any wrongdoing. Consequently, there was no reason why an honest and reasonable police officer might not decide against commencing or continuing an investigation. when viewed in relation to the full spectrum of criminal behaviour, it would be difficult to classify this complaint as a relatively major matter. The relatively small penalty attached to such a breach would relegate it to a low priority matter. While such a breach would at least constitute an invasion of privacy, when the degree of individual and social harm likely involved in such a breach is compared to the harm associated with more serious crimes, it is clear that a reasonable and honest police officer might consider the matter to be of such low priority as to warrant the devotion of no further resources to it. the lack and difficulty of obtaining any legally admissible evidence identifying those responsible for the alleged interference with Mr. O’Malley’s home telephone lines, and the long supposed time frame of events, (spanning more than a decade) made it unlikely that the Director of Public Prosecutions would ever be prepared to prosecute the matter. In conclusion, the principle to be derived from the case law is that so long as police officers have exercised their discretion honestly and in an objectively reasonable manner, and can justify their actions rationally, they will not be found culpable for a decision not to investigate since such a decision falls within their legitimate exercise of police discretion. 15.2.2 MP Policies and Directives As was noted by counsel for seven of the subjects in written submissions, the CFPM has issued Technical Directives on the conduct of policing duties and functions. The CFPM has also issued, on behalf of the VCDS , the Military Police Policies and Technical Procedural Manual ( MPPTP ) providing the CFPM ’s technical guidance on policing duties and functions. Finally, the CFPM , through the office of the Deputy Provost Marshal ( DPM ) Police, issues mission specific Technical Directives to the Task Force Senior MP Adviser. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore, the CFPM at the time in question, testified the mission-specific Technical Directives did not have the binding effect of orders. Footnote 1103 In written submissions on behalf of Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore, the status of CFPM Technical Directives was described as follows: These directives were the articulation of the CFPM ’s expectations on policing. They were described as guidelines for the performance of policing functions. Although consequences could flow from a failure to follow a Technical Directive, they did not constitute an Order. (At p. 18) There is some interplay between non-binding police directives and policies relating to the performance of policing functions, and the legal duties and discretion of police officers as defined by the common law. Such directives or policies do not define or limit the common law responsibilities and discretion of police, although they are relevant to the prevailing circumstances under which individual police conduct will be evaluated. In R. v. Beaudry , the Court considered the relationship between directives to police, and the legal duties of police as these are defined by common law: 44 While the existence of administrative directives that apply to the situation in issue is far from being totally irrelevant, it cannot be as conclusive a factor as Doyon J.A. suggests. After quoting the passages from the police practices manual of Repentigny’s public safety service on the procedure to follow in impaired driving cases, he concluded as follows: […] In my opinion, these passages demonstrate the authorities’ clear intention that impaired driving offences should first be thoroughly investigated, although this does not preclude a subsequent decision not to prosecute. It must be noted that the period of time for taking breath samples is relatively short, which means that the investigation must be completed diligently and that this directive should be followed. A police officer who is familiar with such a directive and who has solemnly affirmed, under the Police Act (R.S.Q., c. P-13.1), that he or she will perform the duties of his or her office honestly cannot be unaware of how serious the state considers this type of offence to be. In fact, the appellant’s superior officer himself concluded, after being informed of the events, that breath samples should have been taken. Footnote 1104 45 Doyon J.A. seems to be attributing to the administrative directives set out in the police practices manual a normative value that they do not have. It should be pointed out that these directives do not have the force of law. They therefore cannot alter the scope of a discretion that is founded in the common law or a statute […] 46 In R. v. Jageshur (2002), 169 C.C.C. (3d) 225, the Ontario Court of Appeal addressed this question in a context that was very similar to the one now before us. That case concerned the legality of a police operation carried out in compliance with the applicable law but not with the applicable administrative directives. Doherty J.A. wrote the following for a unanimous court: An officer’s duties and hence his or her responsibilities cannot be equated with instructions as to how those duties and responsibilities should be carried out. Police policies speak to the manner in which police should carry out their responsibilities, but do not define or limit those responsibilities. […] My conclusion that the officers’ responsibilities were not circumscribed by the RCMP policy concerning major drug operations and reverse stings is fortified by a consideration of the nature of these policies. Section 21(1)(b) of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act authorizes the Governor in Council to make regulations for the conduct and performance of duties by members of the RCMP . Section 21(2)( b ) authorizes the Commissioner of the RCMP to make rules (standing orders) for the conduct and performance of duties by members of the RCMP . Section 38 of the same Act authorizes the Governor in Council to make regulations governing the conduct of members (Code of Conduct). The policies in issue on this appeal did not spring from any of these statutory sources… . [Emphasis added; paras 50 and 52.] In short, evidence of the existence of directives of this nature and evidence that the accused was, or is presumed to have been, aware of them at the time of the conduct in issue can shed light on the circumstances of the alleged exercise of his discretion. The same is true of evidence about the police service’s usual procedures, such as the testimony of Assistant Director Rocheleau and retired officer Lapointe in the case at bar. However, such evidence cannot be conclusive. Footnote 1105 Because police policies and directives can shed light on the circumstances which are alleged to give rise to a duty to investigate, they are a relevant factor for the Commission to consider. In the MPPTP , referred to above (Exhibit P-3, tab 3), guidance was given to MP on their roles and responsibilities, and the conduct of investigations, as follows: Chapter One 3. General. The roles and responsibilities of the MP are contained in the Department Administrative Orders and Directives ( DAOD ). The MP tasks and priorities will vary according to the commander’s requirements, geographical location, and the operational environment concerned. Duties include: crime prevention; detection and investigation of service, criminal, and security offences; […] 6. Constraints. The independence of policing is aimed at ensuring the integrity of our judicial system. The purpose and objectives of an investigation are to reconstruct events, gather evidence, identify the elements of the alleged offence, and identify those responsible for it. Each of these purposes must be fulfilled, and each of these objectives must be achieved with integrity and fairness. […] 5. Independence of Investigations. MP authority is derived from the NDA and the C.C.C. [Criminal Code of Canada]. When exercising MP powers under the NDA , the individual MP member is held personally accountable. 6. Ethical Principles. MP investigations shall be conducted IAW accepted CF Military Police policies and procedures, with particular attention to the following: MP shall not accord immunities or undue advantages to any person notwithstanding their rank or position; Investigations and other law enforcement activities must be conducted in such a manner, within the law, that facilitates and supports the Commander’s legitimate mission, and reinforces military values; MP shall not attempt to dissuade a complainant from pursuing a complaint, nor will the MP display scepticism about the allegations. MP may attempt to reconcile inconsistencies in a complainant’s statement(s) of present, however, failure to do so may not prevent the complaint from being pursued; and MP shall investigate complaints without bias or prejudice to any particular individual. Identification and elimination of suspects shall be based on objective evidence and reasonable grounds. 1. [sic] Initiating an Investigation. An MP investigation may be initiated whenever: an MP observes the commission of any criminal or service offence; an MP is in receipt of a complaint originating from any other person in which a criminal or service offence is alleged; at the request of a Commander/ CO ; MP learns of an incident through an informant ( i.e. local police, a witness, a confidential informant, an anonymous tip, etc. ); MP are tasked directly by DPM Police or DPM NIS ; and an authority in the MP Technical Chain so directs. […] 20. General. The CFNIS provides DND and the CF an efficient, accountable, and independent organization for criminal investigation services in Canada and abroad, in support of the military justice system. The direction provided in the MPPTP was amplified by mission-specific Technical Directives issued by the CFPM . During the time period of this complaint, there were three such Technical Directives.
