Footnote 1252 Maj Zybala took the initiative, prior to his deployment, to inform himself of issues related to the treatment of detainees and the conditions in prisons in Afghanistan. Based on his research, he understood Canada had what he often referred to as a residual responsibility towards detainees once transferred, which he described as follows: [...] je crois que le standard légal c’est qu’on ne peut transférer un détenu si on croit qu’il y a un risque substantiel de torture. Donc il y a une certaine responsabilité? Résiduelle, oui. [ unofficial translation ] [...] I think that the legal standard is that we cannot transfer a detainee if we believe that there is a substantial risk of torture. So there is some liability? Residual, yes. Footnote 1253 He also knew, specifically, this responsibility flowed from article 12 of the third Geneva Convention. Footnote 1254 Maj Zybala’s prior research involved reading, for example, the Graeme Smith Globe and Mail articles from April 2007. He did not view DFAIT , US State Department or UN reports, but did read at least one report from the AIHRC , which he downloaded from the AIHRC website. He took from that report the AIHRC was flagging problems that existed of abuse and torture in the Afghan prisons. Footnote 1255 Indeed, the report he consulted contained a chart with statistics on reports of torture by province in Afghanistan, with such reports in Kandahar province being double that of the next worst province. He was careful to point out, though, the statistics and reports were somewhat dated (from one to two years prior to his rotation) and, in his opinion, the situation in Afghanistan could change radically in only six months. The information in the AIHRC report was useful for him, but not determinative of the question of risk of torture and abuse. Footnote 1256 Maj Zybala also knew about the February 21, 2007 complaint before going into theatre. He knew it alleged the military police were perhaps committing a crime by assisting in the transfer of Afghan detainees to an unacceptable risk of torture. It appears he found the complaint, of his own accord, by going to the Complainants’ website. Footnote 1257 From it, he understood that the complaint raised the allegation – conveyed by the UN – that torture was common in NDS institutions. He knew this, and considered it to be historical information that did not necessarily have a bearing on what was happening in the present in Afghanistan. Again, he saw it as useful, but not determinative: Effectivement. C’est de l’information historique qui est d’intérêt, mais non déterminante. [ unofficial translation ] That’s correct. It’s historical information that is of interest, but not determinative. Footnote 1258 As a result of this prior research, and the aforementioned sources, Maj Zybala therefore knew, prior to going into theatre, torture could occur in the Afghan prison system. Footnote 1259 During his training, Maj Zybala familiarized himself with the new Transfer Arrangement created in May 2007. He knew it put in place a site visit process to be carried out by DFAIT , and placed responsibility on the Afghans to investigate all allegations of mistreatment. He would not speculate as to the motive for establishing the new transfer regime. He only knew there had been a suspension of transfers in May 2007. In general, he felt the new arrangement satisfied Canada’s obligations under international law, ensuring, as he understood was required, that Canada’s detainees were treated in accordance with the third Geneva Convention. Footnote 1260 He was also aware there was an arrangement with the AIHRC with respect to reporting on mistreatment of Canadian-transferred detainees, but never saw reports or heard from them in this respect during his time in theatre. Footnote 1261 Maj Zybala was aware of the applicable technical directive during his timeframe in Afghanistan. In similar fashion to Maj Hudson, he described the necessity to converse with the NIS representatives in theatre were there to be a question as to whether the NIS or the regular MP platoon had the mandate to investigate any particular offence, with the debate centering on the serious and sensitive nature of the investigation. Footnote 1262 This is a reference to para 11 of the various Technical Directives. Maj Zybala also knew if he became aware of a possible violation of international law in theatre, it would be his job to refer this to the NIS . Footnote 1263 He was attuned to the possibility the detainee transfer process potentially implicated the Task Force Commander and the chain of command, in a legal sense. He viewed the directive from LGen ( ret’d ) Gauthier to MGen Laroche while in theatre, including paragraph 24 of that directive, which sets out this potential liability. Footnote 1264 In fact, it appears he considered himself potentially subject to the same or similar liabilities as part of that same chain of command. He did not perceive, however, a conflict of interest in the fact he might have been required to report the illegal activity of that chain of command to the NIS for investigation. Footnote 1265 Maj Hudson briefed Maj Zybala prior to their exchange of command. However, he did not convey that he was unduly concerned about the post-transfer process. He may, though, have learned from Maj Hudson there had been one suspension of transfers. He understood the suspension was to allow for a period of adjustment and transition to the new regime. Maj Hudson did not speak to him about allegations that had been received from former CF detainees. Footnote 1266 While in theatre, Maj Zybala followed, obviously from a distance, the ongoing proceedings in Federal Court, commenced by the Complainants. Footnote 1267 Unlike Maj Hudson, Maj Zybala’s troops did not come to him with concerns about their liability with respect to detainees, or about what was going on in Federal Court. If such discussions did occur, they were brief and “ en passant ”. Footnote 1268 In fact, the situation was reversed somewhat. He was the one who was personally a little worried about his potential liability in theatre. This caused him to read up on the applicable international law before he went into theatre, and to brief his troops during training on the importance of treating detainees well. Footnote 1269 His efforts to read up on the human rights situation and the legalities of the transfer regime were grounded in his personal concerns, but also in the general curiosity he felt a military person should have. Footnote 1270 While in theatre, his troops never advised him that detainees had expressed a fear of torture or mistreatment by the NDS if transferred. However, he confirmed Capt Bouchard’s testimony that at least two detainees communicated that they would have preferred to die rather than be transferred to the NDS because they did not have the money to bribe their way out of prison. He described the Afghan request to be killed as a typical Afghan reaction: Est ce que vous avez déjà été mis au courant que des détenus auraient dit, par exemple, qu’ils préféraient mourir que d’être transférés? Oui. Oui? Par qui? Ça aurait été par le Capitaine Bouchard, qui lui était présent très souvent aux transferts. Il m’a rapporté un incident en particulier dont je me souviens; c’est que deux détenus avaient été informés du fait qu’ils allaient être transférés au NDS , et avaient dit qu’ils préféraient mourir. Je vous dirais que c’est là une réaction assez typiquement afghane et que j’ai vue souvent à Kabul en 2004. C’est la réaction assez typique d’un Afghan, lorsque contrarié par un Occidental, surtout quand vous le traitez de menteur. La réaction souvent est « Bien si vous me croyez pas, tuez moi, tuez moi. J’exige d’être tué ». Mais là vous le traitez pas de menteur, là? Non, mais ce qui les achalait c’était pas le fait qu’ils avaient peur du NDS , mais qu’ils n’avaient pas l’argent nécessaire pour donner des pots de vin au NDS pour se faire libérer. Ce n’était pas une question de peur du NDS , mais nous avons tout simplement pas les fonds monétaires pour nous permettre les pots de vin. Est ce qu’ils vous ont dit ça? C’est exactement ce qu’ils ont dit à l’entrevue, au moment du transfert. Ils ont dit ça à M. Bouchard? Est ce qu’ils ont dit qu’ils avaient peur de mourir, ou qu’ils avaient pas l’argent? Non, ils ont dit qu’ils avaient pas l’argent. Ils préféraient la mort, mais n’avaient pas peur de mourir. Comme je vous dis, c’est une réaction typiquement afghane. [ unofficial translation ] Were you ever made aware that some detainees had supposedly said, for example, that they preferred to die rather than to be transferred? Yes. Yes? By whom? That would have been by Captain Bouchard, who attended transfers very often. He told me about an incident in particular that I remember; two detainees had been informed that they were going to be transferred to the NDS , and had said that they preferred to die. I would say that it’s a fairly typical Afghan reaction that I often saw in Kabul in 2004. It’s the fairly typical reaction of an Afghan when upset by a Westerner, especially when you call him a liar. Often the reaction is “ Well, if you don’t believe me, kill me, kill me. I demand to be killed ”. But there you’re not calling him a liar are you? No, but what bothered them was not the fact that they feared the NDS , but that they didn’t have the money to bribe the NDS to secure their release. It wasn’t a question of fear of the NDS , but we simply do not have the funds for bribes. Did they tell you that? It’s exactly what they said at the interview, at the time of transfer. They said that to Mr. Bouchard? Did they say that they were scared to die, or that they didn’t have the money? No, they said that they didn’t have the money. They preferred death, but were not scared of dying. Like I told you, it’s a typically Afghan reaction. Footnote 1271 Whether the interpretation of the Afghan detainees’ reactions was right or wrong, it appears both Maj Zybala and Capt Bouchard took from the detainees’ comments, not that they were frightened of NDS mistreatment or torture, but that they feared indefinite imprisonment due to an inability to bribe their way out of the Afghan prison system. Maj Zybala was sufficiently concerned about this question of detainees paying their way out of custody that he raised it within the command structure and with members of the Manley Panel when they came to Afghanistan to inquire into Canada’s future role. Footnote 1272 Maj Zybala was also receiving information during his time in theatre from Ms. Garwood-Filbert of Correctional Service Canada. She advised Maj Zybala the situation in the Afghan prisons was improving. Footnote 1273 The ROTO 4 TFPM was questioned in a general sense about the nature of his involvement with the decision making process for transfers, in particular with respect to assessments of risk to detainees post transfer. He informed the Commission he was, indeed, consulted on detainee issues, but only intermittently, and never on the question of the risks post transfer to detainees. Footnote 1274 In contrast to MGen Laroche’s perception, but in keeping with BGen Juneau’s evidence, Maj Zybala said no advisory team for transfers existed in any structured sense. He said each advisor with a role in detainee affairs – the MPs , intelligence, legal - would provide their input separately. He did have occasion to meet with his Commander personally about detainee matters, such as on one occasion where it was suggested a Canadian soldier mistreated a detainee, but he said no committee meetings occurred of the nature that General Laroche’s evidence might have led one to believe. Footnote 1275 Maj Zybala agreed if he became aware of mistreatment post transfer he would have an obligation to advise the General. Footnote 1276 That said, he did not become aware of any such information. Moreover, while he knew visits were occurring, including capacity building visits, he did not have access to any actual reports: Parce que généralement qu’est ce qui se passait, c’est que les visites étaient faites en conjonction avec ce qui s’appelait « capacity building visits », par le membre des Services correctionnels du Canada. Alors les équipes comportaient des gens de plusieurs sources: Services correctionnels, Affaires extérieures, GRC , etc. Et de quelle façon vous participiez ou vous étiez mis au courant de ce qui se passait ou des rapports? Je n’avais pas accès aux rapports. Vous n’aviez pas accès d’aucune façon? Non. [ unofficial translation ] Because typically what happened was that visits were made in conjunction with what was called “ capacity building visits ”, by the member of Correctional Services of CanadA. So the teams included people from many sources: Correctional Services, Foreign Affairs, RCMP , etc. And how did you participate or how were you made aware of what was happening or of the reports? I didn’t have access to the reports. You had no access at all? No. Footnote 1277 Maj Zybala knew, to some degree, the distribution of the site visit reports. It appears he deduced this understanding from his review of the DFAIT Standard Operating Procedures. He did not meet with any of the individuals to whom the reports were distributed, such as the POLAD and the deputy commander, to specifically discuss the results. They met, instead, at the weekly “ groupe d’ordres ” referred to by MGen Laroche in his testimony. These meetings rarely involved discussing detainee matters, and they never appear to have involved the discussion of the particular site visit reports. Footnote 1278 Moreover, no one ever told him directly about the site visits while he was in theatre, with the exception of the November 5, 2007 site visit. Maj Zybala did end up seeing some site visit reports, but only because he specifically sought them out on the internet, from the Complainants’ website. It is unclear whether he did this while in Afghanistan, or shortly after his return. In any event, he viewed those reports sometime in 2008, either towards the end of his rotation or immediately after his return from theatre. This was a point in time where transfers had long been stopped, and were not restarted until a series of ameliorative measures had been put in place. Footnote 1280 This exchange leaves the Commission with the impression Maj Zybala knew to some degree about this newspaper article, but either declined to look at it or placed no stock in it - it is difficult for the Commission to conclude one way or the other. In any event, it was not long after this article came out that Maj Zybala learned of the November 5 site visit and that transfers would be suspended. The November site visit was the only site visit that Maj Zybala learned of, prior to the November 2007 suspension of transfers. He did not view the site visit report per se but was made aware verbally of the results. Footnote 1281 This was the report in which DFAIT officials documented evidence from a detainee of physical scarring and found the implements of torture under a chair in the place indicated by the detainee. In addition, the detainee provided a verbal account of his torture. As described in the following passage, Maj Zybala learned about this site visit on November 6, 2007, in a meeting convened specifically for that purpose by Col Juneau, the acting Commander at the time. At this meeting, Col Juneau informed those present that transfers would be suspended: J’ai été mis au courant de cet incident le 6 de novembre. Spécifiquement, c’était une réunion qui a été appelée par le Colonel Juneau. Essentiellement, le Colonel Juneau a ouvert la réunion en disant qu’une visite de la part du Ministère des Affaires extérieures avait déterminé qu’il y avait des raisons fort probables de croire qu’un détenu avait été maltraité et qu’il cherchait un avis quant à la procédure à suivre. Footnote 1282 At that meeting with Col Juneau, Maj Zybala’s recollection was that the reasons for suspension were only discussed in the sense it was conveyed to him the allegations received on November 5, 2007 were credible. Colonel Juneau had decided to suspend and my impression my intervention was that it was effectively exactly what was required on our part to satisfy our obligations under the law, international humanitarian law. Footnote 1283 Maj Zybala was not privy to the discussions occurring prior to this meeting relating to the Commander and the Deputy Commander’s concerns that transfers might not be able to proceed. He was not privy to the draft letter dated November 4, 2007 in which those concerns were set out, where the conclusion was that the light was amber for future transfers, but that they could, for the time being, continue. He did not know there were concerns about the frequency of DFAIT visits prior to November 5, 2007. Nor was he aware of the subsequent, related correspondence. Footnote 1284 Thus, Maj Zybala did not view any of the site visit reports until he looked them up for himself on the internet, well past the point when transfers were stopped. He only heard directly about the results of the November 5, 2007 visit. He was not privy to the correspondence on the precariousness of the transfer process in October 2007, and he was not privy to discussions on this point that occurred with MGen Laroche and Col Juneau, and others. Nor did he view or hear about the details of the site visits that occurred prior to his rotation, at least not until he viewed certain site visits on the internet. Footnote 1285 He also heard nothing about any type of investigation conducted by DFAIT or others into the September allegations and the appropriateness of continued transfers. Footnote 1286 Maj Zybala explained why it did not surprise him the site visit reports were not shared with him. First, he thought the mandate to investigate any allegations received during site visits rested with DFAIT . Beyond that, he also knew of the phenomenon of compartmentalization in military affairs. From his point of view, it was to be expected these reports would be compartmentalized, and he felt he did not need to see them so long as someone was dealing with the site visits and any related follow-up activities required. Indeed, he did not think he would have been provided the reports, even if he had asked for them: Après quatre ans dans le renseignement, je savais que ce serait des rapports qui seraient excessivement restreints. [ unofficial translation ] After four years in that area, I knew that they would be excessively restricted reports. Footnote 1287 Returning to Maj Zybala’s involvement with the transfer decision process, he testified he either did not view the risk assessment matrix, or if he did, he saw it once at a point in time the Commission was not able to discern. Other than potentially one time, he viewed only the paper portion of the decision making process entitled the “ Commander’s Review ”. This portion did not contain any type of assessment of the post-transfer risk scenario. Footnote 1288 As noted, in the evidence from BGen Juneau, the Risk Assessment Matrix was only in development prior to November 5, 2007, and was not used until the start of transfers in late February/early March 2008. At that point in time, Maj Zybala was about to leave theatre. It was also a point in time where significant, new steps had been taken to improve the transfer process before starting up again. Maj Zybala’s confidence in the transfer regime, from a legal perspective, was also buttressed for him by the conclusions of the Manley Report. He was interviewed by the Panel members but did not recall speaking to them about post-transfer concerns, except perhaps indirectly. The report reached the conclusion that Canada’s handling of detainees met international standards. Maj Zybala read the report while in theatre, and would have viewed this conclusion around January or early February 2008. Footnote 1289 Major Zybala was generally well informed of the measures put in place before transfers recommenced at the end of February 2008. Footnote 1291 Maj Zybala never asked the NIS to investigate a question related to post-transfer treatment of detainees, nor did he ever hear the NIS was conducting such an inquiry. Footnote 1296 Throughout his time in theatre, Maj Zybala never formulated a reasonable suspicion his Commander acted illegally. He knew the Commander had legal advice, and he had confidence in the decision making process. Footnote 1297 Maj Zybala’s approach to what information one would require in order to establish an unacceptable risk of torture was a bit unclear to the Commission. He seemed to suggest during cross-examination by the Complainants, that reports of mistreatment from 20% of Canadian-transferred detainees would not represent a systemic problem in the Afghan prison system requiring that transfers be halted. He suggested the allegations would need somehow to be better substantiated before reaching such a conclusion, and the ratio would need to be up around 50%. He advised the Commission he acquired his particular analysis of the law from the UN ’s Committee Against Torture Reports and his legal advisor. Footnote 1298 Maj Zybala offered a possible explanation as to how his CEFCOM PM , Maj Laflamme, did not learn about the November 6, 2007 suspension of transfers until early December, by way of the Monthly SITREP . Maj Zybala’s evidence was that this was a particularly intense period of time for him, as commander of the MP company. During ROTO 4, the military police began to be involved in mentoring Afghan police at Police Sub-Stations beyond the wire and much closer to harm’s way. While outside the wire during this timeframe, one of his MP soldiers was seriously wounded, another sustained a less serious injury. His soldiers also had to deal with the trauma of the death by IED of members of the ANP . Maj Zybala also went outside the wire during the time immediately after the halt in transfers, returning only at a point in time when Maj Laflamme was on leave. Maj Zybala took his leave following Maj Laflamme’s return. He therefore does not recall ever having discussed the transfer stoppage with Maj Laflamme. Footnote 1299 He also could not recall a conversation with Maj Laflamme in November 2007 in which Maj Laflamme asked about rumours of detainee abuse, although he said it was highly probable that the conversation happened. Footnote 1300 The Complainants’ Submissions The Complainants submitted Maj Zybala bore responsibility for a number of acts or omissions which they attribute to him during the time period of this complaint. They believe he bore responsibility as one of the TFPM s at the time for the failure to investigate or inquire into whether past and ongoing transfer orders were legal. The Complainants argued in their written submission that Maj Zybala had knowledge of, or had the means of knowing, the following information which should have led him to conduct an investigation: Maj Zybala conducted his own research on human rights conditions in Afghanistan prior to deploying to Afghanistan. Maj Zybala read the Graeme Smith article and was aware of the allegations contained therein prior to deployment. Maj Zybala visited the AIHRC website and reviewed their reports prior to deployment. In so doing, he learned the AIHRC documented ongoing torture of detainees in Afghan prisons. Maj Zybala read the February 2007 complaint on one of the Complainants’ websites prior to deployment. Maj Zybala was informed by Maj Hudson there had been one suspension of transfers during ROTO 3, but was not informed the suspension resulted from report of post-transfer torture and abuse. Maj Zybala was aware the Complainants had begun a Federal Court proceeding involving allegations of detainee abuse. Maj Zybala did not have access to the DFAIT site visit reports, except for that of 5 November 2007. Maj Zybala first learned of the 5 November 2007 report in a meeting with Col Juneau, after which detainee transfers were suspended. Maj Zybala understood the suspension likely occurred because the 5 November 2007 report contained credible allegations of mistreatment. Maj Zybala continued to monitor the Federal Court proceedings while in Afghanistan, and upon his return to Canada, out of personal curiosity. Maj Zybala continued to visit the BCCLA website while in theatre, reading about new developments in the Federal Court proceedings and viewing some of the primary source documents posted there. Although the Comd JTF - Afg ’s detainee committee was disbanded during Maj Zybala’s time in Afghanistan, he retained custody and control over the detainee database and still had access to detainee information, and the written advice provided to the Comd JTF - Afg regarding transfer decisions, despite the creation of the position of “ detainee officer ” during ROTO 3. Maj Zybala conducted research on the requirements imposed by international law regarding the transfers of detainees. He believed Canada was prohibited from transferring detainees to a substantial risk of torture. Maj Zybala indicated he undertook his own research into international law and the state of human rights in Afghanistan because he felt there was a reasonable apprehension there may be questions about his own liability in transferring detainees. Maj Zybala believed such curiosity and prudence were part of being a military police officer. Footnote 1301 Based on this information the Complainants submit Maj Zybala should have made further inquiries or initiated an investigation into the legality of the transfer decisions. The Complainants submitted: Yet despite [ Maj Zybala’s] curiosity about his own potential liability, his awareness of allegations of detainee abuse, and general understanding of international legal obligations, Major Zybala never assessed the possibility that the [ Comd JTF - Afg ] may have acted illegally in ordering the transfer of detainees. Major Zybala never requested that NIS undertake an inquiry or investigation into historical or ongoing detainee transfers. He never assessed whether Brig. Gen . Laroche may have acted illegally in ordering the transfer of the individual interviewed for the November 5, 2007 report. Footnote 1302 The Complainants submit Maj Zybala’s concern regarding the treatment of detainees was focused on his own potential liability, and that “ …none of this concern played a role in how he carried out his policing duties as the commander of the Military Police in Afghanistan ”. Footnote 1303 Additionally, the Complainants submit Maj Zybala placed too much reliance in assuming the Comd JTF - Afg was receiving DFAIT reports and making the correct decision with respect to transfers, and he never tested the veracity of that assumption. The Complainants submitted: There is no evidence that either Major Zybala or any MPs under his command investigated or made any inquiries into the legality of any orders to transfer detainees to Afghan custody. Nor is there any evidence that he made recommendations to the NIS to investigate the legality of the transfers. He also gave no evidence showing that while he was in theatre, he was aware that any NIS investigations – or any investigations of any sort, for that matter – were taking place. As with Major Hudson before him, Major Zybala’s failure to make basic inquiries into the legality of the transfer orders is objectively unreasonable. Footnote 1304 Submissions on Behalf of Maj M. Zybala The submissions on behalf of Maj Zybala pointed to a number of factors which, it is said, demonstrate his actions were reasonable and he met all professional standards. Footnote 1305 Maj Zybala submitted, although he had read the AIHRC reports, he understood them to be generalised reports of torture and mistreatment in Afghan prisons. He argued those reports were “ …useful but not determinative of the situation in Afghan prisons… ”, and the situation in Afghanistan was constantly changing. Footnote 1306 Maj Zybala noted he had not read reports from DFAIT , the US State Department, or the UN High Commission for Human Rights but acknowledged having read the Graeme Smith article. Maj Zybala told the Commission he had conducted his own independent research into international law, and knew Canada had a responsibility “ … to treat detainees humanly and that Canada could not transfer a detainee if there was a belief that there is a substantial risk of torture. ” Footnote 1307 He acknowledged he was aware of the Supplementary Arrangement of 3 May 2007, and it was his belief the Supplementary Arrangement satisfied Canada’s international legal obligation. Similarly, Maj Zybala advised he was generally aware that DFAIT was conducting post-transfer monitoring visits, but he was usually not privy to these reports due to the doctrine of “ compartmentalization ”. Maj Zybala submitted he did become aware of allegations of mistreatment in November 2007 when transfers were suspended, and he read some redacted DFAIT reports on the Complainant’s website. Maj Zybala pointed out the DFAIT reports on the Complainant’s website had the date redacted, and said he would not know, conclusively, if they related or not to monitoring visits during his rotation. Maj Zybala also stated, although he “ […] had some general knowledge of general conditions in Afghan prisons and was aware of generalized allegations of mistreatment[…] ”, his meeting with Linda Garwood-Filbert of CSC alleviated any concerns, as the latter informed him prison conditions were improving. Footnote 1308 Similarly, it was Maj Zybala’s position his meeting with the Manley Panel and the release of its final report while he was in Afghanistan, affirmed his belief Canada was meeting its international legal obligations. Footnote 1309 Maj Zybala submitted he knew detainee transfers were suspended in November 2007 following receipt of the 5 November 2007 DFAIT site visit report. He acknowledged being present at the meeting where the decision to suspend transfers was made, but submitted he did not discuss the suspension of transfers with MWO ( ret’d ) Girard. As a result of attending that meeting, Maj Zybala claimed he was “ […] satisfied the [ Comd JTF - Afg ] was doing exactly what was required to satisfy Canada’s obligations under international law. ” Footnote 1310 Maj Zybala also submitted he was aware the Comd JTF - Afg insisted upon several conditions in order to resume transfers. In making transfer decisions, Maj Zybala was aware the Comd JTF - Afg had many sources of information and advice. Maj Zybala noted he never advised the Comd JTF - Afg on post-transfer treatment of detainees, and was confident the transfer decision process “ … was a good process that worked and that the Commander was making sound decisions. ” Footnote 1311 Regarding what would be required to commence an investigation into the transfer decisions of the Comd JTF - Afg , Maj Zybala said he would require “ a mandate and a reasonable suspicion a crime had been committed. ” Footnote 1312 The written submissions on behalf of Maj Zybala stated: In order to have a mandate to investigate, there must be a connection between the crime and the CF and the matter must not fall within the mandate of the NIS . [ Maj Zybala] never formed a reasonable suspicion that the Commander was making improper or illegal decisions; if he had, he would have requested that the NIS commence an investigation. Footnote 1313 Accordingly, Maj Zybala submitted he acted in a reasonable manner and that his actions met the professional standards expected of an MP . Conclusions Regarding Major M. Zybala Having considered the totality of the evidence and submissions, the Commission is not persuaded that Maj Zybala’s conduct failed to meet the standards expected of a police officer. We note in particular the following points in reaching this conclusion: Maj Zybala attempted to inform himself about the risks to detainees post transfer in Afghanistan and the international legal principles that were potentially applicable to the transfer of detainees, including the nature of Canadian responsibility for detainees post transfer. While the Commission may not agree with his personal assessment of the legal standard, and its potential application to the facts of this case, that is not determinative of whether he had a duty to investigate or ensure the investigation of his Commander. Maj Zybala was aware of his obligations pursuant to the Technical Directive in place during his rotation, and the TSO 321. In particular, he understood it was his duty to either investigate, or more likely, take steps to cause the investigation of any allegations of breaches of international law. Maj Zybala did not receive any direct allegations or complaints that the orders to transfer detainees generally, or to transfer any particular detainee, were or could be illegal. He knew about the substance of the complaint to this Commission in February 2007, the Federal Court process, and some of the media attention the detainee question received. The information he acquired through his own research showed him to be curious about, and aware of the risks of torture in Afghan prisons, but it is reasonable the general information he acquired did not lead him to form a suspicion about the particular legality of any of his Commander’s transfer orders. There was information about the post-transfer situation, such as the site visit reports from prior to his rotation and the site visits that occurred in September 2007, that Maj Zybala did not know. The fact that such information was not known to Maj Zybala is not due to personal failings on his part. Rather, it was a function of the “ siloing ” or “ compartmentalizing ” of information. The first indication Maj Zybala had during his rotation that a Canadian-transferred detainee had been abused was on November 6, 2007 when, in a meeting called for that purpose, his Deputy Commander informed him that a credible allegation of abuse had been received and that transfers would be suspended. Maj Zybala provided his opinion at that meeting that stopping transfers met Canada’s international legal obligations. Therefore, it was reasonable for him not to suspect that the chain of command was behaving illegally, as his personal observations pointed to the contrary conclusion. Maj Zybala was informed about the measures put in place before his Commander was willing to recommence transfers to the NDS , including the fact it took almost four months of activity and reform before the Commander was willing to transfer again. This, too, would have quelled suspicions about the legality of his Commander’s actions. Maj Zybala knew or believed his Commander was getting legal advice on the propriety of transfers, something that, on these facts, could reasonably have assuaged any concerns about the legality of the transfer orders. Finding #3: The Commission finds the allegations made by AIC and BCCLA against Major Michel Zybala in the June 12, 2008 complaint to be unsubstantiated. Viewing the evidence as a whole, the Commission finds no grounds to conclude Maj Zybala should have investigated his Task Force Commander while in theatre, or should have caused such an investigation to occur. The Commission finds his actions under the circumstance prevailing at the time met the standards of a reasonable police officer. 16.4 Master Warrant Officer ( ret’d ) Jean-Yves Girard MWO ( ret’d ) Jean-Yves Girard joined the Canadian Forces as an MP in 1975. He was first posted to Chatham, New Brunswick, then to a number of places in the province of Quebec. His career path touched on most aspects of MP related work, from investigations and patrol work to security. In 2005, he was posted to the Quebec City NIS detachment. This was his first point of entry into the National Investigation Service, where he remained until his retirement in February 2010. MWO ( ret’d ) Girard served overseas on four occasions, first in Cyprus in 1981, in Rwanda in 1994 and in the Golan Heights in 2001-2. His fourth deployment overseas was to Afghanistan during the timeframe of this complaint. He went over with ROTO 4, arriving on July 31, 2007, returning in early March 2008 after approximately one week of overlap with his predecessor, CWO Watson. Footnote 1314 MWO ( ret’d ) Girard also spent a month in Afghanistan at some point prior to his full rotation. Footnote 1315 Like CWO Watson, MWO ( ret’d ) Girard was the NIS detachment commander in the Afghan theatre. His detachment, including him, consisted of four NIS investigators, but given leave and vacations, his effective number was three. As NIS detachment commander, he was not under Maj Zybala’s command, and was independent of the chain of command in Afghanistan in the same sense described by CWO Watson. Like CWO Watson, MWO ( ret’d ) Girard had no contact whatsoever with the CEFCOM PM . His commander was the NIS commanding officer, LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick, but he explained his day to day contact up his chain of command was to Lt Utton and Maj Frei if he had questions about investigations. MWO ( ret’d ) Girard could also go to the regional military prosecutor for advice. Footnote 1316 MWO ( ret’d ) Girard was in contact with LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick before deploying, but did not receive any sort of briefing related to the time he would serve in Afghanistan. Instead, his contact with LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick related to his duties as NIS detachment commander for Quebec City. He had no contact whatsoever with Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore. Footnote 1317 MWO ( ret’d ) Girard had contact with Maj Zybala while in theatre, usually when he attended at Task Force Headquarters for investigations or administrative purposes, or to brief the Task Force Commander, MGen Laroche, on ongoing investigations. MWO ( ret’d ) Girard also briefed Maj Zybala on ongoing investigations where necessary. During these discussions with Maj Zybala and MGen Laroche, the discussion never turned to detainees. Footnote 1318 MWO ( ret’d ) Girard’s training was not identical to that received by Maj Zybala’s troops. One difference was he and his detachment spent a month in Toronto, witnessing autopsies of CF soldiers who had died in combat. This was meant to prepare them for the work they would have to do in Afghanistan, which included investigations into KIA s, escalations of force, and the resulting work in mortuary affairs: Ma job, entre autres, en tant que commandant du détachement là-bas c’était aussi – en plus des enquêtes, c’était d’identifier les soldats qui nous sont amenés à la morgue pour qu’on puisse informer les familles par la suite. [ unofficial translation ] A part of my job as detachment commander over there was – in addition to investigations, identifying the soldiers who were brought to the morgue so that we could then notify the families. Footnote 1319 His NIS detachment also did not receive training in detainee handling and the transfer process, in general, as this was not something they would be doing while in Afghanistan. Footnote 1320 Other than this obviously difficult work, MWO ( ret’d ) Girard described his NIS role in Afghanistan as being similar to his role in Canada. His detachment conducted investigations into serious and sensitive matters, as judged necessary, in addition to the theatre-specific work described above. Footnote 1321 He agreed investigations into mistreatment of detainees and related violations of international law would clearly fall within the NIS mandate to investigate. Footnote 1322 MWO ( ret’d ) Girard was shown the technical directive that would have been applicable to him while in theatre. Footnote 1323 He did not recall seeing it at any point in time, Footnote 1324 and could offer no explanation for how it was he was on the distribution list but did not recall seeing it. He said he might have read it, but simply could not recall. Footnote 1325 MWO ( ret’d ) Girard was referred specifically to the paragraph 11 requirement that the appropriate component of the Canadian military police “ shall ” investigate allegations or instances of violations of international law, the law of armed conflict, or mistreatment of detainees “ regardless of who was alleged to have carried out the mistreatment or when that mistreatment is thought to have occurred. ” Footnote 1326 After seeing this passage, MWO ( ret’d ) Girard still did not recall having seen or read the technical directive, even though he agreed it would have applied to him in theatre. Footnote 1327 MWO ( ret’d ) Girard said he did rely, for investigative guidance, on the Military Police Policy and Technical Procedures manual: Footnote 1328 On se fiait beaucoup avec ce qu’on a dans notre volume des techniques de la police militaire pour les enquêtes, ainsi de suite. [ unofficial translation ] We relied mainly on what was in the Military Police techniques manual for investigations, and so on. Initiating an Investigation. An MP investigation may be initiated whenever: an MP observes the commission of any criminal or service offence; an MP is in receipt of a complaint originating from any other person in which a criminal or service offence is alleged; at the request of a Commander or Commanding Officer; MP learns of an incident through an informant ( i.e. , local police, a witness, a confidential informant, an anonymous tip, etc. ); MP are tasked directly by DPM Police or CFNIS ; or an authority in the MP Technical Chain so directs. Footnote 1330 MWO ( ret’d ) Girard also stated in testimony it would be obligatory for him to investigate allegations of breaches of international law and mistreatment of detainees while in theatre. He further understood, as set out in paragraph 14 of the Technical Directive, the TFPM ’s role was to bring allegations of such breaches to his attention. However, he did not consider himself dependent on the TFPM for this type of information, and emphasized the fact the NIS was completely independent of the chain of command. Footnote 1331 MWO ( ret’d ) Girard did not view the TSO 321A, and, unlike CWO Watson, had no reason to come across it in his investigative work. Footnote 1332 MWO ( ret’d ) Girard knew little about the detainee process. Footnote 1367 The Complainants’ Submissions The Complainants submitted that MWO ( ret’d ) Girard bore responsibility for a number of acts or omissions which they attribute to him during the time period of this complaint. Conclusions Regarding MWO ( ret’d ) J-Y. Girard Having considered the totality of the evidence and submissions, the Commission is not persuaded that MWO ( ret’d ) Girard’s conduct failed to meet the standards expected of a police member. We note in particular the following points in reaching this conclusion: MWO ( ret’d ) Girard was either never provided with the Technical Directive applicable to his work while in theatre, or if it was provided to him, he apparently did not read it. The Commission believes the NIS detachment commander in theatre should have been proactive in finding and reading the Technical Directive applicable to his rotation. That said, MWO ( ret’d ) Girard nonetheless knew it was his obligation to investigate allegations of breaches of international law and mistreatment of detainees. Also, despite not having reviewed the Technical Directive, he used the MP Policy and Technical Procedures manual as his guidance for when to initiate an investigation. Despite not having read the Technical Directive, MWO ( ret’d ) Girard would have initiated an investigation into the Task Force Commander’s transfer decisions if he had received a complaint or if he had developed a reasonable suspicion that those decisions were illegal. It is relevant to take into account the stressful and difficult nature of the work MWO ( ret’d ) Girard had to do while in theatre, in particular, in the area of KIA s and mortuary affairs. Given the demands of this work, and the more reactive role of the NIS , it is reasonable that his acquired knowledge of the detainee process and the treatment of detainees post-transfer was minimal. It was also reasonable for him to rely, to a great degree, on others, such as the TFPM and the MP company, to bring information or concerns to him if they existed. No such concerns were brought to his attention. MWO ( ret’d ) Girard knew Canada’s detainees were to be handled in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, although he did not turn his mind, while in theatre, to Canada’s obligations towards detainees once transferred to the Afghan authorities. MWO ( ret’d ) Girard did not receive any direct allegations or complaints that the orders to transfer detainees generally, or to transfer any detainee in particular, were or could be illegal. He explained, despite his heavy and stressful workload, he would have investigated a complaint that the Commander was acting illegal. He considered it his duty to do so. MWO ( ret’d ) Girard did not have access to important information about the post-transfer process, such as the site visit reports produced during his rotation. He did not even know site visits were occurring, or transfers had been halted in November 2007. His lack of knowledge about these matters was reasonable given his workload, his mandate, and his assertion that, if an allegation were brought to his attention, he would have investigated. Finding #4: The Commission finds the allegations made by AIC and BCCLA against Master Warrant Officer ( ret’d ) Jean-Yves Girard in the June 12, 2008 complaint to be unsubstantiated. Viewing the evidence as a whole, the Commission finds no grounds to conclude that MWO ( ret’d ) Girard should have investigated the Task Force Commander while in theatre, or should have caused such an investigation to occur. The Commission finds his actions under the circumstance prevailing at the time met the standards of a reasonable police member. 16.5 Major Ron Gribble Maj Gribble joined the CF in 1976 as a non-commissioned member. He advanced through the ranks in the Princess Patricia’s Light Infantry, performing many duties. In 1990 he entered the non-commissioned member university program, received his degree and was commissioned into the military police in 1992. He trained in all functions of the MP and worked in patrol operations, investigations, and security operations. He graduated from the MP Academy in 1994 and served as the Deputy Wing Commander – Security MP in Winnipeg for several years. During this period he was deployed to Haiti where he served as the MP commanding officer with the Airfield Security Force. After a brief posting on his return, Maj Gribble was with Air Command Headquarters preparing the MP for operations support in such areas as the Disaster Assistance Response Team. He became the Deputy CO of an MP Platoon at CFB Edmonton and was immediately deployed to Bosnia as the Provost Marshal and CO of the MP Platoon. Upon his return he was the CO of the MP Garrison in Edmonton for approximately three years. He was then posted to the Provost Marshal’s office with 1 Area Support Group where he was mainly involved in operational planning and security oversight for various high security events such as the G8 summit in Kananaskis, where he was second in command. Following this Maj Gribble was posted as CO to 1 MP Platoon and was soon deployed for seven months to Kabul, Afghanistan as the TFPM in Camp Julien. Upon his return he was made part of the CFPM ’s staff at NDHQ where he was responsible for operational planning for deployed operations. Significantly, during this period of time he was responsible for drafting the Technical Directives which provided MPs with guidance during their earliest deployments in Kandahar. Footnote 1377 Maj Gribble returned to Edmonton as commandant of the CF Service Prison and Detention Barracks. While there, he was again deployed to Afghanistan as the TFPM and MP CO for ROTO 5. Following his tour on ROTO 5, Maj Gribble became the CO of 1 MP Unit and also served as the JTF Land Force Western Area Provost Marshal. In total, Maj Gribble served in seven overseas operational tours: Haiti, Bosnia, Egypt, twice in Cyprus, and his two tours in Afghanistan. Footnote 1378 Maj Gribble spent a brief period of time in Kandahar in preparation for ROTO 5 in November, 2007, after the cessation of transfers ordered by Col Juneau had occurred. Footnote 1379 He arrived in Afghanistan for the beginning of ROTO 5 on February 26, 2008 and returned on the 20 th or 21 st of September of that year. During his rotation he was “ double-hatted ”, being both the senior MP adviser to the Task Force Commander and the CO of the MP Company, with oversight of 100-plus MPs in theatre. His MP company performed a wide range of MP duties, including general policing, investigations and security, close support of dignitaries and visitors, close support outside the wire, aircraft security support, and, of course, detainee handling. He reported to the Task Force Commander and spoke to him or the deputy commander almost daily. He advised the Commission he was adequately resourced for the tasks at hand. Footnote 1380 Maj Gribble had no chain of command to the CFPM . He also had no command responsibility over the NIS detachment in Kandahar, although he was responsible for providing them with administrative and logistical support as well as referring investigations to them, and he would interact with NIS personnel on an almost daily basis. He fully understood the independent role of the NIS and indicated he would not hesitate to refer investigations which were outside his own company’s mandate to the NIS . He rejected the contention there was any conflict between his policing obligations and his command responsibilities; he was quite emphatic in stating if he thought his commander had committed an offence, he would refer the matter to the NIS . Footnote 1381 Maj Gribble reported in the technical chain to the CEFCOM Provost Marshal, initially Maj Martin Laflamme, and at the end of his tour Maj Greg Losier. According to him, any issues he referred up the technical chain would also be known to his command chain. He provided monthly SITREP s and would go through the CEFCOM PM if there were specific MP -related resource or personnel issues. The CEFCOM PM could then advise further up the technical chain to the CFPM office as well as champion those issues at CEFCOM . If he required technical direction he would normally consult with the CEFCOM PM although he could consult any MP staff member. Footnote 1382 Maj Gribble was directly involved in the detainee transfer process. If a detainee were being held, he was involved on a daily basis visiting the detention facility, reviewing daily reports, logs and information, and advising the Task Force Commander accordingly. Footnote 1383 In his capacity as adviser to the commander Maj Gribble saw his role as being a factual one – he and others passed information about the detainees on to the Task Force Commander, who then made a decision about release or transfer. Initially during his tour this occurred in writing, independently of other parties’ input into the Task Force Commander’s decision. Later in his tour, sometime late in July 2008, a detainee “ assessment board ” consisting of the TFPM , Chief of Intelligence, JAG , POLAD and others met to compile information and to advise on transfer issues. It was Maj Gribble’s understanding the assessment board was implemented primarily to compile information that would assist the NDS in their further investigations and prosecutions of the detainees, not as a result of post-transfer abuse issues. Footnote 1384 While to some extent he knew what information was being provided by others to the Task Force Commander, he testified it did not include information about the risk of post-transfer abuse and this was not, to his knowledge, something discussed at the assessment meetings. Maj Gribble did not see the written record of the Commander’s risk assessment, although he saw other portions of the transfer decision forms. He agreed if he had so desired he could have accessed the form while in theatre. Footnote 1385 He said he did not know the sources of information that would enter into the Commander’s risk assessment. Footnote 1386 He was aware the Commander made that assessment with the assistance of a team of advisers, including legal advisers. Footnote 1387 Maj Gribble understood the proper handling of detainee processing was considered one of the three most important strategic imperatives for the Task Force Commander. Footnote 1388 He was physically present with some of his key staff for detainee transfers. The POLAD , Ed Jager initially, then Jennie Cheng, was present to represent Canada, the detainee officer was there to represent the Commander, and there would usually be an interpreter present. According to Maj Gribble, NDS personnel were not present during the transfer process; however, he did have significant contact with the NDS . Maj Gribble felt they exhibited a good degree of professionalism, and mentioned the close coordination with them on detainee issues in his end of tour report. Footnote 1389 Maj Gribble also understood as an MP he had independent investigative obligations in addition to his operational obligations. He was trained in the laws of armed conflict and the Geneva Conventions and understood it would be unlawful for a commander to transfer a detainee to a substantial risk of torture or abuse. He had no specific training for investigating human rights abuse allegations, or allegations of unlawful orders by a commander. Maj Gribble’s view was that Canada as a power was responsible for addressing post-transfer abuse. He correctly understood it would be inappropriate to investigate his own commander, but he understood if he had suspicions about allegations of this nature or concerns about the legality of transfer orders he would be obliged to report them to the NIS . Footnote 1390 Maj Gribble indicated if an allegation of a criminal or service offence were brought to his attention which was credible and specific, he would be duty bound to initiate an investigation. If an untested allegation were encountered it would be appropriate to open a GO and conduct an assessment short of a full investigation to determine whether there was a credible basis to broaden the inquiry. He stressed he could not engage in “ fishing expeditions ” based on vague complaints or general discussions, nor could he investigate Afghan authorities themselves. He agreed information might come to his attention which was insufficient to cause a full investigation, but which would trigger an assessment as to whether a full investigation should occur. Footnote 1391 Maj Gribble did not feel it was within his purview to act as a monitor of the commander’s transfer orders or to assess their legality on an ongoing basis, absent a suspicion on his part that something illegal had occurred. Footnote 1392 Although he agreed a repeated pattern of transfers to abuse could lead him to question the legality of transfer orders, Footnote 1393 Maj Gribble qualified his role in investigating previous rotations as follows: […] But in the rotation prior to yours, there were transfer suspensions and there were, in November 2007, some serious and apparently corroborated allegations of abuse. You said you had a general awareness, but did you think that there was any need to investigate the circumstances under which that could have happened, in other words, to look at what they were thinking and why they would have transferred someone who ends up getting tortured, perhaps to find that they didn’t know or couldn’t know. But did you think of looking at that issue from your previous rotation and considering whether it should be investigated? The previous rotation was not my responsibility. I had plenty of work to keep me busy on the ground. I wasn’t looking at - - I actually was carrying some files from the previous roto, so I had plenty of work. So to look at something that was past post, no. Footnote 1394 Maj Gribble indicated he would have pursued such an investigation or referred it to the NIS if it had been brought to his attention. The Commission interprets this as meaning Maj Gribble would continue investigations initiated by his predecessor rotation or specifically brought to him, but he had no duty to independently examine the conduct of personnel during the previous rotation absent a specific complaint or referred file. Maj Gribble had no specific pre-deployment training concerning the human rights situation in Afghanistan. His experience in Kabul left him with the impression the human rights situation with security authorities in Afghanistan was generally positive, although his experience was limited to police and prisons in Kabul, not in Kandahar. Footnote 1395 He had not read the various DFAIT , UN , US State Department, Amnesty International or AIHRC reports on human rights generally in Afghanistan, and unlike Maj Hudson he had no direct interaction with personnel from the AIHRC and was not their point of contact for detainee notification issues. Maj Gribble had a working familiarity with the two Arrangements between Afghan and Canadian authorities for transfer of detainees Footnote 1396 but played no role in their drafting. He was cognizant of the monitoring provisions for DFAIT personnel but he had not seen any DFAIT C4 site visit reports, either earlier ones from Mr. Colvin or later ones which occurred prior to and during his rotation. During his rotation MPs did not attend or accompany DFAIT personnel on these visits. Footnote 1397 Despite the fact the TFPM is mentioned in it, Maj Gribble was not aware of the June 12, 2008 complaint to this Commission by AIC / BCCLA until after he had returned from his rotation. Initially in his testimony Maj Gribble indicated he was not familiar with the February 21, 2007 complaint in which MPs were accused of knowingly transferring detainees to torture or abuse. When reminded that he had been interviewed by MPCC investigators and the RCMP concerning the Attaran complaint and the February 21, 2007 complaint, Maj Gribble agreed he was likely advised of the substance of the complaint as early as March 2007. He pointed out he had been consulted about the command role of the CFPM , not about the substance of the complaints, and he was awaiting deployment so was not in a position to review media reports concerning this complaint. The Commission accepts that the focus of his earlier interviews was not concerning the substance of the allegations but the CFPM ’s role in relation to MP members in theatre. It follows that Maj Gribble would have been aware, due to this interview that the substance of the February 21, 2007 complaint was already being investigated by at least two organizations - the RCMP and the MPCC . Footnote 1398 Maj Gribble had read the April 23, 2007 Globe and Mail article by Graeme Smith outlining specific allegations of post-transfer abuse by Canadian-transferred detainees. He believes he read it around November 2007, a time which roughly coincided with his preparatory visit to Afghanistan during pre-deployment training. Maj Gribble was aware at the time he read the article there had been a suspension of detainee transfers, and he assumed it due to post-transfer abuse allegations. Footnote 1399 He had not read other newspaper articles in the Commission’s record. He expressed a general scepticism as to the reliability of media reports as in his experience they could be inaccurate or false. In his view, one would wish to verify the facts before proceeding based on such a report. Footnote 1400 Maj Gribble was unaware of the existence of the Operation Centipede investigations. He was not asked to provide assistance with this and was unaware of any other ongoing investigation into detainee abuse. Operation Centipede disclosed rumours among CF personnel concerning post-transfer abuse, but Maj Gribble was aware of no such rumours among CF members during his rotation. Nor did he hear any concerns expressed by MPs , such as had occurred during Maj Hudson’s rotation, concerning potential MP liability for such abuse. Footnote 1401 He was aware generally there had been allegations of detainee mistreatment in Afghan prisons, but he was aware of nothing specific. He was not familiar with the reasons delivered by the Federal Court in February 2008. Transfers of detainees resumed shortly after Maj Gribble’s deployment on ROTO 5 and continued throughout his rotation. He did not discuss the reasons for the suspension of transfers or the factors leading to resumption of transfers with either Maj Zybala or MGen Laroche. He knew in a general sense there was an increased frequency of DFAIT monitoring visits, more input from Correctional Service Canada and more interaction with the NDS concerning appropriate interviewing and interrogation techniques. Maj Gribble was asked about his understanding of the legal test for transfer of detainees. He was shown a draft letter of Col Juneau and a directive from LGen ( ret’d ) Gauthier to BGen Laroche (as he then was), neither of which he had seen previously. The following exchanges occurred: […] In the first paragraph, the second sentence, [ Col Juneau] says: The discretion to authorize the detainee transfer may only be exercised where there are not substantial grounds for believing that there is a real risk that a detainee would face subsequent abuse or mistreatment o[n] transfer to the NDS ” Is that test something that you were familiar with or at least in accordance with your understanding of your legal obligations and the legal obligations of commanders who might be subject of an investigation? In other words, is that something you concur with? I am not going to concur with something that wasn’t my responsibility. You would have to ask the commander. That was his responsibility. […] General Gauthier indicates in paragraph 24: The chain of command bears the potential liability should we become aware of torture or mistreatment following the transfer of detainees to Afghan authorities. For that reason, I am particularly concerned about the chain of command obligation to satisfy itself that the follow-up of transferred detainees is sufficiently robust. Then he outlines his expectations of a proactive engagement with DFAIT to ensure the monitoring and reporting and analysis is provided. My question is directed to you because as a police officer, you are a law enforcement officer, and this is a discussion, as is Colonel Juneau’s letter, about a legal obligation on the part of commanders. My question is: As a military police officer, what would your understanding be about the legal obligations of the commanders and the potential legal liability of the commanders for falling short on either of those two passages that we have described? Do you understand my question? It’s a very broad question. Could you narrow it? I’m not sure what you are getting at. Maybe I can draw an analogy. You are a police officer. You have to have some understanding of the law you are enforcing to effectively do your duties. Very much so. For instance, if you are a drug patrol officer, you have to know what drugs fall into a grey area that can be possessed, if you have a prescription, for instance. You have to have some kind of knowledge of the legal kind of framework. General Gauthier has described the potential for legal liability. Colonel Juneau has described his understanding of the legal obligations he has to make a transfer decision. I am just wondering whether you had an understanding at the time you were in theatre of those legal obligations on the part of the transferring commanders and, if you had an understanding of that, what your understanding of their obligations was, their legal obligations. Their obligations are covered quite clearly under international law and Canadian law. And what would they – And I was very confident that they understood their responsibilities and they were acting accordingly. They had a host of advisers and people doing different things for them, a lot more knowledge and in-depth knowledge than I had. So I was satisfied that they were operating within those parameters. Maj Gribble agreed if the Task Force Commander violated these precepts, and knowingly transferred a detainee to abuse it would be a violation of the law. He had no such concerns about the Task Force Commander’s decisions during his rotation. When asked about the previous rotations, Maj Gribble stated: I wasn’t there, so I can’t speak to that. My point being, you had no reason – I had no reason. There was nothing that was brought to my attention, no. You had no reason to suspect that they had violated the law even knowing that the transfers had ceased in November of 2007 because of a post transfer allegation of abuse. No, I had no concerns. I think your explanation was – and correct me if I am paraphrasing incorrectly. The measures that were put in place that you described, a number of measures, satisfied you that the transfers could be done without a risk of post transfer abuse, or without a significant risk. That’s correct. If you had been aware of the complaints levied, the P1 document that I showed you, the February 2007 letter from Amnesty International, or the letter from June 2008, if that had come to your attention that basically your commanders, your predecessor commander or your predecessor provost marshals were accused of unlawful activity, can you advise what your response would have been had those letters been brought to your attention in terms of your investigative duties? It would depend on where I was and what my capacity was. You are asking me to hypothesize on something that you haven’t – the ground work is there, so I really – if I am in a position of responsibility, I am going to address those concerns, yes. If you are the Task Force Provost Marshal, if the allegation is that your commanders have violated international law, I take it your primary responsibility would be at least to bring it to the attention of the NIS because that is within their jurisdiction. Yes. Footnote 1402 Maj Gribble’s position is that he had no information which would give him cause to suspect the Task Force Commander had unlawfully transferred detainees to a substantial risk of torture or abuse. From his perspective, when problems arose the suspensions were stopped, more robust measures were put into place, and assurances were obtained from Afghan authorities. The Task Force Commander was transferring with the assistance of a team of advisers, including legal advisers, and he had no reason to question whether the process was being followed in good faith. It did not enter his mind to question the integrity of the process or the good faith of the responsible parties. Maj Gribble reasonably noted the Commander does not have a crystal ball such that all possibility of harm could be eliminated. In his view, there were mechanisms in place to alleviate the risk, and if a credible allegation of abuse arose, Canada as a power had an obligation to respond. The Complainants’ Submissions The Complainants submit Maj Gribble bore responsibility for a number of acts or omissions which they attribute to him during the time period of this complaint. Generally, they say he bore responsibility as one of the TFPM s during the time in question, for the failure to investigate or inquire into whether past and ongoing transfer orders were legal. The Complainants argue in their written submission that Maj Gribble had, or had the means of knowing, the following information which reasonably should have led him to conduct an investigation: Maj Gribble was generally aware there were allegations of detainee abuse in Afghan prisons. Maj Gribble knew transfers were suspended in November 2007 and understood the suspension of transfers occurred because there were reports of post-transfer abuse. Maj Gribble read an online version of the Graeme Smith article. The Complainants took issue with Maj Gribble’s testimony as to his lack of knowledge. In their written submissions they stated: Unlike his predecessor TFPM s, Major Gribble testified that he had minimal awareness that there were concerns about post-transfer torture or abuse of detainees. He testified that he did not receive any background documents during his pre-deployment training that pertained to the human rights situation in Afghanistan. While in theatre, he claimed to have heard no discussion of potential post-transfer abuse, despite the fact that he started his rotation when transfers were just being resumed after the November 2007 suspension. In his conversations with the two DFAIT Political Advisors stations at KAF , he never discussed concerns about post-transfer abuse. He testified that he had no knowledge of the contents of DFAIT site visit reports; in fact, during his rotation, he was not even aware that DFAIT produced site visit reports. Despite having been interviewed by both MPCC investigators and the RCMP regarding the February 2007 Complaint, Major Gribble denied that he was aware of the substance of the Complaint. Footnote 1403 The Complainants also took issue with the fact Maj Gribble testified initially he did not know the legal test for transferring detainees to a foreign power, despite the fact he received pre-deployment training on the law of armed conflict in the “ detainee package ”. The Complainants submitted Maj Gribble “ refused ” to articulate his understanding of the Comd JTF - Afg ’s legal obligations when ordering a detainee transfer when testifying. Footnote 1404 However, the Complainants noted Maj Gribble did acknowledge under cross-examination he understood it would be impermissible to transfer a detainee to a substantial risk of torture, and such an order would violate the laws of armed conflict. However, the Complainants submit Maj Gribble failed to initiate an investigation because he mistakenly believed the decisions in the previous rotations were not his responsibility. The fact that potentially illegal conduct took place during a prior rotation was no bar to his launching an investigation, but as Major Gribble informed this Commission: The previous rotation was not my responsibility. I had plenty of work to keep me busy on the ground. I wasn’t looking at – I actually was carrying some files from the previous roto, so I have plenty of work. So to look at something that was past post, no. Given the seriousness of the issues at stake – violations of the law of armed conflict and the universal prohibition against torture – “ being busy ” is no excuse for failing to make basic inquiries. Footnote 1405 The Complainants also noted in their submissions Maj Gribble did not attempt to rely on previous investigations, such as Operation Centipede, to justify his failure to investigate, as Maj Gribble testified he was not aware of any investigations into the transfer decisions. The Complainants also submitted Maj Gribble assumed the transfer orders were legal, and took issue with the fact Maj Gribble did not attempt to verify his assumptions. The Complainants relied on these points as providing further evidence Maj Gribble was unreasonable in his responsibilities as an MP and the TFPM . The Complainants concluded: Major Gribble never sought advice along the technical chain of command as to whether past orders to transfer required an investigation, nor did he ever express any concern up the technical chain, either. He gave no evidence that he or any MP under his command ever investigated or inquired into the legality of past orders to transfer. He never asked NIS to investigate or inquire into whether past orders to transfer detainees were unlawful. Given that Major Gribble was aware of reports of post-transfer torture and that transfers had to be halted entirely due to concerns over NDS treatment of CF -transferred detainees, his failure to investigate was also objectively unreasonable. Footnote 1406 Submissions on Behalf of Maj R. Gribble The submissions made on behalf of Maj Gribble point to a number of factors which, it is said, demonstrate his actions were reasonable and he met all professional standards. Footnote 1407 Maj Gribble submitted he understood Canada was responsible to ensure detainees were not mistreated, and the Government of Canada negotiated an arrangement with the Government of Afghanistan. According to the written submissions on behalf of Maj Gribble, “ post-transfer treatment of detainees was not within his area of responsibility. ” Footnote 1408 Maj Gribble submitted prior to arriving in Afghanistan, he became aware detainee transfers had been suspended by the Comd JTF - Afg. Maj Gribble also noted transfers of detainees resumed shortly after his arrival in theatre. The written submissions on behalf of Maj Gribble stated: [h]e was aware that transfers resumed based on an increased capacity to visit detainees more frequently, support to the system through Correctional Services Canada and training provided by civilian police to NDS investigators on how to properly investigate, interrogate or interview subjects. He believed that the Government of Canada had taken action, implemented changes and received reassurances from the Government of Afghanistan before the transfers continued. Footnote 1409 Maj Gribble said he was not aware of the previous complaints relating to detainees before this Commission; nor did he read DFAIT human rights reports or other international human rights reports. Instead, Maj Gribble stated he relied upon his previous experience in Afghanistan during 2004 dealing with Afghan police and conditions in Afghan prisons, and that generally these experiences had been positive. Footnote 1410 Maj Gribble told the Commission he had read the Graeme Smith newspaper article in late 2007, but did not believe the newspaper articles alleging mistreatment of detainees contained allegations a CF member had done something unlawful. As such, Maj Gribble submitted he lacked sufficient basis to initiate an investigation. Maj Gribble also said it was “ … not possible for [him] to investigate allegations regarding previous rotations given that none of the people who would be allegedly involved in a crime were in theatre. ” Similarly, Maj Gribble believed it was beyond his jurisdiction to investigate allegations of abuse of Canadian-transferred detainees at the hands of Afghan authorities. Moreover, Maj Gribble stated allegations of detainee abuse by Afghan authorities “ … would not be a sufficient basis to investigate the Task Force Commander. ” Similarly, Maj Gribble submitted he never received a complaint or allegation the Comd JTF - Afg had violated the laws of armed conflict or international law; but if he had, he said he would have referred the matter to the NIS to investigate. Footnote 1411 Maj Gribble noted he attended every transfer of detainees that occurred during his rotation, and emphasized NDS demonstrated professionalism and concern for the condition of detainees. Footnote 1412 He also said, during his tenure as TFPM , the decision to transfer detainees was an informal paper process and he was responsible for advising the Comd JTF - Afg on whether to transfer, release or hold detainees. Maj Gribble stated he was not privy to information relating to treatment of detainees post-transfer, such as the DFAIT site visit reports, Footnote 1413 nor did he receive a copy of the Commander’s risk assessment. Footnote 1414 Maj Gribble also submitted it was not his role to verify the Comd JTF - Afg was giving orders that were in accordance with the law, and said this would properly be the role of the JAG officer providing the Commander with legal advice. Counsel for Maj Gribble submitted: It was not Maj Gribble’s role to ensure that the Commanders’ orders were in accordance with the law; the Commander had a legal advisor who filled that role. Maj Gribble had full confidence in the propriety of the decisions the Commander was making and believed that he was receiving relevant information and advice to enable him to make those decisions. Footnote 1415 [...] Major Gribble was confident that the Commanders understood their responsibilities and that they had a host of advisors, including legal advisors, to assist them in making the decision to transfer. He had no reason to suspect that the Commanders had violated the law. Maj Gribble would have no issue or concern with laying a complaint about anyone in his chain of command, where warranted. Footnote 1416 Accordingly, Maj Gribble submitted, in all the circumstances, he acted in a reasonable manner and his actions met all professional standards expected of an MP . Conclusions Regarding Maj R. Gribble Having considered the totality of the evidence and submissions, the Commission is not persuaded that Maj Gribble’s conduct failed to meet the standards expected of a police officer. We note in particular the following points in reaching this conclusion: Maj Gribble demonstrated knowledge and awareness of the international legal principles that were potentially applicable to the illegal transfer of detainees, including the nature of Canadian responsibility for detainees post transfer. Maj Gribble was also aware of his obligations pursuant to the Technical Directive in place during his rotation, and the TSO 321. In particular, he understood it was his duty to either investigate, or more likely, ensure the investigation of any allegations of breaches of international law. Maj Gribble did not receive any direct allegations or complaints that the orders to transfer detainees generally, or to transfer any detainee in particular, were or could be illegal. He only had some knowledge of the substance of the complaint to this Commission in February 2007, the Federal Court injunction process, and the media attention the detainee question received. He reasonably balanced these concerns against the measures he observed his Commander and the Government taking to guard against potential mistreatment following transfer, such as the suspension of transfers until a more robust monitoring regime was in place. The Commission concludes Maj Gribble took his duties as TFPM seriously. However, the Commission did have concerns with Maj Gribble’s comments that previous rotations were not his responsibility, as such comments may suggest he construed his duties too narrowly. In the Commission’s view, MPs have a broader obligation as police officers to be alert to potential commission of offences regardless of their timing and how the information of a potential offence is obtained. MPs should be open to the prospect of having to examine or inform themselves about events from previous rotations whether or not they have been specifically assigned this task. That being said, there was insufficient information available to Maj Gribble to obligate him to investigate conduct from the previous rotation. However, had sufficient information of any offence committed on the previous rotations come to his attention, he would have been obligated to respond to it by initiating an assessment or for full investigation by either his own company or the NIS , depending on circumstances. It was reasonable that Maj Gribble did not form a suspicion whether his Task Force Commander was transferring to a known and unacceptable risk of torture. It was reasonable for Maj Gribble to consider that his Commander’s behaviour demonstrated a willingness to stop transfers where necessary, despite the operational obstacles this created.
