Maj Gribble was generally aware of information indicating torture was a serious concern in Afghanistan, from sources such as his general understanding of the February 21, 2007 complaint to this Commission, the fact transfers had been suspended during the previous rotation, and the media attention given to the detainee transfer question, particularly Graeme Smith’s Globe and Mail article from April 2007. Maj Gribble had, on the other hand, information that transfers had been suspended when the Commander thought the risk warranted it, he was aware that DFAIT was monitoring detainees post transfer, and he was of the belief remedial measures were put into place prior to the resumption of transfers in early 2008. These factors would reasonably have militated against the development of a suspicion that transfers were being made illegally. Maj Gribble did not have access to important information about the post-transfer process, such as the site visit reports from May onwards, other C4 traffic, the legal opinions the Commander was receiving, and any discussions his Commander may have been having with respect to post-transfer risk assessment. The fact that Maj Gribble did not have access to this information is not due to personal failings on his part, but rather to factors discussed previously. Maj Gribble reasonably assumed his Commander was getting legal advice on the propriety of transfers. In the absence of any information to the contrary, and given his knowledge of CF operations and command resources, it was not unreasonable for him to expect that his Commander would be receiving appropriate advice as to the Commander’s own liabilities in regards to detainee transfers. Finding #5: The Commission finds the allegations made by AIC and BCCLA against Major Ron Gribble in the June 12, 2008 complaint to be unsubstantiated. Viewing the evidence as a whole, the Commission finds no grounds to conclude Maj Gribble should have investigated the Task Force Commander while in theatre, or should have caused such an investigation to occur. The Commission finds his actions under the circumstances prevailing at the time met the standards of a reasonable police officer. 16.6 Major John Kirschner Maj Kirschner joined the CF on January 4, 1983 as an electronics technician, and in 1986 changed occupations to become an MP . On completing basic MP training Maj Kirschner was posted to 1 MP Platoon in Calgary serving as a field MP and a patrolman on base. In 1989 he was posted to Lahr, Germany as a patrolman, criminal investigator, and shift commander for a patrol crew. In 1991 while on his German deployment he was deployed to support Canada’s contribution to the first Gulf War, Operation SCIMITAR. In 1994 Maj Kirschner was posted to the Militia Training and Support Centre in Meaford for 11 months. He was promoted to sergeant and transferred to Ottawa where he was employed in surveillance with the Special Investigations Unit, and later employed by the NIS . In 1998 Maj Kirschner was deployed to Bosnia as the NIS detachment commander in Coralici. On return he was posted to the NIS Sensitive Investigation Unit as a sergeant, investigating allegations concerning senior public servants and higher ranking officers. In 2000 Maj Kirschner was selected for commissioning from the non-commissioned ranks and was appointed lieutenant. After language training he was posted to the NIS as the officer in charge of the Criminal Intelligence Program. In 2002 he was posted to CFB Halifax as the deputy naval provost marshal of the MP detachment. Three years later he was placed in command of the Halifax NIS detachment, where he remained until his pre-deployment training and deployment as NIS detachment commander in Kandahar. Footnote 1417 Maj Kirschner was the Commanding Officer of the CFNIS detachment in Kandahar for ROTO 5, from 15 February to August 2008. This followed approximately 8.5 months of pre-deployment training. He reported to the Deputy CO of the NIS , who at the time was Maj Frei, with LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick being next up his chain of command. Maj Kirschner had no formal command relationship with non- MP personnel in Kandahar, but had a briefing protocol wherein commanders were kept apprised of investigations in a perfunctory manner insofar as they might impact operations. Maj Kirschner thus had met with MGen Laroche and his successor, but was not under their command. Maj Kirschner had regular contact with the ROTO 5 TFPM , Maj Gribble and received administrative support from the MP Company commanded by him. Maj Gribble and Maj Kirschner did not have a mutual reporting or command relationship, but they shared activities and daily happenings since Maj Gribble was the senior technical adviser to the commander. In Maj Kirschner’s words, he did not report to Maj Gribble, but kept him apprised of what the NIS were doing. Footnote 1418 Other than some brief contact during a Site Inspection Visit, Maj Kirschner had no contact with the CFPM Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore. He neither reported to nor received direction from Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore during his rotation, and his contact with the CEFCOM PM was limited to discussions unrelated to detainee issues. Maj Kirschner said none of the TFPM , CEFCOM PM or any other party impeded the independent investigative duties of the NIS during his rotation, and he in fact described his communications and relationship with the TFPM as “ stellar ”. Footnote 1419 Maj Kirschner expressed confidence in the guidance he was receiving from his chain of command and felt clear and confident about what his duties and responsibilities were. Footnote 1420 Under Maj Kirschner the NIS detachment consisted of a total of four MP personnel. With leave entitlements, for the better part of his rotation the detachment consisted of three MPs including himself, and he said they were “ overwhelmed ”, with a workload including 36 conducted and completed major crime investigations during his deployment. The NIS in theatre was not only responsible for investigating escalations of force and KIA s but also dealt with the undoubtedly difficult and “ thankless ” tasks of mortuary affairs and repatriation of fallen CF soldiers that flowed from these incidents. Footnote 1421 Maj Kirschner did not determine the number of personnel he commanded, but did request additional support through CEFCOM with the assistance of LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick. Logistically, it is difficult to deploy additional personnel because of the length of pre-deployment training although in exceptional situations untrained MPs can be deployed. Unfortunately, with the ceiling on the total number of CF members deployed to Afghanistan and the logistic impediments to increasing the allotment with the NIS , Maj Kirschner’s requests for more personnel were unfulfilled. Footnote 1422 Maj Kirschner was not familiar with the February, 2007 AIC / BCCLA complaint against the military police, nor had he seen the June 12, 2008 complaint underlying this hearing despite the fact it was an allegation against MPs and the NIS in Afghanistan filed during his tenure there. He agreed this would be subject matter for the NIS to investigate. The Commission notes that as a potential subject of the complaint, Maj Kirschner would not be in a position to investigate the issues in the complaint after it had been filed because, in essence, he would have been placed in a clear position of conflict investigating his own conduct. Footnote 1423 Maj Kirschner indicated the detainee issue was “ omnipresent ” during his tour. His pre-deployment training dealt with detainee handling, but not with assessing detainee transfer risks; his NIS commanders did advise him to remain alert to detainee abuse issues. Maj Kirschner was not familiar with general reports from DFAIT , or public reports from the UN , the AIHRC or other organizations, concerning the human rights situation in Afghanistan and he was not exposed to this information in pre-deployment training. Footnote 1424 Maj Kirschner had not specifically read the newspaper accounts of alleged abuse, but was aware through the media of complaints about detainee abuse which included allegations of post-transfer torture. Because the allegations dealt with post-transfer abuse, they did not hold much interest for him since investigating them would be, in his view, outside his jurisdiction unless there was a joint venture with Afghan authorities. Moreover, his office was not tasked with undertaking any such investigation. Maj Kirschner was aware, through the media, implements of torture had been found in the NDS detention facility and advised his troops to be alert to signs of abuse when they had occasion to visit the facility in March, 2008. Since allegations of CF abuse of detainees were also known to him through the media, he encouraged his NIS members to distance themselves from the KAF detention facility in case they were called upon to investigate any issues with detainees arising from it. Footnote 1425 Maj Kirschner was aware transfers were suspended when he arrived in theatre and inferred this was due to post-transfer abuse allegations arising in November 2007. He was unaware of the previous transfer suspensions. Maj Kirschner had no specific discussions with MWO ( ret’d ) Girard about detainee transfer suspensions because detainee transfers were not the NIS ’s responsibility. Maj Kirschner was not aware there were Federal Court proceedings concerning detainee transfers until the Commission’s investigation into this matter began, and he was unaware of the reports from DFAIT either prior to or during his rotation, although he assumed they would be making reports of their site visits. Maj Kirschner was aware of, but not involved in, the investigations collected into Operation Centipede – they were classified investigations and the details were only shared on a “ need to know ” basis. Similarly, he was aware of Insp Gfellner’s investigation into Professor Attaran’s complaint about possible CF abuse of detainees and failure to investigate by MPs (Operation Camel Spider) but was not informed of its subject matter. Footnote 1426 Maj Kirschner’s detachment was involved in investigations concerning detainee abuse, but it was alleged abuse by CF members, and not post-transfer abuse. When his subordinates were sent to the NDS detention facility to interview the detainees in question, Maj Kirschner asked them to look out for signs of post-transfer abuse simply because detainee abuse issues were of international significance. They saw no such signs of abuse. Maj Kirschner never heard negative rumours about the NDS ; to the contrary, at the end of the moratorium on transfers there was a confidence conveyed about the NDS . Maj Kirschner had no concerns about their conduct based on what he heard from his subordinates who had met with the NDS . Footnote 1427 Maj Kirschner was aware that CF personnel had obligations towards detainees under international law and under the applicable TSO which included treatment in accordance with the provisions of the Geneva Conventions. While he did not know Canada had certain post-transfer legal obligations with respect to humane post-transfer treatment, he understood Canada did have a monitoring regime in place to ensure this was the case, and he was satisfied this was in fact occurring. His CF training included some measure of understanding of the laws of armed conflict and the Conventions, and he believed all CF members must have knowledge of and adhere to these legal precepts. He, as a member of the NIS , had access to regional military prosecutors to answer any questions concerning international law principles if he had required such guidance, but he did not feel any need to consult while he was in theatre. Maj Kirschner was never given legal instruction on the test for lawful transfer of detainees, but noted if an investigation had been initiated one of the steps in planning was to outline the essential elements to be investigated, and legal counsel could be consulted on this. He believed Canada’s agreements with Afghan authorities mandated that the latter, not CF members, were obliged to investigate abuse at the hands of Afghans. Maj Kirschner noted he could only investigate persons who fell under MP jurisdiction. He believed he had no peace officer power to compel information from DFAIT personnel and indicated legal counsel might be sought if a writ or warrant was required for an investigation. Footnote 1428 Maj Kirschner agreed he would have jurisdiction to investigate a commander if he suspected the commander had committed an offence with respect to a transfer decision. The test for self-initiating an investigation would be a “ reasonable suspicion ” of wrongdoing, less than reasonable and probable grounds. He noted that for suspicion of illegal transfer orders, this would entail having some knowledge of the commander’s state of mind, and given what he saw in theatre, he believed there was no cause to investigate. From Maj Kirschner’s perspective, when detainee abuse allegations had arisen, the Commander had suspended transfers. He was not informed of the conditions which had changed to permit the resumption of transfers, but he assumed something significant had been done to satisfy the Commander and Government of Canada that they could be safely resumed. Even if he had seen the site visit reports outlining torture or abuse, they would speak to the conditions after transfer but not directly to the commander’s state of mind when making the transfer. Maj Kirschner was in theatre during the latter portion of MGen Laroche’s tenure as Commander and thus in principle could have inquired directly as to his state of mind, but at no time was Maj Kirschner asked to review or investigate the legality of MGen Laroche’s transfer orders, nor did he believe he independently had cause to do so. Footnote 1429 Maj Kirschner agreed investigation of allegations of this nature would be mandatory under the Technical Directives and MP policy. In the Commission’s view, Maj Kirschner is not the kind of MP to shy away from his investigative duties. His approach to policing could fairly be described as proactive or, as he described it, tenacious – in appropriate circumstances he would consider it appropriate to investigate or take steps such as initiating surveillance based on rumours or newspaper accounts of uncertain veracity in order to substantiate or discount the need for further investigation or prosecution. Maj Kirschner simply did not feel that even such a minimal degree of suspicion existed with respect to the legality of the Commanders’ orders; to the contrary, the Commander’s conduct suggested to Maj Kirschner that appropriate precautions were being taken. He did not feel his obligations as an investigator went so far as to require him to play an ongoing oversight role with respect to Commanders’ decisions. Footnote 1430 The Complainants’ Submissions The Complainants submit Maj Kirschner bore responsibility for a number of acts or omissions which they attributed to him during the time period of this complaint. Maj Kirschner served under BGen Laroche and BGen Thompson.During this rotation, Maj Gribble was the JTF -A TFPM . During his pre-deployment training, Maj Kirschner was not briefed about the human rights situation in Afghanistan or the post-transfer risk of abuse. The Complainants submit Maj Kirschner stated he had not been aware of theFebruary 2007 Complaint while he was in theatre. Footnote 1431 T he Globe and Mail , but did read or hear other media reports about detainee mistreatment treatment byAfghan authorities post-transfer. They submit in his testimony before the Commission, Maj Kirschner could not recall who authored, published or transmitted those media reports. Maj Kirschner was also unaware of a proceeding in Federal Court seeking to halt detainee transfers or human rights reports from theAIHRC, UNHCR , Amnesty International and the U.S. Department of State. Footnote 1432 Maj Kirschner was aware Canada had an agreement in place with Afghanistan forvisitation rights to their detention facilities. When he arrived in theatre, he understood DFAIT was conducting site visits in order to interview prisoners who had been transferred from Canadian custody. The Complainants submitted he was aware at least one DFAIT site visit uncovering an allegation of torture. They submit Maj Kirschner never sought to obtain copies of the reports and never questioned any DFAIT officials about the reports. Footnote 1433 The Complainants note that Maj Kirschner testified he was aware of general and specific allegations of post-transfer torture and mistreatment. He told the Commission the detainee issue was “ omnipresent ” during his deployment and it was something of which he was “ very cognizant. ” Footnote 1434 He was also aware of specific allegations of post-transfer torture and was aware that during the previous rotation someone had observed a chair with instruments of torture under it. Maj Kirschner told the Commission he believed this discovery is what prompted the suspension of the transfers. Footnote 1435 Independently of any other investigation, Maj Kirschner deployed investigators around March 2008 to an Afghan prison to collect evidence for an investigation into complaints he had received about MPs who purportedly had mistreated detainees in their custody. According to the Complainants, this suggests he perceived a genuine risk of torture or abuse which they believe should have spurred him to look at the legality of the transfer orders. The Complainants submitted Maj Kirschner gave mixed messages about his understanding of the CF ’s obligations regarding detainee post-transfer abuse under international and domestic law. At one point, Maj Kirschner told the Commission he would be required to investigate pursuant to the technical directive if detainees were knowingly transferred to a risk of torture. However, at a later point, Maj Kirschnerindicated a lack of understanding when questioned by counsel for the Complainants about post-transfer obligations under the Geneva Conventions. Footnote 1436 The Complainants alleged Maj Kirschner’s understanding of the law could not be ascertained with certainty. As well, they were left with “ a troubling impression ” Maj Kirschner did not have a correct understanding of theJTF-A Commander’s legal obligations. Footnote 1437 Counsel for the Complainants submitted: Maj Kirschner did not investigate thelegality of the Commander’s transfer orders and the matter of post-transfer torture. Maj Kirschner did not collect any evidence. Maj Kirschner did not interviewany witnesses. The Complainants submitted Maj Kirschner offered several reasons for his failure to investigate. First, Maj Kirschner testified he was extremely busy and had a limited ability to be curious about such matters. Second, Maj Kirschner believed only the Afghans had jurisdiction to investigate incidents that occurred outside Canadian custody. They stated Maj Kirschner said it was not part of his job to conduct investigations of any abuse suffered by a detainee under Afghan custody. The Complainants submitted Maj Kirschnersimply had confidence in the JTF -A Commander and trusted his judgment when he himself believed there to be a risk of post-transfer abuse. Footnote 1438 For these reasons, the Complainants alleged that Maj Kirschner breached a duty to investigate his Task Force Commander while in theatre. Accordingly, it was their view he breached the professional standard expected of an MP in his position. Submissions on Behalf of Maj J. Kirschner Footnote 1439 The submissions made on behalf of Maj Kirschner point to a number of factors which are said to demonstrate his actions were reasonable and he met all professional standards. Maj Kirschner worked in an office of four people responsible for major criminal investigation and mortuary affairs, which involved the processing and repatriation of human remains of Canadian soldiers. During his rotation, the detachment conducted 36 major crimes investigations. It was not his duty or responsibility to act as a “ watchdog for the Commander’s transfer orders ”. Footnote 1440 Maj Kirschner’s position is that he was very aware of the detainee issue when he deployed. The moratorium on transfers was in place when he arrived in theatre, which suggested to him the process was working and the Commander was exercising due diligence to ensure he was protecting those persons who earlier fell under his responsibility. Footnote 1441 In the course of an ongoing investigation involving CF personnel, Maj Kirschner dispatched two investigators to interview detainees in Afghan prisons. Maj Kirschner instructed the investigators to check for signs of mistreatment. Following a private interview with no NDS personnel present, Maj Kirschner was told the detainees said they were being well treated. This led him to conclude Canadian-transferred detainees were being treated satisfactorily. Maj Kirschner testified investigators were sent outside the wire normally only in cases where there was substantial and significant cause. Most often, this involved investigating a fatality. The risk to CF personnel in going outside the wire to investigate was so great it could not be undertaken unless there were clear grounds to do so. The NIS detachment and Maj Kirschner had no involvement in the detainee transfer process and received no information regarding that process or post-transfer monitoring reports. In fact, Maj Kirschner submitted he explicitly directed MPs under his command to distance themselves from anything to do with the detention facility because it would be their responsibility to investigate MPs for any allegations of mistreatment of detainees. Footnote 1442 The NIS detachment had no involvement with ongoing detainee investigations such as Operation Centipede. Maj Kirschner submitted he was unaware of specific newspaper reports or generalized human rights reports, but was generally aware of allegations of abuse regarding detainees transferred to Afghan authorities. He received no specific complaints or allegations which would spur an investigation. Maj Kirschner noted he was not provided copies of the DFAIT monitoring reports nor was he briefed on their contents. He had no occasion to meet anybody from the NDS . He was aware of some of the content of the reports through open source media reports and did not see a need to request the reports. In fact, there were no reports of allegations of mistreatment by Canadian-transferred detainees following the resumption of transfers during Maj Kirschner’s rotation. In order to self-initiate an investigation into the Commander’s decision to transfer detainees, Maj Kirschner submitted he would have needed some reasonable suspicion of wrongdoing. Maj Kirschner understood dedicated NIS legal counsel could advise him if he had any questions about legal issues related to the transfer of detainees. Footnote 1443 Maj Kirschner speculated he might, in some cases, undertake further inquiries as a result of a newspaper article or rumour, but would not necessarily commence an investigation on that basis alone. Maj Kirschner did not believe it was his responsibility to conduct investigations into the treatment of Afghan detainees under Afghan custody, based on his understanding of his mandate, which was limited to investigating Canadians, and the agreements negotiated between Canada and the Government of Afghanistan. Maj Kirschner testified he never formed a reasonable suspicion during his time in Afghanistan the Task Force Commander had breached the law of armed conflict or international law. On the basis of his understanding of the mandate and the information available to him, it was submitted that Maj Kirschner acted reasonably and appropriately in carrying out his policing mandate. No complaints or allegations were ever received by him regarding the legality of the command decisions to transfer detainees. Based on his experience as an MP and member of the CF deployed in operations, it was reasonable he had full confidence in the command decision-making process. Maj Kirschner had no reason to doubt the appropriateness of decisions made by senior commanders. In conclusion, Maj Kirschner’s position was that he had not failed to investigate any allegation or set of facts which required investigation. Conclusions Regarding Maj J. Kirschner Having considered the totality of the evidence and submissions, the Commission is not persuaded that Maj Kirschner’s conduct failed to meet the standards expected of a police officer. We note in particular the following points in reaching this conclusion: Maj Kirschner demonstrated knowledge and awareness of the international legal principles potentially applicable to the illegal transfer of detainees. His awareness of post-transfer international legal obligations was sufficient to lead him, without prompting or guidance, to direct MPs under his command to watch out for signs of post-transfer abuse at the NDS facility. Maj Kirschner was also aware of his obligations pursuant to the Technical Directive in place during his rotation, and the TSO 321. In particular, he understood it was his duty to either investigate, or more likely, ensure the investigation of any allegations of breaches of international law. Maj Kirschner did not receive any direct allegations or complaints that the orders to transfer detainees generally, or to transfer any detainee in particular, were or could be illegal. He had some understanding of the substance of the reasons for the moratorium on transfers in November 2007 and an awareness of the international attention the detainee question received. He reasonably balanced these concerns against the measures he observed his Commander and the Government taking to guard against potential mistreatment following transfer, such as the suspension of transfers until a more robust monitoring regime was in place and the bolstering of the monitoring regime. Maj Kirschner took his duties as NIS detachment commander seriously, and undertook his extremely demanding and resource-challenged role in a professional manner. It is relevant to take into account the stressful and difficult nature of the work Maj Kirschner had to do while in theatre, in particular, in the area of KIA s and mortuary affairs. Given the demands of this work, and the more reactive role of the NIS , it is reasonable that his acquired knowledge of the detainee process and the treatment of detainees post-transfer was minimal. It was also reasonable for him to rely, to a great degree, on others, such as the TFPM and the MP company, to bring information or concerns to him if they existed. No such concerns were brought to his attention. Maj Kirschner reasonably considered his Commander’s behaviour to have demonstrated a willingness to stop transfers where necessary. Maj Kirschner did not have access to important information about the post-transfer process, such as the site visit reports from May onwards, other C4 traffic, the legal opinions the Commander was receiving, and any discussions his Commander may have been having with respect to post-transfer risk assessment. The Commission does not find Maj Kirschner personally blameworthy for the fact that he did not have access to this information. In the absence of access to information about the post-transfer process, and combined with the Commander’s demonstrated willingness to stop transfers in the face of allegations of mistreatment, it was reasonable that Maj Kirschner did not harbour suspicions whether his Commander was illegally ordering detainee transfers. Maj Kirschner was never asked to review or investigate the legality of the transfer orders. The Commission is satisfied that had he been tasked with this, Maj Kirschner would have initiated a proper investigation. Finding #6: The Commission finds that the allegations made by AIC and BCCLA against Major John Kirschner in the June 12, 2008 complaint are unsubstantiated. Viewing the evidence as a whole, the Commission finds no grounds to conclude Maj Kirschner breached a duty to investigate his Task Force Commander while in theatre, or to cause such an investigation to occur. The Commission concludes his actions under the circumstances prevailing at the time met the standard of a reasonable police officer. 16.7 Lieutenant-Colonel ( ret’d ) William H. Garrick LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick joined the military police in 1981 as a Private. Following basic military police training, he was posted to Edmonton and Cold Lake, Alberta, spending five years in each primarily in the areas of patrols and criminal investigations. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick was accepted into the university training program for NCO ’s and went to the University of Manitoba, completing a degree in criminology. On completion of his military police commissioned officers’ course he was appointed as the section commander with the Special Investigation Unit in Winnipeg. In 1997 on the creation of the NIS LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick was posted as the Operations Officer for NIS central region. He was subsequently posted as the operations officer for the Sensitive Investigations Detachment. During that time LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick was posted to Sarajevo, Bosnia on a tour as a team lead on a multinational investigation. Upon return to Canada, LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick was tasked with standing up the investigation support detachment for the NIS which was the surveillance team, criminal intelligence unit, polygraph unit, and computer crime unit. He was appointed to the rank of Major and stayed as the CO of that unit. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick was then transferred to the position of Deputy Provost Marshal - Police for a year. He was next posted to Greenwood, Nova Scotia as the main Provost Marshal for the base, overseeing MP operations. In 2005 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick was transferred back to Ottawa as the Senior Operations Officer, Deputy Commanding Officer of the National Investigation Service. Upon his promotion to Lieutenant Colonel in 2006 he was appointed as Commanding Officer of the National Investigation Service, a position held until he retired in July, 2008. Footnote 1444 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick’s chain of command was straightforward – he reported exclusively to the CFPM , both on the command and the technical chain. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick had almost daily contact with the CFPM about NIS matters and on strategic planning as a senior MP branch specialist. Below him in the MP chain were a deputy CO and a staff officer, and his detachment commanders. He had contact with the NIS detachment commanders in theatre two or more times per week by email. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick told the Commission the purpose of the NIS was to conduct independent investigations of major crimes – large-scale financial crimes, sexual assaults, homicides – as well as investigations potentially implicating senior members of the CF . LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick agreed the type of investigation described in the AIC / BCCLA complaints to the Commission would fall within the NIS mandate and would not be left for investigation by individual MP detachments or units. The independence of the NIS from the military chain of command was “ of paramount importance ”, and was to ensure there could be no direction of or interference with investigations by non- MP members. Consistent with this independence, LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick had no contact with the Task Force Commander, infrequent contact with the CEFCOM commander and received “ absolutely ” no direction from CEFCOM on how to conduct investigations even when they were being conducted parallel to a commander’s BOI investigation. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick had an information reporting relationship with the CEFCOM PM since the chain of command had to be kept informed of NIS investigations in order to address their operational impact, but the manner of conduct of investigations was left to the NIS . Footnote 1445 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick agreed there was a general sense that MPs in general and the NIS in particular were not always “ welcomed with open arms ” by the chain of command, but did not feel there was genuine resistance to MPs performing their investigative functions once the parameters and needs of investigations were explained. At times the logistics of supporting investigations could put CF members at great risk. Thus, it is understandable the chain of command would wish to be informed of the significance of the investigation prior to offering the support. By and large LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick found commanders and others in the chain of command to be helpful when called upon to provide support to the NIS while balancing this with the operational needs of their mission. Footnote 1446 Asked whether he agreed with the statement from army doctrine that the “ purpose of the NIS is to support chain of command in the execution of the assigned mission ” LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick indicated this was not stated in language he would have chosen since it does not convey the notion the independent investigative mandate of the NIS might sometimes be at odds with the immediate imperatives of the chain of command. Some NIS duties, such as forensic investigations when CF members were killed by IED ’s, directly and clearly supported the mission, but at times investigations might be somewhat disruptive to a mission. Overall, however, the independent investigations of the NIS supported the chain of command by ensuring lawful conduct within the military. Footnote 1447 In LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick’s view, it was not the role of the NIS to ensure ongoing compliance with military orders, and it was not their role to investigate the general risk of detainee torture in Afghanistan. Their primary role is to respond to complaints raised when there is a potential offence to be investigated. Others, such as the chain of command, were responsible for maintaining ongoing compliance with orders. NIS members are not patrol officers whose job is to continuously maintain law and order; they respond to complaints and follow up leads. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick did expect a degree of situational or background awareness such that investigations might arise tangentially out of an existing investigation, or might be self-initiated in appropriate circumstances. He spoke positively about Maj Kirschner’s initiative to have his personnel take note of prison conditions when they were visiting the NDS facility and expected his personnel to look outside the immediate parameters of their investigations. He did not expect proactive efforts to continually monitor legal compliance by commanders – this kind of ongoing “ virtue testing ” as his counsel termed it is beyond the scope of their mandate, and in fact might go beyond their legal authority to gather information. Footnote 1448 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick was aware the CF were transferring detainees to Afghan authorities including the NDS , and he understood it was always the Task Force Commander who made the decision to transfer and MPs who carried out the transfers. He was aware of the transfer agreements from December 2005 and May 2007 and believed it was DFAIT and CSC who were responsible for post-transfer monitoring. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick was familiar with TSO 321 as signed by MGen ( ret’d ) Grant on May 27, 2007 and was familiar with MGen ( ret’d ) Grant’s transfer decision form, although LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick was not certain when he became aware of it and he did not know whether it contained a record of the commander’s transfer risk assessment. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick agreed there was a legal obligation on CF members, including the commander, to ensure detainees were not transferred to a known risk of torture or abuse, although he was not familiar with the particular language of the legal test for transfer articulated by the CEFCOM commander in his directives to the Task Force commander. Footnote 1449 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick had read reports from the U.S. State Department, UN and Amnesty International outlining general concerns about the human rights situation in Afghanistan. He viewed these human rights and Rule of Law issues as the reason the CF was deployed to assist the Afghan government. He had not read the AIHRC reports although he was familiar with the organization. He had never seen any reports from DFAIT , whether produced by Mr. Colvin et al prior to the monitoring arrangement or by Messrs Gosselin and Davison afterward, but he assumed DFAIT was producing a record of their site visits. He did not personally request such information from CEFCOM but he understood the NIS obtained some such information in the course of Operation Camel Spider. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick had read reports at a strategic level concerning the Rule of Law issues that would relate to the NDS but had never personally been in contact with members of the NDS to assess their professionalism. Footnote 1450 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick had received training in the Geneva Conventions and Laws of Armed Combat during his MP training, and he tried to ensure his members attended a legal course prior to deployment. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick was surprised to hear MWO ( ret’d ) Girard had testified he had no such training since his early days in the CF . However, in his view, advanced training in these areas of law was not necessary, since the basic concepts were “ relatively straightforward ” and legal advisers were available on short notice for any areas of uncertainty. Footnote 1451 Responsibility for training NIS personnel for deployment was held jointly by the CFPM , LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick and the CF chain of command. There were clear combat readiness requirements which were non-negotiable, but one week of training was dedicated specifically to NIS duties. Investigation of detainee issues as a whole were the top priority and “ they all knew it was our number one priority ”. Footnote 1452 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick felt there was sufficient opportunity for information to be conveyed from one rotation to the next. Each deployed NIS detachment commander was sent on a pre-deployment visit, although it was usually when the incumbent was on leave. Returning detachment commanders were brought into training to speak about issues and expectations when deployed. There was a one-week overlap period between deployments, and in any event, most detainee investigations were occurring from detachments in Canada. Footnote 1453 In terms of specific allegations, LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick was aware of the first AIC / BCCLA complaint to this Commission, and promptly arranged for the RCMP to investigate these allegations since they involved his direct commander, the CFPM . This resulted in a thorough and detailed investigative report by Inspectors Rideout and Blizard Footnote 1454 with which LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick was also familiar. He was also familiar with the facts underlying Professor Attaran’s allegations from the March 2007 Globe and Mail article since it was the subject of one of the NIS investigations arising out of Col Noonan’s Federal Court affidavit. He read the Graeme Smith articles from the Globe and Mail and launched investigations (canvassed in Operation Centipede) into some of the allegations contained in them. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick was not familiar with the allegations outlined in DFAIT site visit reports from June 2007 or September 2007 although he was aware there had been at least one cessation of transfers in May or June 2007 due to the investigation surrounding conditions one detainee was held in during the hiatus in transfers. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick became aware of the November 2007 suspension of transfers when the CFPM Site Inspection Visit report became available; he did not see the DFAIT site visit reports from November 2007 but assumed the reason for the cessation was post-transfer abuse issues. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick was also not aware of the factors which led to the resumption of transfers. Footnote 1455 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick agreed information such as was contained in the site visit reports, summary of allegations, commander’s letters and DFAIT letters would potentially be relevant to investigators if an investigation were undertaken into the legality of the commander’s transfer decisions. He agreed information concerning the pattern of transfers, visits and abuse allegations would also be worth looking at in assessing allegations of abuse and allegations of unlawful transfer orders. In LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick’s view, the fact transfers were suspended from time to time as a response to abuse allegations, and the fact more robust monitoring measures were implemented, both suggested the commander was “ taking the correct actions that I would have expected to take place. ” Footnote 1456 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick was aware of the Federal Court application brought by Amnesty International Canada and BCCLA for an injunction prohibiting detainee transfers He had read the decision of the Federal Court Footnote 1457 wherein the safety of detainee transfers was questioned, but LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick was satisfied, based on his own knowledge of the general human rights situation in Afghanistan, as well as information on the checks and balances in place (learned through the Camel Spider investigation), sufficient safeguards had been put into place by CanadA. Had problems with the legality arisen, he noted there were many personnel who would be in a position to detect it and inform the NIS - the TF Commander’s staff and legal advisers, CF personnel conducting the transfer, CEFCOM personnel who reviewed the orders, CSC , DFAIT and RCMP personnel on the ground in the prisons. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick felt if there was any legal concern about the transfer decisions or process leading to it, he would be made aware of it. Footnote 1458 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick did not request any information from DFAIT , CSC , RCMP or other CF personnel about prison site visits or prison conditions. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick felt the general information they could provide would be similar to what he already knew from his review of human rights reports, and he did not feel it would be appropriate to request information without an investigation having been initiated: And they just generally are not going to wander through National Defence Headquarters asking if anybody has information relating to an issue so they may then form something to investigate. Footnote 1459 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick said he had shared the Federal Court decision with the investigators on Operation Camel Spider and this resulted in a conversation with Inspector Gfellner about keeping his eyes open for detainee issues beyond the specific complaints Camel Spider was investigating. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick did not provide it to the investigators on Operation Centipede looking into the allegations from the Globe and Mail articles because he originally conceived these would be “ Camel Spider 2 ”, a spin-off investigation, rather than a separate operation. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick agreed that the Federal Court opinion raised some concerns, and felt the ongoing investigations would sufficiently cover the appropriate areas if there were any question about the legality of transfer orders. Footnote 1460 In addition to Operation Camel Spider and other NIS investigations, LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick was aware there was a chain of command Board of Inquiry ( BOI ) into detainee issues, although he was not privy to the particulars of that investigation. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick was aware as well of the MPCC investigation into both Professor Attaran’s complaint matter and the February, 2007 AIC / BCCLA complaint concerning the CFPM . To his knowledge, the NIS was not provided with LCol Boot’s CEFCOM fact-check arising out of the allegations in Graeme Smith’s article, despite the fact that CEFCOM requested an NIS investigation into the allegation CF members encouraged a detainee to provide information to avoid abuse. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick agreed information from the CEFCOM investigations and DFAIT reports would be potentially helpful to the NIS investigations both in terms of verification of facts and prioritizing those investigations. Footnote 1461 Detainee investigations constituted a major proportion, approximately 75%, of the NIS workload during the period covered in this complaint, and were their number one priority. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick’s MPs were also tasked with many other duties, including between 400 and 500 ongoing major investigations, investigation of every instance of escalation of force in theatre, investigation of IED attacks on CF personnel, forensic investigations when CF members were wounded or killed in action, retrieval and identification of fallen CF service members, mortuary duty and repatriation of remains. The workload could fairly be described as overwhelming, and in theatre it took a physical and psychological toll on NIS personnel. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick said no NIS member came back from theatre the same person, and for some rotations three of four returning members would take their leave from the CF . Footnote 1462 Operation Centipede was created to address a backlog of potential investigations stemming from the Camel Spider investigation. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick’s original plan was to direct each incident to an appropriate regional NIS office for assessment and, if warranted, full investigation. The reasoning was the regional offices would be proximate to the returning deployed troops (for example, ROTO 3 consisted of troops based in Edmonton, ROTO 4 were from Valcartier) and thus would be in the best position to conduct interviews. It quickly became apparent to LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick that this plan would not work for various logistic reasons, including the prioritization of Operation Camel Spider. After a period of dormancy, Maj Bolduc’s Central Region NIS detachment was directed to halt or wrap up every investigation save an ongoing major fraud investigation and to proceed with the outstanding detainee investigations under the umbrella of Operation Centipede. Operation Centipede was formally initiated on March 19, 2008. Footnote 1463 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick agreed that the NIS investigations including Operation Camel Spider, Operation Centipede and other detainee-related investigations dealt with allegations both of CF abuse and post-transfer abuse, and did not explicitly deal with the legality of transfer orders. Maj Kirschner testified he was advised by LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick to be alert to detainee issues generally, but had not been asked specifically to look at the legality of the commanders’ transfer orders. Footnote 1464 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick testified he believed the documentary evidence collected during the Operation Camel Spider investigation “ involved the entire holistic detainee process ” even though its specific mandate was an allegation of CF abuse of detainees. Footnote 1465 Overall, LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick expected any detainee related issues, including the legality of the commander’s transfer orders, would be picked up in the course of one of the several ongoing investigations, particularly Operation Camel Spider, Operation Centipede, and the Rideout-Blizard investigation. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick’s comments on particular investigations shed some insight into his reasoning. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick pointed out that GO 2008–6918 dealt with the allegation in Col Noonan’s affidavit of CF members becoming aware of post-transfer abuse and doing nothing, but also in its synopsis posed the question why the chain of command did not report this to MPs . LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick said this meant his investigators would look at: […] if in fact there were any legal issues with respect to the transfer process. And then as a follow on to that, would there have been any issues that would have given rise to the chain of command reporting this to the military police. Footnote 1466 In other words, the conduct of the chain of command was to be examined, albeit not their transfer orders in this particular investigation. Regarding the investigation of Graeme Smith’s Globe and Mail article containing a similar allegation, covered under GO 2008–6920 , LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick described his expectations: I mean, there’s some obvious things; actions of the CF members if in fact they were in the area and did not take any action. Then, you know, following to that is again looking at the whole transfer process. Footnote 1467 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick said he would have expected some factual follow up to this article based on more than simply reading the article – attempts to independently verify the information such as were conducted by CEFCOM , for example. The exclusive focus in this GO on whether CF members had actually abused the detainee and the refusal to consider such allegations as they were “ based on hearsay ” fell short of LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick’s expectations. While LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick agreed with the general proposition expressed in the GO summary that only offences within NIS jurisdiction would merit consideration he disagreed with the investigator’s conclusion that nothing in the article merited NIS consideration. Footnote 1468 In fairness, LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick had retired as NIS commander when Operation Centipede was completed. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick was not ultimately responsible for the fact that the concluded investigations fell well short of his expectations. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick agreed the entirety of Operation Centipede took far longer to complete than would be ideal for a police investigation. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick had difficult decisions to make with the resources at his disposal. Management of NIS priorities was one of his major challenges. At any given time, LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick would have available approximately half of a full-strength contingent of 120-124 personnel. Specific factors which played a role in setting priorities when there were detainee investigations were the degree to which the CF were implicated in the allegations, the time sensitivity of the case, the solvability of the case, attentiveness to victims of sexual assault or other serious violent crimes, attentiveness to the families of murder victims and fallen soldiers, and an assessment of the risks faced by investigators and in fact by the potential victims in conducting investigations. Footnote 1469 During the period May 3, 2007 to June 12, 2008, Operation Camel Spider (the investigation into allegations of detainee abuse raised in January 2007 by Professor Attaran) was given top priority and required a tremendous proportion of NIS resources. Footnote 1470 Further allegations arising from Camel Spider were placed on hold until the primary investigation could be completed. As noted, these allegations were for the most part eventually compiled into Operation Centipede and were not investigated until a year or more after they arose. Another resource challenge was the shut-down of entire detachments for pre-deployment training, deployment to theatre, and post-deployment recovery from such issues as physical or psychological trauma. Transfers into and out of the NIS resulted in loss of personnel for training, and the need for a period of mentorship for some inexperienced officers. In addition, particular task forces (some unrelated to detainees) occupied personnel for extended periods. Footnote 1471 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick was not responsible for determining the level of resources allocated to the NIS . He could, and did, request resources from the CFPM when appropriate, and the CFPM was responsive to the degree possible, but there were limits to the human resources that could be allocated to his purposes. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick indicated it was a problem of human, and not financial, resources that presented him with difficulty. Footnote 1472 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick described the test for launching an investigation: You referred in your testimony to conducting investigations [mis-transcribed “ information ”] based on police evidentiary standards. Can you explain what you mean by that? Yeah, I mean every time we conduct an investigation, we’re conducting it either in support of a potential service offence prosecution, or a Canadian criminal court prosecution. Therefore, all the investigations are held to the same standard we hold in Canadian criminal prosecution for evidentiary purposes. Okay, and what would be the standard to commence such an investigation? We would have to have more than a suspicion. We have to have reasonable grounds to enter into the investigation. […] And once the threshold – I might have asked you this with respect to the duty to investigate. What’s the threshold for commencing a criminal investigation? It would be reasonable grounds to believe that an offence [within the NIS mandate] has taken place […] Footnote 1473 Asked how investigations unfold in practice, LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick described a process involving an assessment of the initial facts or complaint in order to determine whether some sort of more comprehensive or formal investigation ought to be initiated. This assessment phase would potentially involve preliminary interviews, follow-up on leads, and possibly seeking legal advice to determine the merits of conducting a full-fledged investigation with a view to pursuing prosecution for an offence. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick agreed it would be appropriate to consider all facts, both supportive of and counter-indicative of the commission of an offence, in order to properly consider the extent to which an investigation would proceed. The investigative assessment could be undertaken on as little basis as a rumour or an account from a newspaper, depending on the facts and circumstances of the case, but ideally would look at “ all the factors ”. This investigative assessment phase, prior to forming reasonable grounds to investigate, is “ absolutely ” part of the policing function. Footnote 1474 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick also agreed MPs could self-initiate investigations or investigative assessments where appropriate, noting the Operation Centipede investigations, including the investigations into the March and April 2007 Globe and Mail articles, were examples of MP self-initiated investigations. Based on observations or facts which came to their attention during Operation Camel Spider, new investigations were initiated into other detainee-related matters despite the fact nobody had levied a complaint or requested an investigation; Footnote 1475 it goes without saying the initial evidence in some of those investigations fell well short of “ reasonable grounds to believe an offence had taken place ”, yet the matters were appropriately flagged to be further examined. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick said self-initiation of an investigation could come from “ a variety of triggers ” – in essence, if the facts suggest it is appropriate to take a further look into something, an MP could do so. The Commission is satisfied with LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick’s understanding of the appropriate method of determining whether to conduct investigative assessments, full investigations, and self-initiation of investigations. Based on all this testimony, the Commission understands LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick’s position essentially to be that an initial assessment can occur to determine if there are reasonable grounds to pursue a more extensive investigation with a focused end of criminal or service offence prosecution. Care must be exercised when examining LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick’s position to distinguish the right to conduct an assessment or investigation, versus the duty to do so. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick was entirely clear in stating that if an MP formed the reasonable suspicion a commander had committed an offence such as unlawful transfer of a detainee, the MP was under a positive duty to investigate. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick was equally clear and consistent in stating that at no time did he form a reasonable suspicion the Task Force Afghanistan Commander had issued such an illegal order. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick cited the evidence in support of the contrary view, that commanders were taking their transfer decisions quite seriously and were continually taking steps to mitigate the risk of transfer to torture, ceasing to transfer at times when it appeared to be unsafe to do so. He also noted the more broadly based initiatives by the Government of Canada with DFAIT and CSC personnel in place, as well as the fact the Commander had a team of advisers including legal advisers to assist him in making transfer decisions. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick felt, if an unlawful transfer order had been issued, he would have been notified. Footnote 1476 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick noted the NIS was never asked by the Chain of Command during the period May 3, 2007 to June 12, 2008, to examine whether the commander fulfilled his obligation to ensure that monitoring safeguards were in place. As well, there was never a request by any member of the public to investigate the legality of the transfer orders. Footnote 1477 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick agreed if an MP had been provided all of the information contained in the DFAIT site visit reports and summaries, had been aware that DFAIT visits were not occurring for substantial periods of time, and had seen the correspondence from the Commander in November 2007 describing the situation as “ amber ” and expressing concerns about the lack of monitoring information being received, “ it might trigger some further inquiry ” to determine what factors had entered into the transfer decisions leading to the abuse allegation disclosed in Mr. Gosselin’s report of November 5, 2007. Footnote 1478 During a conversation with the CFPM on June 12, 2008, LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick and Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore discussed the fact the AIC / BCCLA complaint to this Commission of June 12, 2008 was about the legality of the commander’s transfer decisions. They felt any illegality with respect to transfer orders would be uncovered by the existing NIS investigations, the BOI and other checks and balances. Footnote 1479 Their approach was to see what information would be derived from the other investigations and then consider whether there was anything about the transfer orders to investigate. Thus, despite the strategic importance of detainee abuse issues and LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick’s view that the legality of transfer orders was implicitly covered by the first AIC / BCCLA complaint, this issue was not directly addressed by LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick or the NIS at any time between May 3, 2007 and June 12, 2008. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore testified he had previously discussed this issue with LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick sometime after the February 21, 2007 AIC / BCCLA complaint: At the same time I had asked him to have a look at the NIS investigations that were ongoing to see if there was anything in there that may suggest a Commander had committed an offence by transferring these detainees; to ask questions or raise the issue with his investigators. And at the same point in time, I told him that I would be taking opportunities in regular conversation with Commanders just to raise the issue to see what they said and would also followup with the Task Force Provost Marshals at the time. Footnote 1480 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick was examined by Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore’s counsel one day prior to Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore’s testimony and was not asked to confirm this conversation. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick otherwise made no mention of such a conversation in his testimony. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick had indicated everyone knew detainee issues in general were a top priority and they were to be aware of detainee issues in general, but direct focus on the legality of the transfer decisions is absent from his testimony and from the NIS records prior to June 12, 2008. It appears to the Commission the commanders’ transfer decisions came into sharp focus for LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick only when the Complainants in this matter issued their second complaint on June 12, 2008. To the degree the issue was being implicitly addressed in the other ongoing investigations, it occurred during the course of investigations which proceeded during his tenure at an unacceptably slow pace as a result of the extreme caseload, resource pressure and prioritization that had to occur. Footnote 1481 The Complainants’ Submissions The Complainants submit LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick bore responsibility for a number of acts or omissions which they attribute to him during the time period of this complaint. Footnote 1482 It was submitted LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick, as the CO of the NIS reporting directly to the CFPM , was responsible for overseeing all serious and/or sensitive criminal investigations by the CF military police. Further, the NIS is vested with independence from the normal CF chain of command and is the branch responsible for investigating allegations related to harm to detainees. The Complainants’ submission points to LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick’s testimony that issues concerning detainees were his top priority and occupied 75% of his time, Footnote 1483 and he was aware of international reports about torture in Afghanistan and had read Graeme Smith’s articles in the Globe and Mail . Footnote 1484 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick testified he was aware Canadian officials were monitoring detainees in Afghan custody. Although LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick did not specifically ask his NIS officers to seek out this information, he believed it appropriate for the MPs to make occasional inquiries into detainee treatment post-transfer. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick indicated this kind of inquisitiveness was part of their job, and he would expect MPs to look outside their general parameters when they’re doing their business. Footnote 1485 It was submitted LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick believed he did not have to look into the DFAIT monitoring visits himself, and said there was no reason to follow up on these reports. The Complainants submit LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick later acknowledged such information would have been useful to his investigators. Footnote 1486 The Complainants submitted that LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick acknowledged a discussion of the February 2007 complaint with the CFPM Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore, where they decided that an outside police force should investigate given that the allegations were directed partly against the CFPM . The RCMP was approached and asked to look into the allegations. Supt. Wayne Rideout and Supt. Wade Blizard were the senior RCMP officers tasked with the investigation. Footnote 1487 Following a three-month investigation of the scope of the CFPM ’s role in detainee transfers (commencing March 13, 2007) and numerous interviews, the RCMP submitted a final report. The investigators stated in the report they would consider “ the existence of any knowledge, information or intelligence of actual detainee abuse, post-handover, known by the Military Police, or indeed DND ” to be significant. Footnote 1488 According to counsel for the Complainants, the RCMP sought any kind of information about post-handover abuse which was known by, or ought to have been known by, the CFPM . The June 2007 final RCMP report concluded there was no evidence of an offence, in part based on their understanding there was no “ knowledge, information or intelligence ” indicating post-transfer torture and abuse by Afghan authorities. Footnote 1489 Counsel for the Complainants submitted it was “ unfortunate ” the RCMP investigators had concluded their investigation in the absence of critical information: namely, the graphic first-hand accounts of torture heard by DFAIT officials in Kabul and Kandahar only a few weeks earlier. Counsel submitted that it appeared all of the RCMP ’s interviews were carried out before the DFAIT visits elicited the disturbing allegations on June 4 and 5, 2007 and it is not known why this information was not shared with the RCMP before they submitted their report. Footnote 1490 The Complainants submit LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick said he could not share the DFAIT reports or discuss the suspension of transfers in June 2007 when he met with the RCMP investigators after reading their conclusions because he did not have such information. They questioned why LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick did not take further action after he learned about the allegations in the DFAIT reports. Footnote 1491 When Operation Centipede commenced to address numerous allegations that CF personnel had illegally or improperly carried out their duties in the handling of Afghan detainees, the Complainants submit LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick, as the CO of the NIS , had overall responsibility for these investigations. They included the following allegations: Footnote 1492 a detainee was executed by Afghan authorities post handover and tossed in a ditch; a soldier reported witnessing a detainee being beaten in the head by Afghan soldiers; a detainee transferred to an Afghan authority was subsequently taken behind a building and executed; CF personnel witnessed a detainee being abused post-handover; and a CF captain alluded in an email that Afghan authorities abused detainees in their custody. Although LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick testified significant resource constraints forced him to prioritize investigations as necessary, the Complainants submitted such “ evidence is troubling given the weight that LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick appeared to place on the investigations in other contexts ”. Footnote 1493 In his testimony, LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick said repeatedly one of the main reasons why he did not look into the subsequent allegations of detainee abuse was the fact the Operation Centipede investigations were underway. The Complainants pointed in particular to LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick’s testimony that he believed the Globe and Mail investigations would look into those issues, and submit this explanation is “ wholly insufficient ”. Footnote 1494 Submissions on Behalf of LCol ( ret’d ) W. Garrick The submissions made on behalf of LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick identified a number of factors which it was said demonstrated his actions were reasonable and that he met all professional standards. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick was Commanding officer of the CFNIS during the period of this complaint. He was not notified he was a subject in this proceeding until after he had retired from the CF . Footnote 1495 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick submitted he was satisfied the NIS detachment in Afghanistan was fulfilling investigative functions which related to operational issues, including the use of force by CF members, and conducting post mortem forensic investigations of CF members killed or injured in the line of duty. He was satisfied all of the subject NIS investigators were trained adequately. He was also satisfied that if NIS investigators encountered a complicated investigative issue or one outside their normal mandate, independent legal advice was available. Footnote 1496 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick submitted he had read some high level strategic material pertaining to the Rule of Law in Afghanistan which discussed the NDS , as well as UN Human Rights Reports, US State Department Reports and some Amnesty International reports. Although familiar with the AIHRC , LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick had not read its reports. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick submitted he believed the CF was in Afghanistan due to the overall atmosphere relating to human rights in that country. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick acknowledged being aware of the transfer of Afghan detainees by the CF to Afghan authorities during the relevant time period and understood the decision to transfer was always made by the Task Force Commander. He submitted he knew there was a process in place for determining whether a detainee would be transferred or released, but he was unaware of the particulars of the decision making process. He was aware of both Canada-Afghanistan detainee transfer arrangements and understood DFAIT and Correctional Service Canada personnel were monitoring detainees post-transfer. Footnote 1497 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick submitted he did not receive any DFAIT site visit reports and was unaware of their contents or their existence. Footnote 1498 He acknowledged being factually aware of how the detainees were handled and stated he was comfortable in knowing that a process was put in place by the Canadian Government to ensure Canada would be aware of any problems. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick submitted he was aware of the February 2007 Amnesty International Canada and British Columbia Civil Liberties Association complaint, and responded by requesting an RCMP investigation into the allegations against the CFPM . LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick submitted that allegations of detainee mistreatment would not be sufficient on their own for him to form a reasonable suspicion the Task Force Commander had committed an offence. Information being uncovered by the NIS through other investigations was leading LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick to a different understanding about detainee abuse allegations than was being portrayed in the newspapers. Footnote 1499 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick submitted that he expressed concern at the time to the CFPM about personnel constraints impeding progress of the ongoing detainee investigations in OP CENTIPEDE. The CFPM agreed to give OP CENTIPEDE investigations low priority. Footnote 1500 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick submitted he had been aware of pauses in detainee transfers during in June and November 2007, although he was unsure of when he became aware of the latter. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick said he assumed an incident had taken place which caused the Commander sufficient concern to cease the transfers. Footnote 1501 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick was confident the situation in the Afghan prison system was monitored by a wide range of government departments and military officials all the way up to the CDS , and any of them could have brought forward a complaint for investigation. On the basis of additional information he had not seen previously, LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick submitted he was satisfied in hindsight that the CF and the whole-of-government were taking appropriate action. Footnote 1502 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick stated he agreed any allegation of detainee mistreatment by CF members would result in a mandatory investigation. During the relevant period, LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick submitted he received no complaint or allegation the Task Force Commander had knowingly ordered the transfer of a detainee to a risk of torture by Afghan authorities. He submitted, if such an allegation had come forth, the NIS would have investigated. Footnote 1503 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick submitted he did not expect the MPs under his command to be collecting information on detainee transfers in the absence of a specific ongoing investigation. He did not expect them to go into Afghanistan prisons to investigate alleged complaints made by detainees about their post-transfer treatment. Footnote 1504 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick submitted there were many other investigations looking at the legality of the Commander’s detainee transfer order, including Boards of Inquiry and this Commission, and any discovery of wrongdoing would have been detected and he would have been informed. Footnote 1505 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick submitted he would have been aware if the Task Force Commander had given an unlawful order because there were ample checks and balances in place. Footnote 1506 LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick submitted that at no time did he form a reasonable suspicion the Task Force Commander had transferred detainees to a real risk of torture. Nor did LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick ever feel any of his subordinates failed in their duties with respect to assessing whether or not an investigation was required. Footnote 1507 In conclusion, LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick submitted he acted reasonably and appropriately in carrying out his policing mandate. No complaints or allegations were ever received by him regarding the legality of the Commander’s decisions to transfer detainees. Based on his experience as an MP and member of the CF deployed in operations, LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick submitted it was reasonable for him to have full confidence in the command decision making process and to have no reason to doubt the appropriateness of the decisions made by senior commanders. Conclusions Regarding LCol (Ret’d) W. Garrick Having considered the totality of the evidence and submissions, the Commission is not persuaded that LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick’s conduct failed to meet the standards expected of a police officer. We note in particular the following points in reaching this conclusion: LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick demonstrated knowledge and awareness of the international legal principles potentially applicable to the illegal transfer of detainees, and he understood it was his duty either to investigate, or more likely, ensure the investigation of any allegations of breaches of international law. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick did not receive any direct allegations or complaints that the orders to transfer detainees generally, or to transfer any detainee in particular, were or could be illegal until the Complainants submitted their letter to this Commission on June 12, 2008. He then believed that the existing investigations, particularly Operation Camel Spider and Operation Centipede, would uncover any evidence of illegal transfer orders if it existed. Just prior to the period of this complaint LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick had exhibited an awareness of the necessity of investigating any allegations concerning detainees by ensuring that investigations into the allegations made in the Globe and Mail articles were included in the NIS investigations which became Operation Centipede. LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick’s tenure as CO of CFNIS ended shortly after receipt of the June 12, 2008 complaint letter and at that time, there were ongoing investigations which he expected would be thoroughly conducted. The Commission does not find that LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick is at fault for the fact that the NIS investigations were not pursued promptly and thoroughly between May 3, 2007 and June 12, 2008. The NIS does not have infinite resources, and he adequately explained to the Commission the profoundly strained resources of the NIS during this period of time. He also adequately explained the manner in which discretion was exercised to prioritize NIS investigations as he did. It was ultimately within his discretion as CO of the CFNIS to consider the disposition of his force and the concentration of his resources on any particular investigation area, so long as this was reasonably done. Based on what he knew, including particularly his reliance on the fact that other Government agencies and components of the CF were involved in detainee monitoring, it was reasonable that LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick did not harbour any suspicions whether Commanders had issued unlawful transfer orders. He was aware of the human rights background, the media attention to the issue, and ongoing investigations of complaints into related issues, and reasonably balanced these concerns against the measures he understood were being taken to guard against potential mistreatment following transfer. Finding #7: The Commission finds the allegations made by AIC and BCCLA against LCol ( ret’d ) William Garrick in the June 12, 2008 complaint are unsubstantiated. Viewing the evidence as a whole, the Commission finds no grounds to conclude that LCol William ( ret’d ) Garrick breached a duty to investigate the Task Force Commander while in theatre, or to cause such an investigation to occur. The Commission concludes his actions under the circumstances prevailing at the time met the standard of a reasonable police officer. 16.8 Captain (N) ( ret’d ) Steven Moore Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore was appointed CFPM in June 2005 and served in that capacity until June 15, 2009, a year after the end date of this complaint. Shortly thereafter, he took full retirement from the Canadian Forces. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore was the CFPM for the entire period of the Amnesty/ BCCLA complaint, being May 3, 2007 to June 12, 2008. In this capacity, Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore reported directly to the Vice Chief of the Defence Staff. Footnote 1508 In November 2007, Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore took command, in his capacity as CFPM , of a formation called the Canadian Forces Military Police Group. This group consisted of the National Investigation Service, the Military Police Security Service, the Canadian Forces Prison and Detention Barracks and the Canadian Forces Military Police Academy. Footnote 1509 Except for members of the NIS , at no point during the timeframe of this complaint did Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore have command responsibilities for the MPs involved in or with the Afghanistan deployment, such as the TFPM and other members of the MP company in theatre, and the CEFCOM PM . Footnote 1510 Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore’s evidence can be divided into three subject areas within the context of this failure to investigate complaint. First, as with all subjects, the Commission has looked at the extent to which Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore had access to information about the detainee transfer process, the risks post transfer in Afghanistan, and the Task Force Commanders’ decisions to transfer, and whether the information he had access to should have caused him to investigate the transfer decisions. Second, the Commission will address the evidence as it relates to Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore’s command responsibility for the NIS , in particular, the nature of his involvement with Operation Centipede. The third subject area relates to concerns raised by the CFPM about the MP command and control structure, and the impact this may have had on the ability of the military police to carry out its policing work. Of note, as of April 1, 2011, the MP command structure changed. As the Commission understands it, the CFPM now has a command relationship with MPs in theatre when they are carrying out their policing functions. 16.8.1 Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore’s Access to Information about the Detainee Process and Detainee Treatment During the time relevant to this complaint, Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore held the most senior position within the MP organization, but testified he was not kept in the loop on basic detainee information coming to Ottawa from in-theatre. For example, he was unaware of early information about the detainee process, such as the fact the ROTO 1 TFPM had been designated as the national point of contact for detainee issues in-theatre. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore had no access to the C4 reports generated in 2006 and 2007 by Richard Colvin, on topics such as ICRC cooperation concerns and the conditions in Afghan prisons. Footnote 1511 Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore said the CEFCOM Provost Marshals and the TFPM s did not generally come to him to discuss issues related to the post-transfer treatment of detainees, or raise such issues in meetings. Footnote 1512 Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore was not aware of the high-level discussions occurring in early 2007 between DND , DFAIT and others about changes to the detainee transfer process. He was aware of the more major media reports coming out about the detainee process, including the Globe and Mail articles from Graeme Smith so often discussed in these proceedings. Footnote 1513 Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore was not informed of the April 2007 suspension of transfers until well after the fact. Footnote 1514 He was aware the original transfer arrangement was revised, but could not say exactly when he acquired this knowledge, agreeing he may have learned of the new arrangement through the media. Footnote 1515 The fact a new monitoring regime was being implemented, though, did not cause him to question whether a particular individual, such as the Task Force Commander, had committed a criminal offence.
