Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore felt, instead, the need to implement a new regime spoke to a need to improve government policy: “ I felt that the improvements or previous insufficiencies, if you want to call them that, spoke to government policy rather than [an] offence by any particular individual. ” Footnote 1516 Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore was not aware around this time certain MPs under Maj Hudson’s command had concerns about their own personal liability in actually doing the handovers. This was something he would have liked to have known. Footnote 1517 When the new site visit regime was put in place, Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore did not see any of the site visit reports until seeing them as a result of disclosure from this Commission. Footnote 1518 He knew site visits were occurring, but felt, if individuals within the process saw what they felt constituted negligence or an offence, it would be reported to the military police. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore did not feel so curious about the process that he needed to ask to see the results of those visits, and, as discussed below, he felt this would have been seen as an “ intrusion ”. Footnote 1519 Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore did not learn about the November 2007 suspension of detainee transfers until January 2008, as a result of an in-theatre MP Staff Inspection Visit. As noted in the Commission’s discussion about CEFCOM , the fact he learned so late was likely due to a snag in information flow somewhere along the technical chain between the CEFCOM PM , Maj Laflamme, the CANOSCOM PM , LCol Taylor, and the CFPM . Footnote 1520 Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore lamented the convoluted nature of the technical chain flowing from the TFPM in Afghanistan to himself, suggesting it was something he tried regularly to improve during his tenure. Footnote 1521 Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore was unaware of the November 25, 2007 letter from MGen Laroche (then BGen ) setting out his decision to suspend transfers and the reasons for doing so, until he was shown it during his appearance before the Commission on December 1, 2010. Similarly, Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore did not view any of the correspondence drafted by BGen Juneau (then Col ) and MGen Laroche, in which they set out their concerns about the transfer process, and the lack of visits in October 2007. Footnote 1522 When Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore learned of the suspension of transfers in January 2008, he was not advised of the reasons behind the suspension. He did recall a discussion around Christmas 2007 with the Vice Chief of the Defence Staff about the possibility of MPs conducting inspections of Afghan prisons, which he advised the VCDS the military police had the expertise to conduct. In fact, he noted the TFPM at the time, Maj Zybala, was a former Commandant of the CF Service Prison and Detention Barracks. Nothing seems to have developed from this discussion, and the military police were never tasked with this role. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore inquired with the VCDS as to whether he should begin to work on the possibility of the military police doing the visits, but was told by the VCDS the military was stretched too thin, and he was negotiating with other branches of the government, to have them do the monitoring: “ … if that failed, then he would come back to me. ” Footnote 1523 While Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore testified he did not learn of the specific reasons for suspension, in the context of his conversations with the VCDS , he learned some of the site visits to transferred detainees had created some concern, and so they were dealing with this by exploring more ways to look at the monitoring program. The VCDS was not more specific about the reports, and did not mention allegations of abuse. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore’s perception was the military police were potentially being sought out for background and experience “ that could potentially be complementary to that process. ” Footnote 1524 Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore testified that around the same time, he also had a conversation with Maj Zybala about how the TFPM felt the detainee process was working, and if there were any issues to be examined. Maj Zybala told the Commission he spoke twice with the CFPM while in theatre, but Maj Zybala did not expand, nor was he asked to expand, on the nature of those conversations. Footnote 1525 It seems likely one of the conversations to which Maj Zybala was referring was this one, mentioned by Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore described the nature of the conversation as follows: Well, I did have a conversation as well with Major Zybala who’s Task Force Provost Marshal at the time. Talked to him about the process itself, if he had confidence in the process, if he saw issues that we should be investigating and also make him alive to the fact that it was being discussed now that we may need some of his people to do these visits. Footnote 1526 Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore recalled specifically he contacted Maj Zybala at home around Christmas time, i.e. , while Maj Zybala was on leave in Canada, to have the particular conversation about MPs assisting with the site visit process. Footnote 1527 Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore said he followed the proceedings launched by Amnesty/ BCCLA in Federal Court, but did not read the 2008 judgments at any point prior to the end date of this complaint. Footnote 1528 Despite the limited nature of his information, Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore said he asked questions of a number of people about the detainee process, including detainee treatment post-transfer. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore had concerns about this issue from the time it began to attract scrutiny, which, for him, started with the first Amnesty/ BCCLA complaint dated February 21, 2007. Footnote 1529 The Complainants cited what they called “ highly credible reports on Afghanistan ” from bodies such as the AIHRC , the UN , and the US State Department. These reports described a risk of torture and abuse in the Afghan prison system. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore said he had actually heard general reports about torture in Afghanistan even before reading the first Amnesty/ BCCLA complaint, although he did not read the reports first hand. Footnote 1530 The particular reports cited within this complaint letter did not cause Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore particular concern because it was his assumption the Government of Canada, in crafting its detainee policy, would have taken all of this information into account: What I felt was that the government, when they craft their policy would take, they would have access to all of these and much more … my assumption was that they would be taking specific measures and negotiations with the government of Afghanistan to develop a process and get reassurances that where Canadian Forces were transferring detainees that they would be free of risk of torture. Footnote 1531 Nevertheless, Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore took several steps after seeing the first complaint. He viewed it as a criminal allegation against himself personally, so he ordered LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick to report it to the NIS , and to request they investigate it, if they felt appropriate. Ultimately, this task would be taken on by RCMP investigators. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore intentionally asked not to be briefed on the matter. At the same time, he asked LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick to have a look at any of the existing NIS investigations to see if they revealed information suggesting a need to investigate post-transfer abuse. At the same point in time, he advised LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick he would take the opportunity in regular conversation with Commanders to raise the issue, and would likewise talk to the Task Force Provost Marshals to see if they had concerns about the detainee process, or saw things which needed to be investigated. As such, Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore testified, by the time the Graeme Smith Globe and Mail articles had come out, he had already set certain things in motion: So at the time the article came out, I was aware that the RCMP investigation was underway as well and had also felt that should any of these questions or inquiries turn something up at that point to indicate that there may in fact be an offence that we would in all likelihood have to turn it over to the RCMP as long as I was the subject of their investigation. Footnote 1532 On June 29, 2007, Superintendents Rideout and Blizard of the RCMP concluded (N) ( ret’d ) Moore had done no wrong. They found, at the time of their investigation, no information or intelligence existing within DND to substantiate any allegations of abuse post handover, and, as such, the CFPM could also not have possessed such knowledge. Footnote 1533 Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore was verbally briefed on the results of this investigation, but did not read the actual report himself. Footnote 1534 Even after the completion of the RCMP investigation, Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore continued to have questions about the detainee process. The RCMP investigators advised him they had found nothing to incriminate him, and reiterated what he felt he was hearing from other sources, namely, the detainee process was solid. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore said this raised his confidence level, but he kept on asking questions: “ I did carry on listening, you know, talking to commanders about the issue, asking questions of Task Force Provost Marshals after that time. ” Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore spoke to the operations officer at CEFCOM at some point, the TFPM at various points, and to MGen ( ret’d ) Grant when he was at CEFCOM shortly after his return from theatre: So essentially, if I was dealing with somebody or happened to run into somebody that I felt might be knowledgeable about the process, then I would try and work that into the conversation. And to be clear here, I wasn’t going around accusing people of things here, but working in questions about, you know, how was your tour and what were the big issues and we’ve seen a lot about the detainee issues in the paper, what were your thoughts on that and, you know, listening for somebody to perhaps say, well, you know, actually that caused me some concern or something, which they did not. Footnote 1535 Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore testified that to his knowledge the JAG was involved in monitoring some of the ongoing court cases. He expected them to report any criminal offences they thought might have occurred in relation to the detainee process. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore referred, as well, to the ongoing processes before this Commission (both the Attaran and the Amnesty/ BCCLA complaints), and expected the MPCC would document and report any criminal offence thought to have occurred. Footnote 1536 Finally, Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore knew other investigations into the detainee issue were ongoing, including Camel Spider and internal boards of inquiry on the detainee topic within the Canadian Forces. Footnote 1537 Throughout the course of his testimony, Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore was shown documents, such as the correspondence from MGen Laroche and BGen Juneau, the site visit reports alleging abuse from June 2007 to November 2007, and the DFAIT chart indicating almost 30 percent of detainees interviewed from May 2007 to February 2008 had alleged abuse. This was information Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore had not viewed during the timeframe covered by this complaint, and he agreed some of it was troubling. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore said if he had seen this information during the timeframe of the complaint, it would have given him a different perspective on the detainee transfer question, and could have caused him to make more inquiries than he did. Footnote 1538 With respect to the MP role in enforcing international law, Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore agreed MPs handling detainees had a responsibility to be familiar with the Geneva Conventions. Footnote 1539 Furthermore, he expected MPs engaged in operational functions, such as detainee handling, to nonetheless investigate, or report for investigation, suspected offences of any stripe: Does that mean that, again, any member of the military police regardless of their rank or the position they happen to be posted to have a duty to investigate possible offences? Generally, yes. I’d say within that, I know if someone, if a military police person comes across an offence and is not employed at that time during an investigations section will probably report that offence and cause it to be investigated by somebody else within that unit. But generally, yes. Without talking about any of the subjects or any person in particular, just put it in the abstract. Supposing you’re a Master Corporal MP , and you get some concerns about something you see or you may have read about or somehow you get some information that you think maybe should be looked at a little further, see if there’s any reason for concern there or not. Would that Master Corporal MP be expected to just go about and start asking questions or would there be some protocol they should follow within the MP technical chain to raise that matter to an appropriate level? It would depend on what their specific functions were at the time. Some functions that they would be providing may not allow them time to properly go out and conduct an investigation wholly on their own. I would say that they would be expected, if they came across information that they believed may be an offence, then they need to either investigate that or pass it to somebody in the military police to be investigated. Footnote 1540 What, for Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore, would have constituted an allegation he would have expected his military police to investigate? He was asked whether allegations of possible breaches of international law, found in newspapers, court actions, written reports from diplomats, court judgments, and site visit reports, would invoke a duty to investigate the transfer decisions. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore said it depended on the circumstances, and required some evidence of the Task Force Commander’s state of mind: It would wholly depend on what was in those documents, but if you had allegations that caused you to form a belief that a Canadian detainee was transferred by Commander X, was subsequently tortured post transfer, and Commander X had information that he knew that this person was going to be tortured or would face a substantial risk of torture and transferred him anyway, then that would constitute an offence and require an investigation. So what I think what I seem to be hearing you say is that in your opinion, one of the elements that there would have to be some information about is the knowledge of the Commander at the pertinent time? The Commander’s state of knowledge would be crucial at the pertinent time. Footnote 1541 Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore expected, if any MPs had issues with how to carry out their duties, they would consult the Military Police Policies and Technical Procedures manual. Footnote 1542 Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore was asked about the notion of a pre-investigation investigation, i.e. , an initial duty to ask questions before commencing an actual investigation. He thought it was “ fair to say there are situations that you come across that you’re not ready yet to say there’s an offence associated with this, but it prompts you to start asking more questions. ” Footnote 1543 Based on everything he knew and everything he was hearing during the timeframe of this complaint, Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore never developed the suspicion the Commander had a culpable state of mind at the time of transfer. He saw nothing to “ suggest that the Commander’s state of knowledge at the time he did a specific transfer was such that he should have halted the transfer and he carried on anyway. ” Footnote 1544 Had he received a direct accusation against a commander, Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore would have caused an investigation to take place. He never did. Footnote 1545 To the extent Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore was aware there were reports of torture, such as reports in the media and possibly through the court process, he also had information the transfers were halted on two occasions. This indicated to him people were keeping an eye on the process and doing what they were supposed to do. Footnote 1546 All told, Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore never formed a reasonable suspicion the Task Force Commanders in Afghanistan had committed an offence. Footnote 1547 He would not have expected his military police to self-initiate an investigation if they themselves had not formulated a reasonable suspicion of criminal behaviour. In the same vein, given he personally did not have such a suspicion, Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore felt he had not incurred a professional responsibility to conduct an investigation. He made inquiries in a general sense about the detainee process, but did not feel, for example, he had a professional obligation to seek out the site visit reports or additional information on the detainee process. Footnote 1548 On a final note, Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore received copies of some type of legal advice on the detainee question, which seems to have come via CEFCOM and JAG . In this respect, then, he appears to have been privy to some of the legal advice the Canadian Forces were receiving on the detainee issue. Footnote 1549 16.8.2 Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore’s Responsibility for the NIS The Commission heard evidence from Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore he met with the Commanding Officer of the NIS , LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick, to discuss the allegations in the Amnesty/ BCCLA complaint after it was filed on June 12, 2008. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore testified the purpose of this meeting was to consider whether, given the allegations in the Amnesty/ BCCLA complaint, there should be some police investigative action specifically into the issue whether Commanders had acted illegally by ordering the transfer of detainees. It was concluded at this meeting, in light of ongoing NIS investigations, if there was evidence or allegations against a Commander and his state of knowledge when he ordered the transfer of a detainee, this would come to light and prompt further investigation into that issue. Footnote 1550 This, Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore said, was a reference to everything under the OP CENTIPEDE umbrella, as well as the work done by Inspector Gfellner in Camel Spider, which, at the time, was wrapping up. Footnote 1551 Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore stated the following: I do remember discussing this with Lieutenant Colonel Garrick and he felt that a number of the allegations that were referred to in the Amnesty complaint were already under investigation. I believe we also at that time discussed with respect to CAMEL SPIDER that inspector George Gfellner was being sent into theatre as well and that Lieutenant Colonel Garrick had asked him specifically to have a look, as we had asked others, ask questions about the transfer process and see what people say. Footnote 1552 Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore does not appear to have had the notion of an investigation into the Globe and Mail articles in mind during this conversation with LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick. It appears from LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick’s evidence that it was under LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick’s supervision in late April 2007 that these articles were added to the collection of investigations which eventually became Operation Centipede. Footnote 1553 By all indications, therefore, Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore was not personally even aware of this at the time the articles were released, or at any point during the timeframe of this complaint. This is confirmed by the fact Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore did not recall the Globe and Mail investigation was one of the investigations discussed on June 12, 2008 as being part of the Op Centipede fold. Footnote 1554 Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore expected, as of June 12, 2008 and, indeed, prior to then, the ongoing NIS investigations would answer the question of the legality of the transfers, even though he understood post-transfer abuse was not the specific subject of those investigations: “ … we had a number of investigations now that were focusing on issues around that, enough so that if there were allegations against a specific Commander and his state of knowledge when he transferred a detainee, that those would come to light and then prompt an investigation into that very issue. ” Footnote 1555 Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore’s expectation was seemingly based on certain assumptions about the quality of the ensuing NIS investigative effort. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore testified he was not satisfied with the pace of the NIS ’ Op Centipede investigation. He ascribed this in part to a resourcing issue, which meant some investigations were just taking longer than anyone would have liked. Footnote 1556 With particular reference to the “ investigation ” into the Graeme Smith articles contained within Op Centipede, Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore was even hesitant to call it an investigation. As described in the earlier NIS section, the closing comments of the Globe and Mail investigation would seem to suggest the investigator(s) never considered the possibility the transfer decisions themselves may have been illegal. The following is a passage from what Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore referred to as a decision not to investigate, as opposed to an actual investigation into the Globe and Mail articles: Footnote 1557 2. Although these newspaper journalists are reporting that they have interviewed former Afghan captives or at least received information concerning their treatment at the hands of the Afghan authorities, considering the general rules of evidence, the inadmissibility of statements as they pertain to hearsay information, and the lack of any other credible evidence, there is no satisfactory justification to continue to investigate. Likewise, if these reports were some how deemed to be credible, the allegations of ill-treatment are directed against the Afghan authorities. This alone excludes our jurisdictional interests and the mandate of the CFNIS … 3. To that end, any pending media reports/articles concerning the treatment of Afghan prisoners by Afghan authorities which are void of any direct accusations of criminal wrongdoings of CF members, will not be investigated by this office. This file is concluded. Footnote 1558 Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore was not sure whether he read these closing comments about the Globe and Mail articles before his term ended as CFPM . Moreover, Op Centipede came to a close after the timeframe of this complaint. During the timeframe of this complaint, it appears Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore was not even aware LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick had asked to have these articles added to the Op Centipede fold. Footnote 1559 Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore agreed, ultimately, during his tenure, no investigation was ever completed which answered the question whether the detainee transfers were legal. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore specified an NIS investigation would not have looked broadly at the legality of the detainee regime as a whole. Rather, this would be more in the nature of an investigation against the Government of Canada as a whole, and would have been within the RCMP purview. An NIS investigation, he explained, would have looked at whether a particular Commander, who transferred a particular detainee to torture, had prior knowledge to indicate the detainee would be tortured, but did it anyway. Footnote 1560 16.8.3 Issues Related to Command and Control Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore suggested his lack of command capacity over non- NIS MPs left him with no control over critical decisions being made by and about MPs . Footnote 1561 The CFPM ’s lack of command authority over MPs in theatre and at CEFCOM is a structural feature of the chain of command in the CF , and a significant consideration within the context of this complaint. The Commission notes this appears to have been addressed by a change implemented as of April 1, 2011, whereby the CFPM now has command of MPs in theatre when performing their policing duties. However, the command structure during the timeframe of this complaint seemed to dictate the flow of information (or lack of it) to the CFPM and to MPs generally. For another, it created a concern for the CFPM about the mindset of members of the MP and the perceived independence of MPs to carry out policing tasks. In particular, the CFPM expressed concern about the fact the TFPM in theatre was under the operational command of the Task Force Commander, and yet, could be called upon to question the actions of that Commander, the same individual who would later prepare his performance evaluation reports. Footnote 1562 While the Commission heard no evidence during these hearings indicating MPs felt constrained in their policing decisions by the influence the Task Force Commander could exert over him, this remained a point of concern for Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore throughout his tenure as CFPM : The major issue in my view is having the military police officers cut off from the senior MP chain of command … the sole decision maker within a different chain of command responding to a commander that then writes their evaluation. So the incentive for them is to please that Commander before anybody else. […] And then when it comes to them seeking advice from senior police officers in their chain of command, because there is no formal command link, that seeking advice is at their discretion. Footnote 1563 The reason for the lack of information flow for the military police, on the detainee question, according to Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore, was that information relating to “ operational matters ” took place within a closed circle, of which the MPs , and the CFPM , were not a part. The chain of command viewed detainees as an operational issue, not a policing issue, and therefore believed the CFPM (and by extension other MPs ) need not be involved in that process. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore testified he pushed for a different command structure during his tenure, which would see all MPs under his direct command. He felt this would have enhanced information flow among MPs and increased the chances the military police would be invited to the table for operational matters like detainees. Without this type of command and control, Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore felt left out of a lot of important operational discussions, and indicated to the Commission that requesting documents on detainees would have been seen as an intrusion into the operational field: “ … I believe, my requesting any documents without the authority of an investigation behind me would have been seen as an intrusion and I would have been pushed off. ” Footnote 1564 Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore also had no involvement or input into the role the Afghanistan Task Force Provost Marshals, and the MPs in theatre, would play in the detainee process. He was seen as a policing entity by the operational chain of command, who therefore felt he did not need to be part of the process of determining the proper role for MPs in theatre. Footnote 1565 The CFPM also had no direct input into the number of MPs to be deployed to Afghanistan, although it could be assumed his input would come through the influence he could exert on the CEFCOM PM : So you have no input into the number of MP ’s deployed? No. CEFCOM had their own military police adviser, Provost Marshal assigned to them. Typically, the way the many people within the chain of command viewed it is they wanted their MP advice from the MP that worked for them. They didn’t want to take their MP advice from somebody that was outside their system, including myself. So the result was you got the training, the experience, and the opinion of one military police person, in this case, at the Major level injected into that operation. I could try to influence that Major, but I was working against quite an information deficit. Footnote 1566 The chain of command and reporting structure was a serious concern for Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore for a considerable period of time, with senior MPs in theatre not reporting to him, and information not being forwarded to him for action he, as CFPM , may have considered necessary to take. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore referred in his testimony to the chain of command for MPs being “ siloed ”, resulting in the command structure itself having a detrimental effect on the system of policing in the CF : I’ve, well, I’ve written numerous letters, papers, conducted many presentations on the topic. But from the time I took over as Canadian Forces Provost Marshal, I think this was probably the issue that took up the majority of my time. I tried to focus on, tried to stay away from chasing symptoms of problems and go after the problem itself. And in my view, the chain of command for the military police was siloed in such a way that you did not have one formed unit, you had a whole bunch of series, pockets of them across the country. So you had military police men and women, some of them senior, some of them not terribly senior that are reporting directly to a Commander. And that Commander writes their evaluation at the end of the year and that Commander has, in many cases, a limited knowledge of policing and you know, let’s face it, a police investigation is never a convenient thing. So it could often be perceived as an inhibitor in certain situations when operations are moving very, very fast. So in my view, having the military police siloed off in many different chains of command, it effected a number of issues. All that I’ve outlined in the documents that I’ve referred to the Vice, to the Chief of Defence Staff. But the overall result was that in my view, the policing system in the Canadian Forces was not was below that of Canada and not because of the men and women in the military police. It was because of the system that we were working under. Footnote 1567 Finally, the Commission heard evidence, throughout the hearings, about the MP technical chain of command and the MP ‘technet’. The MP technical net is a set of vertical and lateral channels of communication between MPs at all levels. It is designed to facilitate the resolution of MP matters related to law enforcement and security inquiries. The technet is comprised of the CFPM and staff, Formation Senior MP Advisors and MP organizations. The responsibility of the MP technical chain is oversight, audit and review of MP functions. Footnote 1568 It is the only formally recognized channel of communications which allows for influencing policing across different chains of command. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore described it as an essential, but sometimes awkward, way of influencing MP decision making on policing matters. He viewed technical control as “ [...] a loose association connected by subject matter expertise. [...] But there is no, there is no command associated with technical control. You are essentially trying to influence people that are getting their taskings and directions from somebody else. ” Footnote 1569 In short, he felt the technical chain was an unwieldy way in which to run a police force for the Canadian Forces. It depended on the day-to-day discretion of each and every MP as to whether each particular piece of information coming their way should also go up the technical chain, as opposed to, or in addition to the regular CF chain of command: “ [...] we had a lot of very intelligent, responsive and dedicated people within the military police as well that would make every effort to advise us if something important was going on, but that was at their discretion. ” Footnote 1570 As described earlier, the Commission heard evidence from individuals at CEFCOM , such as LGen ( ret’d ) Gauthier, LGen Deschamps, and Ms. Duschner. These witnesses described a debate or discussions occurring in the first half of 2007 about the extent to which MPs should be the repository of information about the detainee process, and about disciplining the MP technet. At first, it appeared to the Commission the CEFCOM hierarchy wished somehow to limit or entirely shut down the flow of information through the MP technical net, at least on the detainee issue. LGen Deschamps and LGen ( ret’d ) Gauthier made it clear this was not the case. The intent was merely to ensure all information relevant to operations made its way up the operational chain of command, and did not somehow remain exclusively within the MP ranks where operations personnel would have no access to it. This was what MGen Deschamps and LGen ( ret’d ) Gauthier suggested had occurred in relation to the Attaran complaint, and the information about those detainees. Nevertheless, in hearing this evidence, it was clear to the Commission discussion had occurred, at senior levels within the CEFCOM chain of command, about the role MPs would play in the detainee information retention process, and about disciplining the technical chain in order to ensure operationally important information made its way up the operational chain of command. These discussions related to the mission-critical question of detainees, and the role MPs would play in the process. The CFPM was not a participant in this process, Footnote 1571 nor was the CEFCOM PM . Clearly, this was an important decision-making stage not only in relation to the role of the military police in the new site visit regime, but also in relation to the role they would play in assisting with the investigation and retention of information about detainees who might, one day, be prosecuted within the Afghan system. Key decisions about the MP function, and the information they would retain, were made in the absence of input from key figures in the MP hierarchy. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore’s efforts to improve the flow of information and the command structure for the military police culminated with his address to the Commander’s Council on October 17, 2008. Footnote 1572 Indeed, LGen ( ret’d ) Gauthier recalled Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore had raised these concerns in the meeting. Footnote 1573 These very fundamental issues emerged as major concerns in Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore’s testimony, and he evidently struggled with them throughout his tenure as CFPM . Throughout his tenure, he worked diligently within the CF command structure to bring about meaningful changes for the MP branch and the improvement of CF policing. Accordingly, Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore did not believe the command and control structure as it existed during the timeframe of this complaint purposefully prevented him or the other subjects of this complaint from investigating the Task Force Commanders and their decisions to transfer. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore’s concerns in this respect spoke mainly to the system in a general sense and the overall flow of information, which may have been different if his efforts to reform the command structure had succeeded during the timeframe of this complaint. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore was not implying, however, the Task Force Commanders, such as MGen Laroche and MGen ( ret’d ) Grant, in any way purposefully prevented the TFPM s in theatre from investigating the transfer decisions. Footnote 1574 The Complainants’ Submissions The Complainants submit Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore bears responsibility for a number of acts or omissions which they ascribe to him during the time period of this complaint. Generally, they say he bore ultimate responsibility as the CFPM , and as the most senior member of the military police, for a lack of investigative activity and for failures of MP education and training. In general, their written submissions state the failings for which Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore was responsible include the following, which the Complainants consider tantamount to a leadership failure: None of the allegations of detainee abuse documented throughout 2007 resulted in any review of the transfer orders. There was no MP inquiry following the allegations of torture leading to the November 2007 suspension of transfers, despite the fact the detainee interviewed for the November 5, 2007 DFAIT report was very likely tortured by the NDS . Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore was aware of reports of NDS torture and testified as to his concern, but this concern amounted to a cursory and inadequate investigation. When further reports of post-transfer abuse emerged, he declined to devote any resources for further inquiry and failed to take the necessary steps to ensure Canadian commanders were fulfilling their legal obligations. During his command there was virtually no activity on the Globe and Mail investigations for a significant period of time, a problem for which Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore was ultimately responsible. He failed to provide adequate training and education for MPs , and briefings for NIS commanders, on reports of post-transfer abuse and the potential legal issues concerning the post-transfer treatment of detainees. Submissions on Behalf of Capt(N) ( ret’d ) S. Moore The submissions of Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore point to a number of factors which, he submits, demonstrate his actions were reasonable in the circumstances. In those submissions, Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore referred throughout his evidence to what he saw as a problem with the chain of command structure. Under that structure, although he was CFPM he had no command authority over the majority of the military police in the Canadian Forces. This significant impediment was noted by the Commission in the Attaran complaint, where the Commission recommended a new and more complete command and control structure which allowed the CFPM to fulfill the important responsibilities of that office (Recommendation 1(a)). Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore had made considerable efforts to try to change the status quo. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore submitted, because detainee handling was seen as an operational and not a policing matter, the CFPM had very little, if any, input. He lobbied for a role to be played by the CFPM in decisions with respect to processes involving detainees similar to that played by the Royal Provost Marshal in Great Britain. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore submits that the view detainee handling was an operational matter drove the flow of information concerning detainees post-transfer. The military police were not provided with post-transfer information. The C4 communications which would have included site visit reports and the concerns of Richard Colvin were not distributed to the CEFCOM PM , and therefore could not be forwarded by them to the CFPM . Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore testified he was not consulted on the arrangement for the transfer of detainees between the Canadian Forces and Afghanistan signed on December 18, 2005. However, he submits it was reasonable for him to assume the Government had done its due diligence in crafting the agreement and it was legal. The subsequent arrangement of May 3, 2007 strengthened the original agreement in a number of ways. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore submits the evidence shows a commitment to the human rights of detainees by all concerned with the transfer policy and process. When problems were identified, they were not ignored but assessed and responded to with thought and care. This is evidenced by monitoring, suspending transfers when there were concerns, improving agreements and monitoring procedures. The process was taken seriously, overseen at very high levels, and subject to extensive legal review. Around the time of the first AIC / BCCLA complaint, Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore started to think about the issue of post-transfer treatment of detainees. He assumed in formulating its transfer policy, the Government had crafted a legal regime and it would develop a process where detainees would not face a risk of torture. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore submits these were reasonable assumptions. According to Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore, the legality of a transfer order depends on the Task Force Commander’s state of knowledge with respect to the risk of torture associated with that particular transfer. The fact an allegation of torture is subsequently made does not reveal the Task Force Commander’s knowledge at the time of transfer. This information would be necessary to cause an investigation since, without it, there would be nothing on which to base a reasonable suspicion a crime had been committed. The factors influencing the CFPM ’s thinking an investigation was not required are said to include the following: The Rideout/Blizard Report dated June 27, 2007. Following the original AIC / BCCLA complaint, he directed the CO / NIS to examine current and past investigations to see if there was any link between them and the issue of post-transfer abuse. He was told there was no need for an investigation. No concerns were brought to the attention of Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore by the TFPM s. He knew the TFPM s and had confidence in their integrity and commitment to duty. The MPCC did not refer any evidence of an offence to him during its investigation of the original AIC / BCCLA complaint. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore reasonably expected existing investigations, including Camel Spider and Centipede (which was actually a collection of investigations), would uncover any allegations around transfer orders and the Task Force Commander’s state of knowledge, although this was not their actual subject matter. The broadening of the Camel Spider mandate showed an effort on the part of the CFPM to become aware of the situation. He acknowledges in his submissions it appears Centipede “ was lacking in vigour ”, and the shape of the investigation envisaged by the CO / NIS did not square with what appeared to have actually been done. However, there was at the time an expectation these investigations would uncover any issue around the transfer orders. It was reasonable for Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore to believe, with respect to the Federal Court litigation, the cases were being monitored by JAG lawyers who knew more about the issue than he did. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore had a level of confidence in the Task Force Commanders and a belief they would follow the law. He knew decisions were being made with the advice of lawyers and other advisors. Because the process involved a number of people, if something were wrong it would be brought to the attention of the MPs . No complaint or allegation was ever made to the military police about Task Force Commanders “ illegally ” ordering transfers. In the absence of a complaint, there was no cause to launch a formal investigation. Simply requesting documents short of a formal investigation would have been seen as an “ intrusion ”. Conclusions Regarding Captain (N) ( ret’d ) S. Moore Having considered the totality of the evidence and submissions, the Commission is not persuaded that Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore’s conduct failed to meet the standards expected of a police officer. We note in particular the following points in reaching this conclusion: Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore knew Canada’s detainees were to be handled in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, and from the outset of the timeframe of this complaint was attuned to the legal issues surrounding the transfer of detainees to a potential risk of torture. For various reasons for which the Commission concludes he is not personally responsible, Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore had a limited degree of information about the detainee process and the potential risks of mistreatment of detainees post transfer. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore was not provided the site visit reports from DFAIT visits, nor was he privy to core correspondence and the high-level decision-making process with respect to detainee policy. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore was conscious of the February 21, 2007 Amnesty/ BCCLA complaint, and from then forward, he took several steps to monitor the detainee process and address the allegations against him personally. These steps included the following: Requesting, via LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick, his NIS Commander, an independent body investigate his role in the detainee transfer decisions Directing LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick to review existing NIS investigations to see whether they raised concerns about post-transfer abuse Making inquiries of individuals involved with the detainee process in theatre to canvass their confidence in the process Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore reasonably expected that if there was evidence the Task Force Commanders were knowingly transferring detainees to a real risk of torture, or wilfully blind to this risk, someone involved with this process would report this information to the police. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore also reasonably expected the existing investigations into the detainee question would uncover any such information if it existed. On top of this, he took, of his own accord, the steps described above to further monitor any potential legal issues related to the detainee transfer regime. It was reasonable that Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore did not develop a suspicion whether the Task Force Commanders were behaving illegally. He eventually saw evidence that when problems arose with the transfer regime, the transfers were suspended, and improvements implemented. His decision to nevertheless monitor the situation in various ways showed him to possess foresight and a proactive attitude. During the timeframe of this complaint, Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore was not aware the Globe and Mail articles on post-transfer abuse were being considered within the context of Operation Centipede. Therefore, he could not have provided any input or direction with respect to an investigation of the allegations contained therein and would have had no reason to expect, during the timeframe of this complaint, that the ultimate investigation into those articles would leave much to be desired. With respect to command and control issues, the CFPM was significantly disengaged from the post-transfer follow-up process, even though at one point it was contemplated the military police might be involved in the post-transfer monitoring regime. This was not due to personal failings on the part of Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore. In contrast, the Commission notes the significant responsibilities for detainees assigned to the UK Royal Military Police, including monitoring post-transfer treatment and follow-ups. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore cannot be personally faulted for the fact he was kept out of the loop, since this seems to have been a product of the very command structure he was attempting to change. The technical chain was an unwieldy way for the CFPM to gather information about potential concerns and illegalities related to the detainee transfer process in theatre. Indeed, the Commission saw much evidence to indicate, not only were the military police structurally “ siloed ” away from operational information potentially relevant to their policing function, but also, from one rotation to the next, there were deficiencies in the information flow between the military police leaving theatre and those arriving. The Commission also has very serious concerns about the workload of the NIS and their ability, given the workload, to fully realize their mandate as a serious crimes investigation unit in theatre. The Commission notes the CFPM continually attempted to exert greater control over the MP information and decision-making environment in order to enhance MP policing capabilities, and perhaps address these deficiencies with respect to staffing and information flow, both in theatre and in other contexts. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore testified that throughout his tenure as CFPM he worked diligently to bring about meaningful changes for the MP branch and the improvement of CF policing. He had serious concerns about the command and control structure within which the military police worked, and the ability of his police force to balance the operational priorities of their various commanders against policing concerns. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore did not believe those within the operational command and control structure deliberately prevented him or the other subjects of this complaint from investigating the Task Force Commanders and their decisions to transfer. His concerns about the command and control system were more general and systemic in nature. Finding #8: The Commission finds the allegations made by AIC and BCCLA against Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Steven Moore in the June 12, 2008 complaint to be unsubstantiated. Viewing the evidence as a whole, the Commission finds no grounds to conclude Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore should have investigated the Task Force Commanders while in theatre, or should have caused such an investigation to occur. The Commission finds his actions under the circumstances prevailing at the time met the standard of a reasonable police officer. XVII. The Commission's Findings and Recommendations 17.1 Commission Commentary on the Hearing Process The Commission believes it important to state its views on the significant obstacles encountered in obtaining necessary documentary disclosure and witness testimony. As described earlier, these obstacles included: the Government refusing to consider options to expedite the s. 38 process, such as negotiating a disclosure agreement with security cleared Commission counsel; the Government invoking s. 38 of the Canada Evidence Act to block Commission interviews of witnesses and access to their testimony, notably Mr. Colvin; the Government’s initial refusal to provide any redacted documents to the Commission until all of the documents had been vetted; significant delays in documentary disclosure, and in many instances, the outright refusal to act on document requests; ongoing disputes over relevance of documents and unilateral determinations by Government officials based on opaque screening criteria; the Government’s invoking s. 38 to attempt to have questioning of witnesses take place in secret and out of public view; and the Government requiring an undertaking from Mr. Wallace not to give documents to the Commission. Unfortunately, this Commission is not the first tribunal to encounter these types of difficulties. In fact, many parallels were found between this Commission’s experiences and those commented on by the Somalia Commission of Inquiry in its 1997 Report, as discussed below. 17.1.1 Commission Comments on the Documentary Disclosure Process With the Commission’s decision to conduct public interest hearings in March 2008, and through to November 2009, the doors were basically slammed shut on document disclosure. The Commission did not receive a single, new document from the Government throughout that time period despite many requests. Many excuses were given for this approximately 21 month dry spell in document production and none were very convincing from the Commission’s perspective. For example, the Government took the unreasonable position it did not need to produce documents to the Commission if it unilaterally considered them to be outside the Commission’s mandate. This stance disregarded the authority of the Commission, under Rule 7 of the Rules of Procedure for Hearings Before the Military Police Complaints Commission , SOR/2002-241, to make its own independent determinations as to its jurisdiction. It also disregarded the authority given to the Commission under section 250.41(1) of the National Defence Act , which gives the Commission, not the Government, the power to decide what documents and things are considered necessary to the full investigation and consideration of the matters before the Commission. Justice de Montigny of the Federal Court of Canada affirmed this important principle, and validated the scope of the Commision’s information/documentation requests, when he said: “ [...] it is for the Commission, not for the government, to determine ultimately what documents are relevant to its inquiry. If it were otherwise, the Commission would be at the mercy of the body it is supposed to investigate. This was clearly not the intent of Parliament. ” Footnote 1575 Unfortunately, throughout a significant portion of these proceedings, the Commission believes Parliament’s intent was confounded. While the Commission recognizes there were jurisdictional challenges throughout these proceedings, this still did not explain why documents relating to such clearly relevant matters as NIS investigations into detainee handling were not disclosed or provided to the Commission for a lengthy period of time, despite the fact they clearly related to an unchallenged and central aspect of the Commission’s jurisdiction. The first request for such documents was made as far back as November 2008, Footnote 1576 yet it was not until a meeting on September 25, 2009, that Government counsel advised Commission counsel of the existence of documents relating to MP investigations. Footnote 1577 The Commission regularly offered to cooperate and assist in speeding up document production and redaction, for example by pre-reviewing documents to eliminate those it did not consider necessary and thereby reduce the redaction tasks. Even though the Commission is not an entity on the s. 38 Schedule to which protected information could be disclosed during public interest hearings (despite having requested, without success, to be added to the Schedule), s. 38.031 of the Canada Evidence Act still permitted the Attorney General of Canada to enter into a disclosure agreement. Such a compromise was refused and there simply appeared to be no desire to look at alternatives that would have expedited the Commission’s work. Moreover, even though document production eventually occurred, the Commission remained concerned throughout the whole course of the public hearings with the Government’s unilateral approach to document production and the screening out of documents, as described inter alia in the testimony of Maj Gagnon, and in numerous subsequent interchanges between the Commission and Government counsel. The Commission understands some document screening must take place to avoid having the Commission swamped with masses of irrelevant documents, and the Government devoting time to unnecessarily redacting documents for which the Commission has no need. Precisely for that reason, Commission counsel offered to assist with document review, and the offer was soundly rejected. The Commission believes that the process of document selection and production must be transparent to the Commission if it is to properly discharge its mandate and maintain public confidence in its independence. Where, as happened here, the Commission increasingly lacks confidence in the document screening and production process; the Government asserts a unilateral right to issue guidelines for production and to make decisions as to the relevance or necessity of documents; and the Government appears to view the Commission as an adversary, there are important implications for the independence of the Commission. It was particularly disturbing for the Commission to learn decisions not to produce documents were taken by a committee of the highest ranking civil servants, from various branches of the Government of Canada. Added to this was the fact that, at times, comments made by Government counsel (who simultaneously acted as counsel for seven of the subjects) towards the Commission’s need for documentary disclosure verged on antipathy. At one point, after some pressing from the Commission on how long it would take to produce documents, the Government counsel responded curtly that the Commission would get the documents “ …when they are good and ready ”. Footnote 1578 Counsel later apologized for this remark. It is understandable in the heat of the moment remarks might be made spontaneously that are immediately regretted. However, the Commission did consider that this comment, when coupled with the other issues and exchanges around timely document disclosure, reflected an overall attitude of antipathy on the part of the Government towards the Commission and its task, and a general, adversarial approach. In the Commission’s opinion, the business of the Government during a public inquiry should be to advance the public interest in having a full and fair process, and to uphold the Rule of Law, not to be unnecessarily adversarial: see, e.g. , Adam M. Dodek, Lawyering at the Intersection of Public Law and Legal Ethics: Government Lawyers as Custodians of the Rule of Law , 2010 Dal. L.J. 1, at p. 11. It bears repeating that this Commission is an independent, quasi-judicial body established by Parliament under Part IV of the National Defence Act to provide oversight and greater accountability on the part of the Canadian Forces’ military police. The Commission reports to Parliament through the Minister of National Defence, but in the discharge of its functions the Commission is independent from both the Department of National Defence and the Canadian Forces. This independence is critical to the proper exercise of the Commission’s statutory mandate – a mandate intended to foster public confidence in the military police. To support the Commission’s mandate, the National Defence Act grants the Commission significant powers to summon and enforce the attendance of witnesses to give evidence under oath, and to require the production of documents and things under their control the Commission considers necessary for the full investigation and consideration of the matters before it. The Commission’s power to issue a summons and require the production of documents considered necessary for its investigation is found in section 250.41 of the National Defence Act . These powers are given to the Commission to serve the public interest. It is self-evident that the ability to obtain timely production of documentation is absolutely fundamental to the Commission being able to conduct the full, independent investigation that the National Defence Act requires. Section 250.41(1)(a) of that Act grants the Commission significant powers to require the production of documents that it [ i.e. , the Commission and not the Government] considers necessary to a full investigation. This is a decision the Commission is authorized by statute to make based on the Commission’s own assessment of the needs of its investigative effort. During a tribunal’s investigative stage, the test for relevance should be applied broadly by Commission counsel, as stated by Professor Ed Ratushny in his text, The Conduct of Public Inquiries: Law, Policy and Practice (2009) : “ In such inquiries, hearings counsel should cast the net of potential relevance very broadly. ” Footnote 1579 The “ failure to investigate ” complaint alleged the existence of awareness of likely torture, and of reports pertaining to the alleged torture of detainees after they were ordered transferred. This included awareness on the part of the military police and the senior military officers who ordered the transfers. Put more bluntly, the Complainants alleged crimes were or may have been committed that warranted a police investigation. Allegations of possible criminal conduct based on “ awareness ” of the likelihood of torture, and “ ordering the transfer of detainees ” despite “ compelling first-hand reports ” that previous CF detainees were tortured (to quote the specific wording of this complaint, P2), were thus matters before the Commission. The Commission had a public duty to cast its net broadly enough to get a sense of the overall information environment, and the degree to which the MP were branched into that environment. This was necessary to conduct a full and thorough investigation into the serious allegations against the subjects. It is therefore unfortunate that the document production process carried out by the Government in response to this inquiry was characterized by an attitude of aversion to, or antipathy towards, the public hearing, and that the Government’s actions discussed above led to unnecessary costs and significant delays to the Commission and the other parties. The reasonableness of the Commission’s position on disclosure is confirmed in the comments of the Federal Court indicating documents are the “ lifeblood ” of an inquiry, and it is for the Commission, not the Government, to determine what documents are necessary to fulfil its mandate. Footnote 1580 17.1.2 Commission Comments on Access to Witnesses In addition to document issues, the Government’s uncooperative stance was also demonstrated in the difficulties experienced by the Commission in accessing witnesses for pre-hearing interviews and even into the hearings themselves. Government counsel took the position early in the process that any interviews with Government employees must be arranged only through his office since he claimed to be the legal counsel for these Government employees, and in particular the 38 individuals whom the Commission had advised it wished to interview. This position caused difficulties for Commission counsel, as described earlier. Richard Colvin was one witness who was willing to attend a pre-hearing interview with the Commission and to testify at the hearing. Subsequently the Government issued a section 38 notice over all the information that Mr. Colvin could have provided to the Commission in September 2009. He was thus prevented from providing information to the Commission even though he considered it relevant and necessary to the Commission’s investigation. Mr. Colvin could not provide documents to the Commission, be interviewed by Commission counsel, or testify before the Commission due to the s. 38 notice. Subsequently, Government counsel advised during a meeting on September 25, 2009 that s. 38 notices would likely be issued over all anticipated Government witness testimony, unless a compromise could be reached not involving public airing of their evidence. Indeed, the Government’s position would have required most of the questioning of witnesses to take place in private. Footnote 1581 Such a process is inimical to the very purpose of a public inquiry. It is significant to the Commission that, only months later, the s. 38 notice over the entirety of Mr. Colvin’s anticipated evidence was retracted, and Mr. Colvin eventually testified, in public. Albeit with some remaining constraints imposed by s. 38 of the Canada Evidence Act , on October 13, 2009 the National Security Group confirmed that the affidavit Mr. Colvin had tendered to the Commission contained no sensitive information at all. This clearly put into question the justification for the earlier blanket s. 38 claim over all of Mr. Colvin’s evidence. Justice Mactavish opined in her decision refusing a stay of these proceedings, that the Government’s stated security concerns were overblown with respect to witness testimony. She determined any risks of disclosure during witness testimony could be addressed by: (1) careful preparation of witnesses; (2) summaries of anticipated evidence; (3) alert counsel ready to make timely objections; and (4) Commission counsel awareness of s. 38 obligations. She also noted public testimony had been heard numerous times, even where those witnesses were privy to protected information and required to filter what they made public through that lens: Counsel for the Attorney General conceded that witnesses in the possession of potentially injurious information do testify in various types of public hearings, including high-profile proceedings that garner a great deal of media attention. Examples of this include security certificate proceedings in this Court, as well as Commissions of Inquiry such as those involving the Air India bombing and the Maher Arar affair. Indeed, Brigadier General Joseph Paul André Deschamps testified before this Court in Amnesty #1 , in the presence of the media, with respect to issues relating to the transfer of detainees by the Canadian Forces in Afghanistan, see paras. 32–36 . There is no evidence before me that any potentially injurious information has inadvertently been disclosed by witnesses in any of these proceedings. Footnote 1582 The Commission understands there is no obligation on the part of a witness to meet with Commission counsel, but this is a form of cooperation usually extended. Such pre-hearing interviews can assist both sides by eliminating the element of surprise and, in this case, assisting to identify any valid s. 38 concerns ahead of time. The Commission concludes it did not receive Government cooperation with respect to accessing potential witnesses from the time that public interest hearings were called in March 2008 through to the end of 2009/early 2010. Indeed, the Government’s actions during that time appeared more designed to delay or prevent Commission access to witnesses, as exemplified by the case of Mr. Colvin. This impeded the Commission’s work during that timeframe. 17.1.3 Commission Comments on Government of Canada Use of s. 38 of the Canada Evidence Act In the Commission’s view, this case illustrates the real dangers that s. 38 of the Canada Evidence Act poses to independent commissions of inquiry being able to access relevant and necessary information, as well as witnesses. Broadly invoked, as it was here, s. 38 has the potential to completely stymie a public inquiry. Section 38 is intended to protect sensitive and potentially injurious information from public disclosure. The type of information meant to be protected includes information relating to international relations, national defence, or national security. The Commission is bound by law to ensure such sensitive or potentially injurious information is not released publicly, and takes this responsibility seriously. Given the continuing deployment of Canada’s troops in Afghanistan, the Commission was keenly aware of the need to ensure sensitive or potentially injurious information would not be compromised as a result of its hearings. The Commission thus fully understands the importance of protecting the type of information covered by s. 38. The danger lies in the potential for overreaching, that is, invoking s. 38 to prevent disclosure of information belonging, and which can safely be placed in, the public domain. Both the Arar Inquiry and the Air India Inquiry dealt with s. 38 and national security information, and were still able to address significant issues in public, contributing to the national debate on civil liberties, the obligations of government, the public’s right to know, and national security in the 21st century. The list of scheduled entities entitled to receive information under s. 38 includes such entities as boards of inquiry under the National Defence Act , the Public Service Relations Board, the Information Commissioner, the Privacy Commissioner, the Security Intelligence Review Committee, the Arar Inquiry, the Air India Inquiry, the Almalki Inquiry and the Public Sector Integrity Commissioner. However, in the course of the AIC / BCCLA complaint, the Commission’s two requests to be added to this list of like agencies were turned down. The Commission has already noted that in advance of announcing public hearings, it did receive non-redacted material during the investigation portion of the first Transfer Complaint. The Commission was thus able to view that material and safeguard it. Section S18 of the Afghanistan Public Interest Hearings Rules, issued for the public hearings, contemplated that some evidence might need to be kept confidential and not be publicly released. For this reason, the Commission’s hearing procedures called for evidence to be classified as either public “ P ” or confidential “ C ”. This designation of confidentiality extended to the transcripts of evidence heard in camera . The Rules also provided documents filed with the Commission in the course of a hearing in private had to be kept separate from the public record. Accordingly, the fact information was disclosed to the Commission in the course of the public hearings did not mean the information would inevitably become public. Sensitive information would be kept confidential in accordance with the Rules governing the hearing. The issue of the Government invoking s. 38 over documents and witnesses during the public hearing obviously became a major point of contention. The Commission faced significant delays and obstacles related to s. 38 of the Canada Evidence Act , and the need for documents to be screened and redacted before receiving them. The process was time-consuming and could have been avoided, or at least shortened, had the Government adopted a more cooperative posture. The opportunities for compromise existed. On two occasions the Commission wrote to the Minister of National Defence to request the Commission be designated as an entity on the s. 38 schedule of designated entities to the Canada Evidence Act pursuant to sections 38.01(6)(d) and 38.01(8) of that Act. The dates of these requests were July 18, 2008 and November 28, 2008. The Chairperson at the time indicated this would clearly allow the Commission to efficiently obtain information relevant to the discharge of its statutory mandate of providing independent oversight of military policing. By letter dated January 16, 2009, the Minister replied stating: Having reviewed this matter, I am satisfied that the existing scheme continues to be appropriate for the Commission at this time. As you have pointed out, your request would have both policy and legislative implications which would require further study. As your letters also touch on matters concerning the application of section 38 of the Canada Evidence Act , I am forwarding your letters to the Assistant Deputy Attorney General, Mr. Donald J. Rennie, who exercises delegated authority under the Act. The Assistant Deputy Attorney General did not respond further to the Commission’s request. However, even without the Commission being scheduled, it was always open to the Attorney General of Canada to negotiate a disclosure arrangement with the Commission pursuant to s. 38.031, something that the Attorney General consistently refused to do. The Commission has thus been left with the abiding impression that s. 38 became a litigation tool throughout these proceedings, whose purpose became at least as much to delay the work of the Commission as it was to protect truly sensitive information. The former Chairperson summarized the Commission’s concerns as follows: Again, this case is not about national security. It is about the government invoking its own review processes, which have been in progress for almost 11 months [as of October 2009] now without producing any results, to refuse the production of documents that would assist the subjects and the Commission. It is about the government insisting on distinguishing between formal and informal reviews, refusing to produce over-redacted documents, constantly revising the processes and timelines necessary to review documents, and attempting to explain the delay away on the ground of lack of clarity or overbreadth of the document requests made, even where subsets of clearly relevant materials have been identified and reviewed. Footnote 1583 All told, the Commission holds the view that the Government’s actions with respect to the s. 38 process promoted “ […] public suspicion and cynicism about legitimate claims by the Government of national security confidentiality ”, the same concern stated by Commissioner O’Connor in the Arar Policy Report. Footnote 1584 The other elephant in the room during the entire hearing process, of course, was the ever-present question as to exactly what information was being removed from the documents in the name of national security. This issue sometimes took on surreal proportions, as was exemplified by the following exchange between Mr. Colvin, Mr. Préfontaine and the Commission, in which Mr. Préfontaine cross-examined Mr. Colvin on information behind a redaction in his reports, information which Mr. Préfontaine had seen, but counsel representing other parties, and the Commission, had not: So this is your subtle signal? I would disagree with you there, Mr. Préfontaine. If we had access to the unredacted version, then there would be some crucial information, additional information, which obviously we don’t have because of the redactions. Yes. -- which would -- I have had access to the unredacted document. Yes. I don’t see there anything that is missing or crucial or important, Mr. Colvin. Oh, then I am afraid, then, you would be acknowledging your -- that you are new to this issue, because if you were someone who was involved in this file, involved in Afghanistan involved on this issue, what has been redacted is extremely important, and it is critical to understanding that there is nothing particularly subtle about this message. I don’t agree it is a subtle signal. Okay. And the substance of what you in this message -- not in your head, but in this message -- what you impart to the reader and the substance of what you have to say about treatment of detainees is contained in paragraphs 20 to 23; correct? Correct, and in the summary and conclusions. And in the summary where you repeat the introduction? The conclusion, yes. The conclusion, sorry. Yes, that’s correct. Which echoes word for word? Yes. And there is also the follow up that also relates to that issue. That is paragraph 25. Yes. And the Commission will decide whether it was too subtle for the reader to pick up your meaning. I think the Commissioner is only given the redacted version, so he may have some difficulty fully assessing the subtlety, or lack thereof, of these reports. And I recognize it is difficult for the Commission to have to contend with -- without ability of independent verification what you say or, for that matter, what I say. Yes. I am fully prepared for the Commission to see the unredacted version and to form his own opinion. So would I, but it is not my call to make, Mr. Colvin. THE CHAIR: Can I just ask, did you say that the information contained in the unredacted really isn’t critical, or did I misread that? MR. PRÉFONTAINE: No, you didn’t, Mr. Stannard. THE CHAIR: Just a real silly question, then. Any reason why we don’t have it? MR. PRÉFONTAINE: Because it would be injurious to either national defence, international relations or national security. THE CHAIR: Even though it is not critical information? MR. PRÉFONTAINE: It might be the information has nothing to do with what Mr. Colvin makes it out to be. Footnote 1585 This exemplified how s. 38 claims pose problems for tribunals, since in the absence of the redacted information the Commission could not resolve for itself the disagreement that erupted over the significance of the redacted information. It was manifestly unfair to try to impugn Mr. Colvin’s testimony by purporting to refer to the substance of redacted information that Mr. Colvin himself was prohibited from disclosing or discussing. It was also inappropriate, in the Commission’s opinion, for counsel for seven of the subjects to have seen behind the redactions, while counsel for all other parties, and the Commission, had not. This essentially meant that the subjects represented by Department of Justice counsel had the benefit of privileged access to information that the other parties and the Commission itself did not have. Finally, it should also be noted Mr. Colvin was testifying under oath, whereas the unsworn opinion of counsel as to the content of the redactions did not comprise evidence. 17.1.4 Claims of Cabinet Confidentiality Under s. 39 of the Canada Evidence Act In late spring 2009, the Commission challenged in Federal Court certain redactions made to the documents. Through negotiations, counsel for the Commission and counsel for the Government reached compromises to the point where the Commission felt it could proceed with the redacted documents. The Commission recognized that a Court challenge to Government redactions was only likely to add further to the delays the Commission wanted to avoid. One claim of privilege advanced by the Government was the claim certain redactions were justified under s. 39 of the Canada Evidence Act . This section deals with confidences of the Queen’s Privy Council for Canada. Under s. 39, a Minister of the Crown or the Clerk of the Privy Council can object to the disclosure of information by certifying in writing the information constitutes a confidence of the Queen’s Privy Council of Canada. Disclosure of that information shall then be refused without examining the information or hearing it. However, although the Government made redactions citing s. 39 grounds, no certificate in writing under s. 39 was provided to the Commission until January 20, 2012. Although the certificate itself appears to have been completed on December 7, 2011, it was not provided to the Commission until January 20, 2012, which was after the Interim Report had already been issued by the Commission. 17.1.5 Looking Back on the Somalia Inquiry: The Parallels and a Chance to Move Beyond This Commission is not the first tribunal to be confronted with difficulties in obtaining access to Government documents and evidence. As former Chairperson Peter Tinsley stated at an early stage of this Commission’s proceedings, it seemed that some of the key lessons from the Somalia experience had not been learned. This Commission was indeed struck by a number of similarities between the process issues which it faced, and the experiences reported by the Somalia Inquiry. The Somalia Inquiry mainly had to do with the actions of the Canadian military in Somalia. The Somalia Inquiry felt compelled in its Report to tell the story of DND ’s apparent reluctance to cooperate with the Inquiry when it came to transparency and disclosure of documents. The comments made by the Somalia Commission in Chapter 39 of its Report on this issue could, in many respects, be adopted almost word for word to describe the issues this Commission faced in obtaining disclosure of relevant information from the Government during these proceedings. Footnote 1586 At the outset of the Chapter on openness and disclosure, the Somalia Commission stated, “ [t]hrough its actions, DND hampered the progress and effectiveness of our Inquiry and left us with no choice but to resort to extraordinary investigative processes to discharge our mandate appropriately. ” Footnote 1587 The progress and effectiveness of this Commission were similarly hampered by the Government’s overall approach to document production, which resulted in delays and disagreements, and meant that a great deal of time and effort had to be expended pursuing documentary evidence. It should not have become necessary, in the Commission’s view, for witnesses to have to be summonsed from DND and DFAIT to explain the process of document selection and production to the Commission. The Somalia Inquiry also had to deal with DND ’s failure to comply with orders for production of documents and with what it referred to as a “ long and disillusioning process ” surrounding document production. Footnote 1588 This Commission, too, faced a “ long and disillusioning process ” of document production. Promises of cooperation, while made, were not manifested in practice. Like this Commission, the Somalia Inquiry was confronted with unilateral decision-making by the Government of Canada on the relevance of document requests to the Commission’s mandate, Footnote 1589 and repeated requests for clarification from those within DND dealing with document disclosure. Footnote 1590 On this subject the Somalia Inquiry Report said, “ [...] the Inquiry and SILT [the group created within DND to manage document production during the Somalia Inquiry] had very different views about what was important in terms of documents. ” Footnote 1591 The Somalia Commission further stated, “ … it was our role to decide what information was of importance to us, not the Department’s [...] ” Footnote 1592 This Commission was compelled to make precisely the same point on numerous occasions during its dealings with the Government over document production.
