The Somalia Inquiry also had to deal with late and last minute disclosure of documents and, in some instances, after all testimony had been heard. This Commission, too, was forced to scramble at the last minute to quickly review and assess the relevance of disclosure provided to the Commission very late in the day. Footnote 1593 One of the most striking parallels between the Somalia Inquiry and this Commission is that both inquiries found it necessary to start their hearings without having obtained complete production of documents. Both subsequently had to call witnesses to explain the delays in document production and related issues. The Somalia Report states: [...] we had no choice but to begin hearings before we had received all the documents. Evidentiary hearings began in October 1995, and as they proceeded through the fall of 1995 and continued through the winter of 1996, we continued to receive, process, and review new documents, including documents of direct relevance to the hearings already under way. Because of the serious difficulties that we had encountered in obtaining disclosure [...] we were obliged to hold public hearings to determine why we were not receiving documents necessary for us to fulfill our mandate and whether this deficiency was deliberate. Footnote 1594 These words could be applied directly to the Commission’s own public interest hearings. After encountering delays in beginning its substantive hearings due to document issues, the Commission had no choice but to begin substantive hearings with the documents that it had in March 2010. Full document production had still not been received at that time; however, the scope and pace of production continued to be an issue during the hearings proper, even as witnesses were being called to testify. As pointed out earlier, a period of 21 months passed during the early stage of the hearings without a single new document being produced by the Government. The Somalia Inquiry wrote that searches for a key set of documents only became “ frantic ” Footnote 1595 and focused when the Department of National Defence faced the possibility that the Chief of the Defence Staff would be called as a witness. This is similar to the Commission’s experience in the fall of 2009, when the extent of the Government’s non-cooperation was made publicly evident by Commission counsel and the former Chairperson, when Parliamentary Committee hearings into the detainee question began, and when both the Commission’s dilemma and the detainee questions received intense media coverage. For both inquiries, it seems it was only increasing public exposure that caused the Government to become more forthcoming with its disclosure. Also analogous are the concerns of both the Somalia Commission and this Commission about the Government’s litigious and seemingly adversarial approach to document production. The Commission was mindful of the existence of a potential or actual conflict of interest between the Government’s duty to produce documents to the Commission on the one hand, and, on the other hand, the self-interest it might have in slowing down or inhibiting disclosure of information deemed harmful to itself. The Somalia Report described the dilemma thus: [...] the purpose and design of SILT placed everyone within it in an impossible position, caught between adherence to our order of production and respect for the public inquiry process, and loyalty to their own institution and leadership – a leadership by its own admission disinclined to recognize the public’s right to information and willing to resort to legalistic hair-splitting and subterfuge to avoid divulging that information. Footnote 1596 The Commission feels obliged to call on the CFPM , the Chief of the Defence Staff, the Minister of National Defence, and the Government of Canada as a whole to review the process section of this Report in detail to understand the full extent to which the actions described above severely impeded the Commission’s ability to carry out the mandate prescribed to it by Parliament. The Complainants, the subjects, the Department of National Defence, and the public would have been much better served by a more transparent and cooperative approach. The Commission holds out the hope that future public interest investigations and hearings will be carried out in the spirit of cooperation and respect that the public has a right to expect. XVIII. Recommendations The Commission was struck throughout the hearings by the evidence it heard indicating a lack of continuity of knowledge for the military police from one Afghanistan rotation to the next. This was the case for detainee issues, in particular, but also for policing issues generally. A non-exhaustive list of examples includes the following: MP knowledge about the human rights situation in Afghanistan, and, in particular, the risk to detainees post transfer, varied from one MP to the next and from one rotation to the next, and appears to have depended on whether a particular MP showed the initiative to inform him or herself on the issue. Maj Gribble’s evidence suggested he felt he had no duty to independently examine the conduct of personnel during the previous rotation absent a specific complaint or referred file. CWO Watson ( ROTO 3) was aware that he was assisting with the investigation stemming from the Attaran complaint, but by ROTO 4, MWO ( ret’d ) Girard assisted briefly with that investigation, without knowing that he was doing so. Thus, from one NIS Detachment Commander to the next there was a serious disconnect in knowledge about an important and on-going investigation into detainee matters in Afghanistan. Knowledge of previous suspensions of transfers varied widely among the MPs interviewed, as did knowledge about Federal Court proceedings with respect to detainees and the complaints filed with this Commission. MWO ( ret’d ) Girard did not recall reviewing the technical directive applicable to his rotation, despite its importance (although LCol ( ret’d ) Garrick said the substantive information necessary to performance of his duties was reviewed in pre-deployment training). In order for an in-theatre police force to function effectively it must have a degree of continuity of knowledge and information from one rotation to the next. Important policing issues and potential crimes may go uninvestigated if in-coming MPs know too little about what went on during the rotations before them. To borrow an analogy, it would be unacceptable for the police officers of a local detachment or city police force to change entirely every six months without taking serious measures to transfer the existing knowledge base to the newcomers. And yet, the Commission saw repeated examples of MPs coming into theatre with serious information deficits on matters relevant to their policing duties arising during the previous rotation. While there was a slight overlap between successive TFPM s and NIS Detachment Commanders, the focus during that overlap appears to have been task-based and forward-looking. To allow MPs to function at their optimum level of awareness and diligence, or close to it, there must be a robust process for ensuring the transfer of theatre-specific policing knowledge from one rotation to the next. In the Commission’s view, this is not a radical or even controversial proposition. Frequently this Commission encounters reference to the significance of communicating “ lessons learned ” within the military from one rotation or operation to another. In the Commission’s view, it is in the interests of the CF and the MP branch that greater attention be paid to the transfer of information down successive rotations. It will inevitably assist the MP branch in supporting the CF ’s operational objectives. The Commission therefore makes the following recommendations: Recommendation #1: The Commission recommends that the Canadian Forces Provost Marshal implement measures and standards to ensure that MPs deployed during future conflicts are provided the necessary baseline information to be fully educated on potential policing issues stemming from the previous rotation. In order for the MP units in theatre to perform as a seamless policing unit, this baseline information should include: End of Tour reports provided to the incoming TFPM and NIS Detachment Commander before or soon after they arrive in theatre; A brief summary of on-going investigations and investigations completed in the previous rotation; A brief summary of all applicable orders and/or directives particularly applicable to the MP in theatre, such as technical directives and theatre standing orders; Pre-deployment training on the humanitarian and human rights situation and risks in theatre, and how this might impact on MP policing duties and expectations; Information on potential policing issues for the incoming MP units, based on the policing environment in the previous rotation and any information available to the CFPM ; and Given the sensitivity and mission critical importance of detainee issues, an assessment of potential policing issues relative to the treatment and transfer of detainees in theatre, and a briefing on any current or past investigations into this or related subject matter. The CFPM should ensure this information is made available to any MP for whom it is relevant to their duties, and in particular the CEFCOM PM , the CO NIS and the TFPM . In accepting this recommendation, the CDS responded: “This recommendation has already been implemented to place greater emphasis on training taken to ensure that Military Police ( MP ) deployed during future conflicts are provided the necessary baseline information to be fully educated on potential policing issues. With the CFPM ’s assumption of command of all police assets in the CF , the CFPM ensures that MP command teams and all CFMP personnel deployed have been provided with policing information that is relevant to their duties. The CFPM also maintains situational awareness and oversight of all policing issues facing MP in Canada and abroad. All MP deploying to theatre are required to undergo pre-deployment training which includes all of the theatre-specific issues with which MP need to be familiarized in order to perform their duties. This would include but not be limited to training on the humanitarian and human rights situation and risks in theatre. The staff of the Canadian Forces National Investigation Service deploying to theatre receives a handover brief of ongoing investigations and investigations completed in the previous rotation where applicable. As part of pre-deployment training where required, MP undertake a five-day course provided by the staff of the Canadian Forces Service Prison and Detention Barracks related to potential policing issues relative to the handling, treatment and transfer of detainees in theatre.” The Commission is satisfied with this response to its recommendation. The Commission also identified serious problems with reporting, accountability and information flow from MPs in theatre up through the technical chain to the CO NIS and the CFPM . It appeared there was a “ silo ” effect such that information about what the military police were doing tended to stay within the chain of command in Afghanistan or at CEFCOM , and only intermittently made its way up the technical chain to the CFPM . The following is an illustrative list of these problems: Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore was not aware that detainee transfers had ceased until long after the fact, nor did he learn until much later about the fact that implements of torture had been found during the site visit that led to the stoppage. Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore was not aware that, at one point in time, Maj Fraser (the ROTO 1 TFPM ) had been identified as the national point of contact on detainee issues in Afghanistan. No information went through the technical chain from LCol Boot about the CEFCOM investigation/fact-check into the Graeme Smith Globe and Mail articles, even though this information would clearly have been of significance to some of the NIS ’s investigations. The CFPM was not aware that from January to May 2007 significant discussions were occurring at CEFCOM about the role that MPs would play in the detainee process and the degree to which they would be the repository of information stemming from that process. This was despite the fact the CEFCOM PM was consulted on this question during those months. At one point in early 2007, Maj Hudson provided the chain of command with his opinion that his military police were not in a position to assist with post-transfer monitoring, whereas later in 2007, the CFPM was saying just the opposite to the VCDS when asked his opinion about a potential role for the MP post-transfer. There appears not to have been a coordinated MP position on this issue. The CFPM was never informed of the concerns raised by MPs in theatre during ROTO 3 about their potential liability with respect to detainees. All told, it appeared to the Commission that military police involved with in-theatre matters, at CEFCOM and in Afghanistan, had no guidance as to when they should be ensuring that information with potential policing applications made it up the military police chain of command for assessment and guidance as to the appropriate MP response. As LGen ( ret’d ) Gauthier noted for operations issues, centralizing information allows commanders to make appropriate decisions and to properly instruct people under their command in their essential duties. MPs in theatre can at times face all-consuming workloads and highly focused operational demands. They cannot always be expected to maintain a comprehensive overview of trends or developments which may require their attention. Because of this, the CFPM or his designates should become the central repository of all information relevant to the execution of deployed MPs ’ essential policing duties so that they can be provided with proper guidance. The CFPM should ensure that he or his designates maintain sufficient information to have a “ big picture view ” on all policing issues of strategic or high importance, with a view to ensuring that appropriate engagement and direction on policing issues is forthcoming when appropriate. The Commission therefore makes the following recommendation: Recommendation #2: The Commission recommends that the Canadian Forces Provost Marshal review the MP reporting structure for all military missions, in theatre and at CEFCOM , to address the problem of information sharing on policing matters. The goal should be to provide a greater degree of MP command oversight in relation to policing matters in theatre. In accepting this recommendation, the CDS noted: “ By way of update significant steps have already been taken to ensure MP command oversight in relation to policing matters in theatre. The CFPM assumed full command of all MP involved in policing duties on 01 Apr 11. Since that time, the CFPM has attached MP assets to environmental, operational and other commanders under an operational command (OPCOM) relationship for operational support (non-police) duties. In short, with the revised command and control structure the technical chain of command has become the formal chain of command. Accordingly, the CFPM chain of command now has direct knowledge and oversight of all policing matters conducted by MP at the tactical level, both domestically and while on international operations. ” The Commission is satisfied with this response to its recommendation. The Commission notes the steps taken to enhance MP command oversight capabilities by the move to convert the MP technical chain into a command chain, effective April 1, 2011, and the Commission welcomes these reforms as a move in the right direction. Time will tell how well the bifurcation of MP command between policing and non-policing roles functions in practice and, in particular, how well it serves the CFPM in ensuring the highest level of professionalism in military policing in the CF . The Commission will certainly do its utmost to support the CFPM in this goal. A significant part of the discussion in this Report is devoted to process obstacles. These included difficulties in obtaining requested documents, accessing witnesses and government redaction of documents on the basis of alleged national security concerns. As noted, all of these contributed to delays and, in fact, led to protracted periods where the Federal Court heard arguments relating to challenges to the Commission’s jurisdiction in respect of a public interest hearing on the matters before it. To remedy these concerns for future public interest hearings and to seek greater clarification of the matters that led to delays, the Commission makes two additional recommendations: Recommendation#3: The Commission recommends that the Chief of the Defence Staff and the Canadian Forces Provost Marshal review the process sections of this Report in detail with a view to eliminating barriers to efficiently and effectively conducting future public interest hearings, and developing a cooperative approach to document production, witness access, and national security issues. Such an approach would save costs, expedite hearings, and help ensure the Commission is able to properly fulfill its mandate. In accepting this recommendation, the CDS wrote: “The Canadian Forces and departmental authorities strive to ensure a fully cooperative approach, within the limits of the law, in support of the public interest inquiries conducted by the Commission. It must be noted that the law recognizes the right to challenge decisions of the Commission to investigate matters beyond its statutory mandate, as confirmed by the Federal Court in this case. The law also provides a procedure for protecting information that is subject to public interest immunity or legal privilege. In this matter there were thousands of pages that had to be reviewed by multiple departments. Finally, past and present members of the CF and past and present employees of the Government are entitled to receive legal representation in accordance with the Government’s policy, and in a manner that accords with the ethical obligations of lawyers. Despite its restricted access to confidential information, the Commission was able to fulfill its mandate, and conduct a thorough and independent investigation of the complaints against members of the military police in the performance of their policing duties and functions.” The Commission recognizes that parties have the right to raise bona fide jurisdictional questions in the course of a hearing, and have the right of recourse to the Courts when and if such questions arise. The Commission also recognizes that there are protections under the Canada Evidence Act that are afforded to certain types of information. The concern being expressed by the Commission through this recommendation and supporting observations is that more could have been done by representatives of the CF and the government to assist the work of the Commission without prejudicing the above interests. Recommendation#4: The Commission recommends that the Minister of National Defence take steps to cause the addition of the Commission by the Governor in Council to the schedule of designated entities as prescribed by section 38.01(8) of the Canada Evidence Act . This would allow the Commission to more effectively obtain information relevant to the discharge of its statutory mandate of providing independent oversight of military policing while at the same time maintaining strict control over any information the disclosure of which has the potential to negatively affect Canada’s national security interests or international relations. In accepting this recommendation, the CDS responded: “ It is within the mandate of the Commission to review, and where warranted in the public interest, investigate complaints regarding the conduct of members of the military police. It is recognized that, in appropriate circumstances, the Canada Evidence Act permits an investigative body to be given access to sensitive or potentially injurious information. This is best determined on a case-by-case basis. ” It remains unclear to the Commission why the government considers it inappropriate to include the Commission on the Schedule of designated entities under section 38.01(8) of the Canada Evidence Act . Moreover, the standards by which the government would make a determination on a “ case by case basis ” whether to give the Commission access to sensitive or potentially injurious information within the meaning of section 38 of the Canada Evidence Act have not been explained. If the Afghanistan Public Interest Hearing was not such a case, then what is? The CDS ’s response to this recommendation appears to indicate that the Commission might be considered for addition to the Schedule of entities referred to in section 38.01(8) of the Canada Evidence Act, but only for specific cases as and when determined by the government. Such temporary scheduling on an ad hoc basis seems inconsistent with the practice of scheduling standing Commissions as designated entities under the Canada Evidence Act . At present, no standing Commission or Committee on the Schedule has been designated only in respect of a specific case, with the arguable exception of certain Commissions of Inquiry whose mandate is expressly limited to investigating only one particular subject: e.g. , the Commission of Inquiry into the Investigation of the Bombing of Air India Flight 182. The reason for this approach is that all of the entities designated to date are tribunals or administrative investigators who, like this Commission, must necessarily enjoy independence from government influence in the handling of their cases. The purpose of the Schedule of designated entities in the Canada Evidence Act is to facilitate the proper functioning of such independent bodies whose mandate anticipates that they will have, and require, regular and ongoing access to sensitive information relating to national defence, security or international relations in order to do their job. If such scheduling were only approached on a case-by-case basis, it would not only be less efficient, but also would undermine the purpose behind the scheduling mechanism. While the Canada Evidence Act does permit ad hoc disclosure authorizations and agreements by the Attorney General of Canada under Canada Evidence Act sections 38.03, 38.031 and 38.04(6), the very fact that the Act provides for a Schedule of designated entities indicates that these ad hoc authorizations are not appropriate for certain bodies. Scheduling of entities specifically allows these entities to receive sensitive information in an expeditious manner that respects the need for the entity to operate independent of government influence, and the need to effectively safeguard sensitive information from inappropriate public disclosure. As such, the Commission does not consider ad hoc scheduling under the Canada Evidence Act in respect of individual complaint files would provide a satisfactory response to the difficulties that were encountered in this case. It is also possible that the CDS ’s response to this recommendation intended to refer to the use of disclosure authorizations and agreements under sections 38.03 and 38.031 of the Canada Evidence Act as an alternative to scheduling under that Act . In this case, the Commission would make the following observations. First, as discussed above, ad hoc authorizations and agreements are not truly an alternative to scheduling an entity under section 38.01(8). If they were, then there would seemingly be no use in having a Schedule of entities at all. Secondly, the nature of military policing, particularly in the context of deployed operations, is such that the Commission’s review or investigation of complaints under Part IV of the National Defence Act , whether by way of public interest hearing or otherwise, frequently requires access to information which would ordinarily be considered to be at least “ sensitive information ” under section 38 of the Canada Evidence Act . As suggested above, it diminishes the public perception of the Commission as an independent oversight body if the government can selectively decide to cooperate, or not, with the Commission’s discharge of its mandate in respect of particular complaints. It is for these reasons that the Commission has twice, and without success, written to the Minister of National Defence requesting that he sponsor or otherwise facilitate an Order-in-Council to add the Commission to the Canada Evidence Act Schedule of designated entities. Thirdly, in the case of the Afghanistan Public Interest Hearing, the Commission’s inquiry necessitated reviewing a large number of documents which the government deemed to contain “ sensitive information ” or “ potentially injurious information ” under section 38 of the Canada Evidence Act . Despite numerous invitations by the Commission, the government declined to exercise its authority under sections 38.03 or 38.031 to disclose relevant “ sensitive ” or “ potentially injurious ” information to the Commission even under conditions that the Attorney General considered appropriate. It is therefore difficult for the Commission to conceive of another case when the government might agree to exercise its authority under these sections. In light of its experience during this hearing, the Commission admits to having doubts that the response to this recommendation will lead to a viable resolution of the problems identified by the Commission. XIX. Summary of Findings and Recommendations Finding #1: The Commission finds the allegations made by AIC and BCCLA against Major Hudson in the June 12, 2008 complaint to be unsubstantiated. Viewing the evidence as a whole, the Commission finds no grounds to conclude that Maj Hudson should have investigated his Task Force Commander while in theatre, or should have caused such an investigation to occur. The Commission finds his actions under the circumstances prevailing at the time met the standard of a reasonable police officer. Finding #2: The Commission finds the allegations made by AIC and BCCLA against Chief Warrant Officer Barry Watson in the June 12, 2008 complaint to be unsubstantiated. Viewing the evidence as a whole, the Commission finds no grounds to conclude that CWO Watson should have investigated the Task Force Commander while in theatre, or should have caused such an investigation to occur. The Commission finds his actions under the circumstances prevailing at the time met the standard of a reasonable police member. Finding #3: The Commission finds the allegations made by AIC and BCCLA against Major Michel Zybala in the June 12, 2008 complaint to be unsubstantiated. Viewing the evidence as a whole, the Commission finds no grounds to conclude Maj Zybala should have investigated his Task Force Commander while in theatre, or should have caused such an investigation to occur. The Commission finds his actions under the circumstance prevailing at the time met the standards of a reasonable police officer. Finding #4: The Commission finds the allegations made by AIC and BCCLA against Master Warrant Officer ( ret’d ) Jean-Yves Girard in the June 12, 2008 complaint to be unsubstantiated. Viewing the evidence as a whole, the Commission finds no grounds to conclude that MWO ( ret’d ) Girard should have investigated the Task Force Commander while in theatre, or should have caused such an investigation to occur. The Commission finds his actions under the circumstance prevailing at the time met the standards of a reasonable police member. Finding #5: The Commission finds the allegations made by AIC and BCCLA against Major Ron Gribble in the June 12, 2008 complaint to be unsubstantiated. Viewing the evidence as a whole, the Commission finds no grounds to conclude Maj Gribble should have investigated the Task Force Commander while in theatre, or should have caused such an investigation to occur. The Commission finds his actions under the circumstances prevailing at the time met the standards of a reasonable police officer. Finding #6: The Commission finds that the allegations made by AIC and BCCLA against Major John Kirschner in the June 12, 2008 complaint are unsubstantiated. Viewing the evidence as a whole, the Commission finds no grounds to conclude Maj Kirschner breached a duty to investigate his Task Force Commander while in theatre, or to cause such an investigation to occur. The Commission concludes his actions under the circumstances prevailing at the time met the standard of a reasonable police officer. Finding #7: The Commission finds the allegations made by AIC and BCCLA against LCol ( ret’d ) William Garrick in the June 12, 2008 complaint are unsubstantiated. Viewing the evidence as a whole, the Commission finds no grounds to conclude that LCol ( ret’d ) William Garrick breached a duty to investigate the Task Force Commander while in theatre, or to cause such an investigation to occur. The Commission concludes his actions under the circumstances prevailing at the time met the standard of a reasonable police officer. Finding #8: The Commission finds the allegations made by AIC and BCCLA against Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Steven Moore in the June 12, 2008 complaint to be unsubstantiated. Viewing the evidence as a whole, the Commission finds no grounds to conclude Capt(N) ( ret’d ) Moore should have investigated the Task Force Commanders while in theatre, or should have caused such an investigation to occur. The Commission finds his actions under the circumstances prevailing at the time met the standard of a reasonable police officer. Recommendation #1: The Commission recommends that the Canadian Forces Provost Marshal implement measures and standards to ensure that MPs deployed during future conflicts are provided the necessary baseline information to be fully educated on potential policing issues stemming from the previous rotation. In order for the MP units in theatre to perform as a seamless policing unit, this baseline information should include: End of Tour reports provided to the incoming TFPM and NIS Detachment Commander before or soon after they arrive in theatre; A brief summary of on-going investigations and investigations completed in the previous rotation; A brief summary of all applicable orders and/or directives particularly applicable to the MP in theatre, such as technical directives and theatre standing orders; Pre-deployment training on the humanitarian and human rights situation and risks in theatre, and how this might impact on MP policing duties and expectations; Information on potential policing issues for the incoming MP units, based on the policing environment in the previous rotation and any information available to the CFPM ; and Given the sensitivity and mission critical importance of detainee issues, an assessment of potential policing issues relative to the treatment and transfer of detainees in theatre, and a briefing on any current or past investigations into this or related subject matter. The CFPM should ensure this information is made available to any MP for whom it is relevant to their duties, and in particular the CEFCOM PM , the CO NIS and the TFPM . Recommendation #2: The Commission recommends that the Canadian Forces Provost Marshal review the MP reporting structure for all military missions, in theatre and at CEFCOM , to address the problem of information sharing on policing matters. The goal should be to provide a greater degree of MP command oversight in relation to policing matters in theatre. Recommendation#3: The Commission recommends that the Chief of the Defence Staff and the Canadian Forces Provost Marshal review the process sections of this Report in detail with a view to eliminating barriers to efficiently and effectively conducting future public interest hearings, and developing a cooperative approach to document production, witness access, and national security issues. Such an approach would save costs, expedite hearings, and help ensure the Commission is able to properly fulfill its mandate. Recommendation#4: The Commission recommends that the Minister of National Defence take steps to cause the addition of the Commission by the Governor in Council to the schedule of designated entities as prescribed by section 38.01(8) of the Canada Evidence Act . This would allow the Commission to more effectively obtain information relevant to the discharge of its statutory mandate of providing independent oversight of military policing while at the same time maintaining strict control over any information the disclosure of which has the potential to negatively affect Canada’s national security interests or international relations.
